verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains al-ʿuqūd as the plural of al-ʿaqd, literally a binding that joins two things so firmly that separation is difficult. Having first denoted a physical tying, it came to denote abstract bindings such as offer and acceptance in commerce, employment, and every covenant or agreement. Because the plural is joined to the comprehensive al, the command to fulfil the covenants embraces everything properly called a ʿaqd: God’s covenants with His servants—monotheism, fundamental beliefs, worship, and divinely legislated laws—as well as human transactions and commitments.

The commentary therefore rejects attempts to restrict the verse to private contracts, oaths, pre-Islamic defensive pacts, or the covenants of the People of the Book. Neither the wording nor the ordinary breadth of al-ʿaqd supports such limitations. A covenant includes every word or act that establishes an inseparable relation: a sale transfers authority over merchandise from seller to buyer; marriage binds the woman to the man in the stated marital relation; and an employment agreement binds a person to perform the agreed work.

The Qur’an strongly praises fidelity and condemns breach because covenants are indispensable to both individual and social life. Social rights, privileges, duties, and claims rest upon explicit or implicit practical agreements. If a person breaks a freely undertaken agreement merely because he has gained power to do so, social justice—the basis by which people escape exploitation and servitude—is first destroyed. The obligation includes individual promises and collective agreements between peoples; collective agreements are still more important because their fulfilment more fully establishes justice and their violation causes wider harm.

Al-Mizan notes that the Qur’an preserves a treaty even where breaking it would be easy and advantageous. After the conquest of Mecca, Muslims were commanded to fulfil to its term a valid non-aggression agreement with idolaters who had not violated it or aided others against them, even though those idolaters had become weak and defenceless. This upholds the sanctity of covenant out of piety. If one party breaks its confirmed agreement, however, the other may respond only to the same extent. Thus Islam requires fidelity whether a pact benefits or harms one’s private interest, because social justice takes precedence over private gain; reciprocal response to breach protects society from exploitation and the arrogance of the powerful.

The commentary contrasts this religious logic—preserving truth and reality by every possible means so that society may prosper—with the logic of societies that protect national interest even by crushing truth. Islam’s ruling is not confined to formal legal contracts: it includes every explicit or implicit bond on which an edifice is built.

The verse then makes the meat of the cattle quadrupeds lawful, referring to the eight pairs, except what is later recited as forbidden. The lawful category does not include game hunted while one is in ihrām. The circumstantial clause is related to those addressed by “are made lawful for you”: even an otherwise lawful wild deer, cow, or zebra becomes forbidden if hunted in that state. Al-sayd here means hunted game, and al-hurum denotes those who have put themselves under the restrictions of pilgrimage.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan says that the renewed address to believers emphasizes respect for what God has sanctified. Al-ihlāl, literally making lawful, is used here metaphorically for violating or treating sacred things without due honour; its precise application follows its object. Thus God’s signs are violated by neglecting their reverence, and a sacred month by commencing fighting in it.

Al-shaʾāir probably denotes the guideposts and rites of hajj. The sacred months in which fighting is prohibited are al-Muharram, Rajab, Dhi al-qiʾdah, and Dhi al-hijjah. Al-hady denotes goats, sheep, cattle, and camels taken for pilgrimage, while al-qalāid are the garlands placed on sacrificial animals so that none may appropriate them. Al-āmmīn are those heading for the Sacred House; their seeking of grace may mean material gain, reward in the hereafter, or both. These meanings best suit the context.

The command to hunt once free from pilgrimage restrictions merely lifts the earlier prohibition; it does not independently make hunting obligatory. Al-hall and al-ihlāl both mean release from ihrām. Nor may hatred of a people who barred the believers from the Sacred Mosque induce them to transgress once they have overcome them.

The command to cooperate in righteousness and piety is, according to the commentary, a foundation of Islamic culture and ethics. Righteousness consists of true belief and good works in worship and mutual dealings, while al-taqwā is guarding oneself in relation to God’s commands and prohibitions. Such cooperation is collective faith and good action grounded in fear of God. Its opposite is cooperation in sin—evil conduct that impairs a felicitous life—and aggression, which usurps people’s real rights and produces insecurity for their lives, honour, and property. The warning that Allah is severe in punishment emphatically forbids such cooperation.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan holds that the initial four prohibitions—carrion, blood, swine flesh, and that over which a name other than Allah’s has been invoked—had repeatedly been revealed long before this chapter, in Meccan and early Medinan revelations. This verse consequently reinforces, rather than first legislates, their prohibition; the early prohibition of uncleanness also shows that the first three were forbidden from the earliest Meccan period. The strangled animal, that beaten to death, that killed by a fall, that gored to death, and that partly eaten by wild beasts are not new legislation either: they are particular, less usual forms of al-maytah, listed separately to prevent doubt about their inclusion.

The verse newly mentions flesh sacrificed upon stones set up for idols and division by arrows, although transgression and sin had already been forbidden generally. Sacrificing upon such stones prohibits an idolatrous practice of the Days of Ignorance: Arabs venerated stones around the Kaʾbah and sacrificed over them. Division by arrows, al-istiqsām bi al-azlām, concerns gambling for portions of a camel or other animal: headless arrows determined who received a share and how many shares. Although the literal sense is seeking division by means of arrows, the context of forbidden foods requires this meaning, not divination about whether a future journey, marriage, or undertaking will prove beneficial. The phrase “that is a transgression” may grammatically refer to the whole list, the final two items after “except what you slaughter,” or the last item alone; the middle possibility is probably best.

Al-Munkhaniqah is an animal that dies by strangulation, whether intentional or accidental and regardless of the means. Al-mawqūdhah is beaten until it dies; al-mutaraddiyah falls from a height; al-natīhah dies after being gored by another animal; and the animal eaten by wild beasts dies from a beast of prey eating its flesh. “Except what you slaughter” applies to all five categories, not only the last. If one of these animals still displays life—for example, breathing or movement of its tail—and is immediately slaughtered according to the sharīʾah, by cutting its four jugular veins, it may be eaten. An animal is prohibited under the categories of falling or goring only if it dies from that fall or injury without valid slaughter; an animal recovered alive and uninjured is not so described if it later dies or is slaughtered.

The words, “This day have those who disbelieve despaired of your religion … This day have I perfected for you your religion,” are, in Al-Mizan’s view, a single, internally connected parenthetical speech within the food laws. Removing them leaves a complete prohibition-and-emergency clause like earlier verses. The parenthesis may have been revealed at that point, placed there on the Prophet’s order although separately revealed, or inserted at compilation; in every case, it remains parenthetical. Traditions on its occasion of revelation generally discuss these words alone, without mentioning the food prohibitions, which supports their independent character. A report in al-Durr al-manthūr from ʿAbd b. Hamīd, transmitting al-Shaʾbī, says that “This day I have perfected for you your religion” was revealed at ʿArafāt and that the Prophet placed verses which pleased him at the beginning of a chapter, with Jibrīl teaching him how. Yet the two sentences concerning the despair of the disbelievers and the perfection of religion have one theme, and exegetes from early times have accordingly treated them together. The repeated “this day” denotes one day.

The commentary rejects several proposed identifications of that day. It cannot be the beginning of Islam, because the verse presupposes an existing religion which enemies hoped to destroy, believers feared for, and God then perfected. It cannot be the conquest of Mecca, because many laws were still revealed afterwards and not all Arabian idolaters had despaired while pre-Islamic pilgrimage customs and valid treaties remained. Nor can it be the period after the revelation of the chapter of “Repentance”: although Arabian polytheism and its customs had then been removed, later laws, including laws in this last detailed chapter, were still revealed.

Nor does Al-Mizan accept the commonly reported day of ʿArafāt in the Farewell Pilgrimage merely because the Prophet taught the manāsik there. The Quraysh had despaired at the conquest, Arabian idolaters after “Repentance,” while the unrestricted phrase “those who disbelieve” includes Jews, Christians, fire-worshippers, and others who had not then despaired of overcoming Islam. Teaching one obligatory rite cannot be the perfection of the entire religion, and it supplies no connection between the disbelievers’ despair and the religion’s perfection. The claim that all remaining lawful and unlawful matters were then revealed is contradicted by reports of legislation after that day, including the verse of al-kalālah and verses concerning interest. ʿUmar is reported to have said in a sermon that the verse of interest was among the last revealed and that the Messenger died without explaining it; al-Bukhārī reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that the verse of interest was the last verse revealed. The suggestion that perfection means exclusive Muslim possession of the Kaʾbah also fails: this had occurred a year earlier, and removing obstacles to implementing religion is not the same as perfecting the religion, which consists of beliefs and laws.

The commentary also rejects the view that the detailed food rulings were gradually delayed until Islam became powerful, so that this disclosure itself perfected religion and caused the enemies’ despair. The disbelievers’ defeat had occurred earlier; the verse adds no food prohibition beyond the already prohibited four, since the five other dead-animal cases are their details; and the earlier prohibitions concerned more common foods and therefore would have provoked greater resistance if gradual accommodation were the purpose. In any event, the legislation or explanation of a few food laws cannot perfect the whole religion, complete every favour, or explain why Islam was then chosen as religion. Nor can perfection mean the closing of legislation, because rulings followed this verse and even occur later in the same chapter.

Al-Mizan instead explains that the disbelievers had persistently sought the extinction of Islam because it challenged their supremacy, curtailed their accustomed indulgence, and undermined polytheism. They tried to weaken the Prophet through wealth and honour, then through conciliation and flattery, and worked to spread hypocrisy and doubts among the believers. Even when Islam’s strength had frustrated these efforts, they retained the hope that the religion would perish with the Prophet, who had no male offspring to succeed him. They imagined prophethood to be a kind of kingship whose traces and laws would vanish with its founder.

A religion, however complete in sharīʾah and doctrine, cannot preserve itself after its protector is gone. It requires appointed protectors to prevent deterioration and manage its affairs. Thus the disbelievers could fully despair only when God appointed one to take the Prophet’s place in safeguarding religion and guiding the ummah. The religion would then cease to be transient and gain continuity and permanence; this would be both its perfection and the completion of Divine favour. This interpretation supports traditions that the verse was revealed at Ghadīr Khumm, on 18 Dhi al-hijjah, 10 AH, concerning the successorship of ʿAlī. On that day, the religion passed from the Prophet’s personal guardianship to the collective guardianship of the Imāms.

“Those who disbelieve” is unrestricted and includes idolaters, Jews, Christians, and others. “So fear them not, and fear Me” is advisory rather than a new obligatory command. The believers had properly feared the enemies in regard to their religion while those enemies still hoped to divert them from it; once that cause disappeared, they had no need to fear them. They must instead fear God concerning that same religion: they must beware lest, through ingratitude, He remove the perfected bounty from them. The warning is therefore not merely a statement of favour. The religion is secured from destruction originating with disbelievers, but Muslims themselves may corrupt it by rejecting or showing ingratitude toward the complete Divine favour, whereupon it may be replaced by affliction, hunger, and fear. Al-Mizan says that Muslims have in fact done this and suffered its consequences. The Qur’anic warnings connected with al-wilāyah are closely related to this threat.

Al-ikmāl, perfection, and al-itmām, completion, are close but distinct. A thing is perfect when it fulfils its intended purpose; it is complete when it no longer needs anything additional. Completion applies where an effect depends on all its parts and conditions, as a fast is invalid if one of its conditions fails. Perfection applies where partial effects arise from individual parts and the full intended effect appears when all parts are present. Thus the verse indicates that something was added to the body of religious beliefs, perceptions, and laws, making it perfect, and that a spiritual Divine favour which had not yet yielded its full effect was completed.

A bounty is truly a bounty only when it serves the Divine purpose for which it was given: enabling human beings to attain felicity through worship and nearness to God. Things and faculties used in submission to God are blessings; otherwise, they become trial and affliction. The real Divine favour is therefore Divine wilāyah—His guardianship and management of the servants’ affairs—and things are blessings insofar as they partake of it. Islam is both a religion, as the revealed guidance for worship, and a Divine favour because it contains the wilāyah of Allah, His Messenger, and those vested with authority after him.

The wilāyah of Allah, exercised through religion, is not complete without the wilāyah of the Messenger; nor is the Messenger’s wilāyah complete without that of those vested with authority, who manage the religious affairs of the ummah by Divine permission. Accordingly, God perfected the believers’ religious perceptions by making wilāyah obligatory and completed His favour by appointing after the Messenger the authority who would safeguard religion when revelation ceased and the Prophet was no longer present. Wilāyah was one project, incomplete until this appointment. Islam was thereby chosen as the religion of monotheism: none is worshipped except God, and none is obeyed—obedience itself being a kind of worship—except God and those whose obedience He has made obligatory, namely the Messenger and the waliyy. Al-Mizan regards this as fulfilment of the promise of security after fear and of established religion, whose purpose is worship without association.

The emergency permission at the end is secondary and applies only in necessity. One compelled by hunger may take only enough unlawful food to remove the hunger and avert the emergency, without wilfully inclining to sin. Divine forgiveness and mercy may be connected both with sins liable to punishment and with the law whose contravention produces those sins.

In its discourse on slaughter, Al-Mizan says that human nature permits eating what can be digested except what is physically or spiritually harmful or naturally repulsive. Physical harm and spiritual harm require rational restraint; aversion arises from perceived filth and may also reflect religious and social habit. Human communities range from complete prohibition of animal food to unrestricted consumption. Buddhism represents one extreme, while peoples who eat every meat, even human flesh, represent the other. Pre-Islamic Arabs ate many animals, blood, carrion, strangled and beaten animals, animals killed by falls or goring, and prey killed by beasts. They objected that Muslims ate what they themselves killed but not what God had killed.

Islam follows a middle course based on normal human nature. It permits agreeable meats: cattle such as sheep, goats, cows, and camels; horses and donkeys with dislike; permitted birds rather than birds of prey; and specified fish. It nevertheless forbids blood, carrion, and animals over which Allah’s name was not invoked. In doing so it restores the natural order while respecting reason’s judgment against bodily and spiritual harm, natural aversion to foul things, and social harms such as idolatrous sacrifice and gambling by arrows.

Against the objection that mercy should prevent killing sentient animals, the commentary replies that legislation follows humanity’s real welfare rather than feeling alone. The material world is a system of continual transformation, exchange, eater and eaten: earthly compounds draw from the earth and return to it; plants draw nourishment from earth and air; animals eat plants or other animals; and all return to the earth. Human bodily constitution—teeth adapted for cutting, tearing, breaking, and grinding, and an appetite and digestion suited to animal as well as vegetable food—is creative guidance indicating permission to eat meat. Islamic legislation, as a natural religion, restores what creation guides human beings toward while restraining what is physically, spiritually, or socially harmful or naturally repellent.

Mercy is a fine created disposition, but it has not been granted absolute rule over all affairs. If mercy in this sense governed without qualification, punishment of oppressors and criminals and proportionate response to aggression would be impossible. Divine mercy is not material tenderness or emotional pity; it is God’s bestowal of good upon one who deserves it in the measure he deserves. What appears punishment may thus be mercy, and what appears mercy may be otherwise. False mercy cannot justify neglecting a beneficial act or disregarding the realities on which sharīʾah must be legislated.

Islam nonetheless gives mercy its proper place in slaughter. It forbids torturing the animal, cutting its limbs or skinning it before death, strangling it or beating it to death, and slaughtering one animal in another’s sight; it also prescribes humane practices such as giving the animal water. Islam is a religion of reason rather than sentiments, accepting sentiments only insofar as reason approves them and they serve social reform.

Finally, restricting lawful meat to animals already dead would not be required by mercy and would contradict the realities of creation. It would also spread disease and physical harm, itself contrary to mercy and reason. Proper slaughter, with its merciful conditions, is therefore required rather than reliance on carrion.
verses.4: Al-Mizan treats “good things” in (5:4) as an unrestricted general rule: normal intellect identifies what is good, and every good is lawful. It prefers reading “what you have taught” independently, with “what” introducing a condition and “so eat” its result, rather than assuming an omitted “prey of.” Although al-Jawārih covers hunting birds and beasts, the restriction mukallibīn may indicate that this ruling is confined to trained hunting dogs. Lawfulness requires a properly trained dog to catch for its owner, not itself, an otherwise lawful wild animal, with God’s name mentioned when the dog is released. If it kills before the hunter arrives, that invocation counts as slaughter; if the animal remains alive, it must be slaughtered properly with God’s name, a case outside this rule. The closing warning requires fear of God: hunting must not cause excessive loss of life or serve mere game, arrogance, or amusement, for God is swift in reckoning and requites oppression and transgression in this world before the hereafter.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that the renewed declaration that good things are lawful, introduced by “This day,” manifests God’s favor in permitting the food and chaste women of the People of the Book. Since believers had been strongly warned against intimate friendship with them, they may have doubted these permissions. Joining them to the unqualified lawfulness of good things reassures them that this food, and marriage with these women, are a genuine divinely granted ease.

The statement that the food of the People of the Book is lawful to Muslims and Muslim food lawful to them is one utterance with one meaning, not two independent laws. The latter clause is not a command addressed to the People of the Book, who do not accept the Prophet’s authority; rather, the wording establishes lawfulness between the two groups without a restriction on either side, just as the reciprocal wording of 60:10 establishes unlawfulness on both sides.

Although al-Taʾām can philologically mean all nourishment, usage without a contextual qualification may mean wheat and similar grains. This is supported by statements in Lisān al-ʾArab and al-Nihāyah and by most ahādīth from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, though a few traditions give another meaning. In any event, the permission cannot include animals intrinsically forbidden, such as swine, or otherwise lawful animals not slaughtered properly, including those over which God’s name was not pronounced. God has called such things uncleanness, transgression, and sin, and would not permit them as a favor; they have also just been enumerated in this sūrah. They cannot be deemed abrogated, especially since traditions describe “The Table” as abrogating but not abrogated.

The expression “those who have been given the Book before you,” rather than simply Jews, Christians, or the People of the Book, indicates the reason for this easing: they are nearer to believers than other non-Muslim communities because they received a Book and believed in one God and the prophets, unlike idol-worshippers and polytheists. The addition “before you” also suggests mixing and intermingling. As an act of favor and relaxation, this ruling cannot be abrogated by “And do not marry the idolatresses until they believe” (2:221) or “and hold not to the ties of marriage of unbelieving women” (60:10). Both verses preceded this later revelation, and earlier verses cannot abrogate a later one; moreover, traditions state that “The Table” was the last sūrah revealed, abrogating earlier rulings but not itself abrogated. Nor do those earlier verses concern marriage with Christian or Jewish women. Even if 60:10 were taken to prohibit such marriage, (5:5) would abrogate it, not the reverse.

Al-Mizan holds that al-muhsanāt here means chaste women. The parallel mention of believing women and women of the People of the Book requires the same sense in both cases; it cannot mean Islam, since women of the People of the Book are included, nor free women, since then the stated favor would be incomplete by excluding slave girls. The verse concerns unmarried chaste women. It permits marriage with chaste women of the People of the Book upon payment of their dowries and a true marital relation, not fornication or secret paramours. It imposes no condition that the marriage be permanent rather than mutʾah, since mutʾah is marriage like permanent marriage. The requirement of marriage and dowry also shows that the verse does not concern slave girls.

“Whoever denies faith” concerns al-kufr of imān: covering a firmly rooted, true faith that gives rise to good deeds. It means knowingly failing to act upon what one knows to be true—for example, neglecting prayer, zakāt, fasting, and hajj while knowing their status, or associating with and participating in the affairs of polytheists while knowing Islam to be the truth. Because kufr is a covering that keeps its object hidden, this description applies only to one who persists in abandoning faith’s demands; a person who commits such a violation once or twice without persistence is guilty of fisq, not called a denier of faith. Thus, the verse means that one who continually refuses to adhere to known truth and the pillars of religion forfeits all good works and becomes a loser in the hereafter. This accords with the descriptions of those who knowingly choose error over rectitude and reject God’s signs and the meeting of the hereafter in (7:146–7), and of those whose works are lost while they think themselves virtuous in (18:103–5).

The warning completes the legislation. Permission concerning the People of the Book is meant to ease believers’ lives, spread piety, and enable Islamic morality, beneficial knowledge, and good deeds to reach non-Muslim society. It is not permission for unrestricted mingling, sexual indulgence, or infatuation with their women, by which their culture and misconduct might overcome Islamic righteousness. Such a favor could then become a destructive trial and a curse. Believers must not exploit this relaxation so as to neglect faith and its pillars, thereby nullifying their deeds.

The commentary rejects interpretations unsupported by the wording and context: that “good things” refers to bahīrah, sāibah, wasīlah, and hāmī; that the People of the Book’s food includes meat slaughtered according to their own rites; that the verse merely permits eating at one table; that their women had always been lawful under “and lawful for you is (all) besides that” (4:24); or that the final warning means only that believers must not reject these permissions. Such readings disregard “This day” and the verse’s character as favor and relaxation. In particular, 4:23–24 deals with prohibitions and permissions based on consanguinity and marriage, not religious difference.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that “when you rise up to prayer” means when you intend prayer, since rising toward an act ordinarily accompanies intending it. The verse establishes purification as a prerequisite for prayer: wudūʾ in the ordinary state and a total ablution in al-janābah. Yet its opening is not to be read as requiring a new wudūʾ before every prayer without qualification; the later purpose of purification helps explain the obligation.

Washing means pouring water over the organ. Traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt define the face as extending lengthwise from the beginning of the forehead hairline to the chin, and breadthwise as what is covered by the thumb and middle finger. Because al-yad can denote the entire arm or lesser portions, “as far as the elbows” specifies that the hand to be washed extends from the fingertips to the elbows. The preposition ilā marks the limit of the required organ but does not itself determine whether the elbows are included; traditions establish their washing. It does not mean “together with,” and reports of the Prophet’s action cannot by themselves fix the lexical meaning of the verse.

The phrase “as far as the elbows” qualifies “your hands,” not the direction of washing. Thus the verse alone permits either direction, while traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt direct washing from the elbows down to the fingertips. The reported consensus that such wudūʾ is valid likewise depends on reading the phrase as delimiting the hands rather than prescribing a direction.

Al-Mizan holds that mash with bi denotes wiping only part of the object; hence only part of the head is required, and correct traditions identify this as its front part. Both readings of wa arjulakum support wiping the feet: with kasrah, the feet are plainly joined to “your heads”; with fathah, they are joined to the grammatical position of bi-ruʾūsikum. To connect the feet instead to the earlier command to wash the faces, despite the intervening command to wipe the head, would violate the verse’s eloquent construction. The many traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt likewise require wiping the feet. Sunni reports describe the Prophet’s practice or rulings of companions and conflict among themselves, some supporting wiping and others washing; Al-Mizan says that preferring reports of washing and forcing the verse to fit them distorts its manifest sense.

It rejects the claims that a genitive reading is merely an inferior grammatical following, that wiping is a reduced form of washing, or that the mention of the ankles proves washing. Wiping and washing are distinct acts, and such arguments impose meanings through analogy. If advocates of washing hold that the Sunnah superseded the Qur’anic ruling—as Anas and al-Shaʾbī are reported to have said, that Gabriel brought wiping while the sunnah is washing—the issue becomes whether the Sunnah can abrogate the Book, rather than an interpretation of the verse. Saying that a report conflicts with the Book means that its import conflicts with the Qur’an’s apparent meaning; it is not itself a legal fatwā. Al-Kaʾb is identified as the bone protruding on the dorsum of the foot, though some identify it with the projecting bones at the leg-foot joint.

The command to wash when junub is coordinated with the command for wudūʾ: if one is not junub, one performs wudūʾ; if one is junub, one performs ghusl, which suffices in place of wudūʾ according to the traditions. The purification signified by this bath is not ordinary removal of bodily dirt, termed al-Tanazzuf, but the very ritual act that removes spiritual uncleanness.

For tayammum, sickness, travel, coming from the privy, and touching women are independent situations, not mutually opposing conditions or combinations in which the latter two merely qualify the former two. Sickness and travel may make water unavailable or unusable; coming from the privy causes small hadath, ordinarily removed by wudūʾ, while “touching the women” alludes to sexual intercourse and causes major hadath, ordinarily removed by ghusl. “You do not find water” metaphorically includes inability to use it and conditions all four cases, including illness. Thus the mention of sickness and travel is not superfluous, and “or” need not be converted into “and.”

The wording “one among you comes from privy” is a deliberately indirect and impersonal allusion to relieving oneself, teaching propriety in speech. Likewise, “you have touched the women” is a modest allusion to intercourse, not mere physical touch. The context begins with wudūʾ for small hadath and ghusl for major hadath, then provides tayammum as the substitute for both when water cannot be used; interpreting the phrase as mere touch would leave no substitute for ghusl. The verse also indicates that one whose tahārah has not been broken by small hadath need not repeat wudūʾ or tayammum for the next prayer.

Al-Ṣaʿīd al-ṭayyib means earth in its natural state, such as soil or common stones, excluding substances separated from earth through burning or other processes, including cement, pottery, and minerals; al-ṭayyib may also mean clean. Tayammum is a mitigated substitute for wudūʾ: its washings of face and hands become partial wipings with earth, while wiping the head and feet is omitted. Since mash with bi again denotes partiality, traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt specify the forehead and the hands from the wrists downward, rejecting both wiping from armpit to fingertips and wiping the whole arm washed in wudūʾ. Minhu indicates that the wiping begins with earth: the hands are struck upon it and then used to wipe the face and hands. It does not require dust to remain attached to the palms, so the contrary restriction concerning smooth stone does not follow from the wording.

“Allah does not desire to put on you any difficulty” negates both commands whose very nature would impose hardship and temporary hardship that may arise when a general command is applied, as illness can prevent standing in prayer. God’s purpose in these rules is purification, not burden; therefore, when wudūʾ or ghusl becomes difficult because water is unavailable or unusable, tayammum replaces it rather than purification being abandoned.

This tahārah is spiritual purification, required for the validity of prayer, rather than removal of al-khabath, whose removal does not require al-niyyah. Its immediate purpose is purification through wudūʾ, ghusl, and tayammum. The completion of divine favor is a wider purpose: favor here is religion as submission to God in every condition and acceptance of His authority, completed when the shariah encompasses its commands. The three purifications are one part of that comprehensive favor, through which believers are to become grateful.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains that the covenant binding the believers is their declaration, “We have heard and we obey”: unconditional hearing and obedience, which is Islam and surrender to God. They must remember God’s favor, understood either as the gracious gifts they received under Islam—peace, well-being, affluence, and purity of heart and deed after the days of ignorance—or as Islam itself, the source that sustains every other favor. Referring to Islam or divine authority identifies instances of the favor, not the dictionary meaning of the word. The command to fear Allah is reinforced by His knowledge of the secrets concealed within hearts.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse commands believers to give testimony with complete justice even against those whom they hate; enmity must not lead them to seek revenge by violating an opponent’s rights. Justice in testimony is therefore explicitly joined to the command to act equitably, because equity is nearer to piety, followed by the warning to fear Allah, who knows what they do.

This differs subtly from the related passage in the chapter “Women.” That verse addresses injustice arising from low desire, love, kinship, friendship, or hoped-for benefit: it commands steadfastness in justice as the basis for witnessing for Allah’s sake, and forbids desire because it causes deviation from justice. Here the order is reversed: uprightness for Allah is the basis for testimony with justice, because the immediate danger is injustice prompted by hatred. Although testimony favouring a loved one or relative against the truth is also unjust, the two verses address distinct motives. Both finally warn against abandoning piety, whether by following desire or by allowing hostility to corrupt justice.
verses.9: Al-Mizan states that Allah’s promise to believers who do good deeds is forgiveness and a mighty reward. It considers this formulation more forceful than the promise in verse 29 of the chapter “Victory,” because here the promise is stated clearly and independently, whereas there it occurs as part of a sentence. The claim that its emphasis results merely from being “news after news” is rejected.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that the threat against those who disbelieve and reject the divine signs stands opposite the preceding promise of forgiveness and mighty reward for believing doers of good. Al-Rāghib is cited as saying that al-Jahmah is intensely searing fire, from which al-jahīm, Hell, is derived.

Disbelief is qualified here by rejection of the divine message, excluding the case of one who recognizes a divine sign as true and does not reject it but does not properly follow it. Such a person’s case remains with God: He may forgive or punish. Between the promised believers who do good and the disbelievers who reject the signs are many intermediate stages whose conditions God has left unspecified.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse is apparently a general reminder of Allah’s protection from the polytheists’ repeated attempts to kill the believers, erase Islam, and annihilate the religion of tawhīd, rather than a reference to one particular conspiracy against the Prophet or an alleged Jewish assassination plot.

The command to fear Allah and rely on Him is an intense warning not to abandon piety or reliance. Its placement before the accounts of the covenants of the Children of Israel and of those who said, “We are Christians,” shows the intended lesson: they broke their covenant of surrender and obedience, were consequently cursed and hardened in heart, neglected part of their religion, and, in the Christian case, were made subject to enduring enmity and hatred. They should have obeyed their Messengers, accepted what God chose, refrained from what He disapproved, and obeyed none but God or one who calls to His obedience—not even religious scholars or monks who demanded submission to themselves.

By casting divine guidance behind their backs, they became remote from divine mercy, distorted divine speech through unacceptable interpretation, and forgot the fundamental portion of religion on which happiness in both worlds depends. Religion is an interdependent whole of beliefs and rules: corruption of one part, especially a foundation, corrupts the rest. Acts such as prayer, charity, or fighting cannot benefit a person when they are no longer for God’s sake, nor can neglected religious fundamentals aid him in the hereafter.

Reliance on God apparently extends to legislative and creative matters, or perhaps to legislation particularly. Believers must entrust religious matters and the Messenger’s sharīʿah to God, without imagining themselves independent or entitled to manipulate it. They must also conform to the causal order God established in creation without ascribing to it independent authority or any share of lordship, always awaiting what God decides and chooses.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan says that this account of the Children of Israel warns this ummah through what befell them. God gave them religious commands, made a covenant requiring steadfastness in religion, appointed twelve chiefains, and promulgated the sharīʿah, thereby completing His proof against them. Yet they broke the covenant, for which they were cursed and their hearts made hard.

Al-Rāghib defines al-Naqīb, translated “chiefain,” as one who investigates his people’s condition. The twelve were apparently heads of the twelve tribes and held worldly and religious authority over them, somewhat as Ulu al-Amr do in this ummah; however, they received no revelation and possessed no authority to legislate a sharīʿah, which belongs to God and His Messenger.

“Surely I am with you” is God’s commitment to protect and care for them, entailing help if they obey and abandonment if they disobey. This was conditional upon maintaining prayer, paying zakāt, believing in and respectfully assisting God’s Messengers, and offering Him a goodly loan. “My Messengers” includes future messengers such as Jesus and Muḥammad, as well as those raised between Moses and Muḥammad. The goodly loan means voluntary spending in God’s way, distinct from obligatory zakāt. The reward promised is the covering of evil deeds and entry into gardens beneath which rivers flow; disbelief after this loses the right way.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan takes the punishment for breaking the covenant as apparently referring to the disbelief just mentioned, which causes one to lose the right way. The curse means exclusion from divine mercy, and hard-heartedness is a state in which the heart neither submits to truth nor is moved by mercy.

This hard-heartedness led them to alter words from their proper places: they misinterpreted divine speech in ways God did not intend, or deleted, added, or changed its words. Thus they lost sight of the clear realities of religion. The portion they neglected consisted of religious fundamentals upon which felicity in both worlds depends; its loss brought misery and hardship. Among the resulting beliefs were that God resembles His creatures, Moses was the final Prophet, the Torah’s sharīʿah would last forever, and badāʾ or abrogation of the sharīʿah was impossible.

The statement that the Prophet will continually discover treachery in them may alternatively mean that he will find a treacherous group among them, with only a few excepted. Al-Mizan adds that the exception of a few does not prevent curse and punishment from attaching to the whole group or nation.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah took a covenant from those who said, “We are Christians,” but, after they forgot part of what they had been admonished with, caused enmity and hatred to adhere among them until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Rāghib is cited as defining Gharā as “became attached,” derived from al-gharāʾ, glue.

Jesus Christ, son of Mary, is described as a Prophet of Mercy who called to peace, love, concern for the hereafter, and detachment from worldly adornment and pleasure. He strictly forbade fighting among themselves for worldly gain; the author notes that this is attributed to statements of Christ in the four Gospels. When they forgot part of this admonition, God turned their hearts from love and peace toward war and fighting, replacing the fraternity they had been taught with enmity and hatred.

Al-Mizan regards this hostility as ingrained in the psyche of Christian nations, like the inescapable fire of the hereafter. It began soon after Jesus was raised up, as his disciples and missionaries, travelling from Jerusalem to Rome, entered one controversy after another. It then spread into wars, raids, banishments, and anathemas, reaching the great world wars that threatened the destruction of the earth and humanity. The account shows how a divine bounty becomes divine revenge and how efforts are wasted; God will soon inform them of the result of what they did.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that the Messenger disclosed what the People of the Book had concealed: the Torah and Gospel contained descriptions by which they recognized the ummī Prophet, as indicated in (7:157), (2:146), and (48:29). He also exposed the ruling of stoning, which they had hidden while seeking to have the Prophet alter it; it remains explicit in Deuteronomy, 22:23–24.

His passing over much means that he left many concealed matters undisclosed. The commentary says that remaining contradictions and errors in the Torah and Gospels show this concealment: the Torah includes assertions about Tawḥīd (Divine Unity) and Prophethood that cannot be ascribed to God, such as bodily existence and entering a place, as well as unacceptable accusations of kufr, sins, and other misconduct against the Prophet. It is also wholly silent about resurrection, without which no religion can stand, while the Gospels—especially that according to St. John—contain idolatrous ideas.

The construction of “there has come to you a light and a clear Book from Allah” apparently makes what has come dependent on God, as speech depends on its speaker and explanation on its explainer. Thus “light” may mean the Qur’an, with “a clear Book” an explicative apposition, so that both denote the Qur’an; this is supported by its description as light in (7:157), (64:8), and (4:174). Alternatively, the light may be the Prophet, supported by the opening of the verse and by his being called a “light-giving torch” in verse 46 of chapter 33.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that “with it” refers to the Book or the Light. Whether the Light is understood as the Prophet or the Qur’an makes no practical difference: both are apparent means of guidance, while God alone is the Guide in reality. The Qur’an and the Prophet revive guidance in the world, but neither is an independent source of it.

This guidance benefits only one who follows God’s pleasure. Here guidance means being conveyed to one’s destination: God leads such people through the way, or successive ways, of peace. Peace is unrestricted safety from every misery and distress that corrupts happiness in this world or the next; it accords with the Qur’anic depiction of Islam, faith, and piety as success, attainment, and security. The many ways of peace are like distinct lanes within one highway, the straight path: they suit differing conditions of the travellers but all lead to one destination. This differs from ungodly ways, whose separate paths lead to different ends. Thus, and God knows better, through His Book or His Prophet God leads those who follow His pleasure along ways that preserve their happiness in both abodes and protect them from what contaminates it.

Since God does not approve of kufr or transgression, pursuit of His pleasure ultimately requires keeping away from injustice and from association with unjust people. Such people are excluded from divine guidance. The verse is therefore parallel in meaning to the statement that those who believe without mixing faith with injustice have security and are rightly guided.

Al-Mizan notes that al-Zulumāt, “darknesses,” is plural, whereas light is singular. This indicates that falsehood has divergent paths, while truth remains one despite the various lanes appropriate to different spiritual levels. When bringing people from darkness into light is attributed to the Prophet or the Book, “by His permission” means God’s approval and pleasure, emphasizing that they are not independent causes and that God is the real cause of guidance. When it is attributed to God, however, permission means His knowledge: al-idhn may be used in the sense of information.

The repeated phrase “guides them” follows the intervening clause, “and brings them out,” and also indicates a comprehensive guidance. Although “a straight path” is grammatically indefinite, it denotes the one unique straight path, ordinarily ascribed to God alone; the indefinite form magnifies its rank and honor.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan takes the verse to address one of the three sects discussed in “The House of ʿImrān” (Ch. 3), which held that God had become one with the Messiah, who was therefore both god and man. The wording may also cover belief in the Messiah’s sonship or in three persons in one god, but in any case it rejects the claim that the Messiah became one with God.

The question whether anyone could prevent Allah from destroying the Messiah, his mother, and all people on earth refutes this claim by exposing its contradiction. Calling him the son of Mary affirms his humanity; as a human being, he is subject to the changes affecting all people. He, his mother, and all creation are owned and controlled by God, who may dispose of them or destroy them as He wills. Yet one who can be destroyed cannot be God. No cause has independent control over its effect, and no one can prevent or overcome God’s control. God alone truly owns; even when He grants someone ownership of something, His own ownership and authority remain.

The specification “son of Mary,” together with the mention of his mother and then all those on earth, establishes the Messiah’s transience: he and his mother share the same human origin, and all people stand under the same law and are liable to the same changes. If others may be destroyed by God’s command, the Messiah may be as well; were he God, destruction would not apply to him.

The statement that Allah possesses the kingdom of the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them supplies the reason. The addition of “what is between them” makes the proof comprehensive, including the Messiah, who is between heaven and earth. Its wording confines unrestricted ownership and authority to God alone, so none can stop His decree. His creating whatever He pleases and having power over all things further explain this kingdom: comprehensive power and an effectual will belong essentially to such dominion. They prove both that no one can prevent His destruction of all things if He wills and that none shares His divinity. Perhaps this is why the Divine name is repeatedly used: if He is God, none shares Godship with Him.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that the Jews and Christians did not here claim literal sonship like the Christian claim made concerning the Messiah. Calling themselves God’s sons was a metaphorical claim to distinction, like the designation of various righteous persons as sons of God in their scriptures. They meant that their relation to God resembled that of a king’s sons to their father: they were specially near, loved, and honoured, exempt from the treatment and laws applicable to ordinary subjects. Thus they supposed that God would neither punish or humiliate them nor make them stand as ordinary people on the Day of Resurrection. “His beloved ones,” following “sons,” is an explicative apposition; the essential implication of both expressions is their alleged complete security from punishment, even if they rejected the call of truth. This is shown by the reply, “He forgives whom He pleases and chastises whom He pleases”; otherwise that reply, and “Nay, you are men from among those whom He has created,” would have no relevance.

The verse refutes them by two proofs. The first is the question, “Why does He then chastise you for your faults?” If their alleged sonship and belovedness made chastisement impossible, they would be safe from punishment in this world and the next. Yet their afflictions for sins disprove this. The commentary describes the Jews as repeatedly committing grave crimes—such as killing prophets and righteous people, breaking covenants, altering and concealing divine communications, and rejecting them—and as consequently suffering disgrace, oppression, destruction, and other bitter effects. It similarly holds that Christian societies and nations had sins and chastisements no less than the Jews, before, during, and after the Prophet’s time.

Al-Mizan addresses the objection that such calamities may be signs of divine love rather than wrath, since prophets, righteous servants, and Muslims also suffer reversals. Worldly afflictions reach believers and unbelievers, righteous and wicked alike, but their name and effect depend on the affected person’s standing before God. For prophets and their true followers, whose virtues are established, they disclose hidden merits, train them spiritually, and raise their rank. For those whose felicity or misery is not yet settled, they are tests that reveal belief or unbelief and lead toward paradise or hell. For people entrenched in corruption, base desire, arrogance, and the corruption of others, disasters that destroy them are divine punishment and the evil consequence of their deeds. The commentary regards the calamities that befell the Jews throughout their history until Muḥammad’s mission, and Christians from the Messiah’s raising until Islam, as chastisement and retribution in view of their persistent sins.

Muslims too are subject to the same divine course. Their afflictions are trials if they remain steadfast on truth, but punishment if they deviate from the straight path. No one possesses a badge of honour or a self-claimed right against God; the Qur’an does not call Muslims God’s sons or beloved ones, and does not give weight to titles people assume. The wording about chastisement could possibly refer to the next world, in which case it would be read in the future tense. The People of the Book did admit some punishment: Jews said, “Fire shall not touch us but for a few days” (2:80), while the Christian doctrine of the Messiah’s atonement itself acknowledges sins and their punishment. Nevertheless, the earlier interpretation—present chastisements—is more appropriate.

The second proof is: “Nay, you are men from among those whom He has created; He forgives whom He pleases and chastises whom He pleases;” and Allah’s is the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to Him is the eventual return. They are merely mortal creatures, without a superiority over other creatures that could secure them from punishment. God alone possesses and rules all who are in the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them, and all return to Him. Their creatureliness, God’s exclusive kingdom, and their eventual return are the three premises; the conclusion is that forgiveness and chastisement rest with God’s will. No claimed distinction, nobility, or shield can obstruct His will or protect anyone from it.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that the Messenger’s coming after a cessation of messengers completes God’s proof against the People of the Book: they can no longer say that no bearer of good news or warning came to them. Citing al-Rāghib, it explains al-futūr as a period of tranquillity, quiet, or weakness after its opposite, here a period in which no messenger came.

The verse completes the preceding address, which announced a Messenger supported by the manifest Book and guiding, by God’s permission, to good and happiness. The present verse states the purpose of that explanation: to remove every excuse. The words “explaining to you” may carry over the qualification in the preceding verse—explaining much of what they concealed of the Book. On this reading, the new religion confirms what they already possessed; its difference lies in unveiling religious realities that their Books had explained but they concealed. The repetition of the earlier announcement is permissible because of the intervening gap, and serves to add the point about completing the proof.

Alternatively, this is an independent announcement whose object has been omitted. The omission may indicate comprehensiveness, namely that the Messenger explains everything requiring explanation, or the greatness of the matter explained. The long cessation of messengers shows why such clarification was needed. “Lest you say” is then connected to “indeed there has come to you,” giving the reason for his coming.

The closing assertion that Allah has power over all things answers an implied Jewish objection: that no new shariah could follow the Torah because abrogation and al-badāʾ were impossible. Such a restriction conflicts with the universality of divine power.

Al-Mizan then maintains that human life is necessarily a life of reflection, perception, and thought. The soundness and comprehensiveness of a person’s thought determine the soundness of his life. The Qur’an repeatedly calls people to knowledge, reflection, remembrance, and consideration; teaches arguments for truth and against falsehood; recounts the arguments of prophets and righteous people; and does not command blind belief in God or in what He sends. It also points to purposes behind religious commands, even where their detailed causes are inaccessible. Its guidance to the most upright path therefore includes guidance to an upright manner of thought: a path free of contradiction, neither opposing truth nor internally pulling in divergent directions.

The Qur’an leaves this correct thought to human common sense, natural reasoning, and the genuine sources of the shariah. Correct thinking is the stable natural perception by which people recognize truth, good, benefit, falsehood, evil, and harm. Apparent disputes about it are like disputes over self-evident principles and arise from misunderstanding the subject. Independent realities—such as matters concerning the world’s origin and end and mathematical or physical principles—are known by returning to self-evident premises and premises inseparably connected with them, arranging these properly, and deriving a conclusion. The basic logical forms involved are self-evident; doubt about them indicates a defect in apprehending what is clear.

Those who dispute logic still employ its forms and materials whenever they argue for their own conclusions. If their premises or forms were altered so that no conclusion followed, they themselves would reject their speech as meaningless. Their natural practice thus affirms the logical principles they verbally deny. Logic prevents error when it is used properly; disagreement among logicians does not disprove it, just as a sword cuts only when used properly. Nor does the historical development of logical principles show that they were invented: development means detailed discovery of principles of which human nature was already vaguely aware.

A system does not become invalid because it has been used to divert people from the Book, the Sunnah, or Ahl al-Bayt, just as a sword or religion may be used for an improper end. Nor do erroneous philosophical conclusions discredit logical form or self-evident truth; the error may result from introducing a false premise among correct ones. Claims that logic cannot guard against mistakes in its material and that one must therefore return only to the maʾsūmīn are also defective. Holding fast to a maʾsūm requires certainty that a report truly came from him and certainty of its meaning. Such certainty is unavailable in akhbār al-āhād, which yield only strong conjecture concerning both transmission and meaning. Certainty may arise from a maʾsūm’s words or from logical premises, but in either case one must know that the argument’s form is sound.

The assertion that rational arguments yield no certainty is itself a rational, logically formed argument seeking a definite conclusion. Likewise, the claim that everything needed is contained in the Book and the traditions of the maʾsūmīn, so that rational inquiry is an unnecessary remnant of unbelievers, relies on reasoning. Logical principles themselves belong to what is stored in the Book and Sunnah, but their depth cannot be reached without independent inquiry. It is one thing to say that the Book and Sunnah need no outside supplement to clarify their meanings, and another to say that a person adhering to them needs no additional intellectual help to reach correct conclusions. The Book and Sunnah themselves summon people to use sound rational arguments based on self-evident premises or what rests upon them.

The Book and the definitely established Sunnah have themselves been confirmed by reason, so the same reason cannot invalidate what it has definitively established. This does not remove the need to distinguish sound rational premises from false ones, just as one must distinguish decisive Qur’anic verses and traditions from ambiguous ones, and genuine reports from forged ones. Truth remains truth regardless of whether its conveyor is a believer or unbeliever, pious or sinful; rejecting it merely because of its conveyor is condemned ignorant prejudice.

Precaution may be necessary for one unable to grasp deep rational questions, but neither the Book, Sunnah, nor reason proves that persons capable of such discernment are barred from their realities. Human nobility and greatness depend on such understanding. The claim that one should adhere only to the apparent meanings of the Book and Sunnah because rational principles may lead to permanent perdition again uses an exceptive syllogism and rational premises. The same is true of arguments that insist on the Book and Sunnah while rejecting logic, philosophy, and rational reflection as foreign inheritances.

Al-Mizan rejects a historical polemic which alleges that the early pious predecessors used only the Book and Sunnah; that Greek philosophy caused Muslim theologians to impose philosophy on the Qur’an and divide into Ashʾarites and Muʾtazilites; and that Sūfīs and philosophers later deceived the Shīʿahs by forcing Qur’an and hadith into the mould of philosophy and taṣawwuf. It regards this history as contrary to established facts. It also distinguishes philosophy from al-kalām: philosophy treats real, objective phenomena and seeks proof through doubt-free premises, whereas scholastic theology treats questions that may be real or mentally posited and may reason from real or subjective considerations. The mutakallimūn were historically in conflict with philosophers and al-ʿurafāʾ, not simply engaged in fitting philosophy to the Qur’an.

The distinction sometimes drawn between theology and philosophy does not make theology religious and philosophy anti-religious. It concerns the kinds of syllogisms used: theological discussion may employ dialectical premises accepted by people, while philosophical discussion seeks truth through demonstrative argument. If a philosophical statement truly conflicts with the clear dictates of religion, it is invalid, but the error belongs to the person who made it and does not condemn philosophy or ʿirfān as disciplines. Disagreement among philosophers or logicians no more invalidates those disciplines than disagreement among Ashʾarites, Muʾtazilites, Shīʿites, jurists, or the many schools within jurisprudence invalidates religion or law.

The alternative sometimes proposed is tadhakkur, or remembrance, a theory attributed to Plato: by freeing oneself from lustful dispositions, acquiring piety and spiritual perfection, and turning inward, one may reach truth. Some hold that all knowledge is actually present from the beginning, so that acquisition is merely remembering. Others say knowledge is only potentially present and becomes actual when one turns from material distractions to the soul; this is attributed to Illuminists, Sūfīs, and similar groups. A further group adds adherence to the shariah in knowledge and practice, but differs from the Sūfīs chiefly in its strict limitation of “following” to apparent Qur’anic and Sunnah meanings; its method is thus a mixture of Sūfī and Akhbārī approaches.

If remembrance is not meant to abolish logic and rational premises, Al-Mizan accepts it to a degree. A person naturally knows himself, his powers, and his weaknesses from the beginning, and this latent knowledge can become acquired knowledge through his faculties. Some knowledge may also be gained through relative withdrawal from material attachments. But if remembrance means that inward turning eliminates the need to arrange premises in order to reach conclusions, it is untenable. Declarative knowledge depends on separately grasping subject and predicate, while many ideas arise from or are abstracted from sensory perception. A person deprived of a sense lacks knowledge dependent on it; this would not occur if all such knowledge were actually present in the essence. To say that blindness or deafness obstructs remembrance contradicts the theory’s claim that withdrawal from material connections removes the obstruction.

Moreover, only some people are thought to possess such remembrance, whereas humanity generally reaches countless correct results in every science, craft, and life activity by combining premises and drawing conclusions. This is a natural human method, not a chance occurrence. The alleged results of remembrance themselves resolve into ordered logical premises; altering the form or material disrupts the result. Its proponents therefore use logic without recognizing it. To establish a distinct way, they would have to present an academic form having no connection with logical principles.

The claim that remembrance through adherence to the shariah is superior because it certainly agrees with the maʾsūm, while logic mostly risks error, also fails. Only a few people can grasp the vast, interconnected purposes, mysteries, beliefs, and practical rulings of the Book and Sunnah in such a direct manner. People are not required to do what lies beyond their capacity; they must understand religion through the ordinary human method of arranging known premises to discover what is unknown. Logic, in accordance with each person’s ability, is as available as remembrance is claimed to be. The advocates of remembrance still use logical arguments to deny logic, and adherents of the supposed path have also differed widely. The disagreements of respected companions of the Prophet and Imams, and of early jurists and muhaddithīn, show that remembrance alone cannot distinguish truth from error.

A view definitely heard from a maʾsūm and perfectly understood is secure from error, but this rests on a demonstrative syllogism: it is the opinion of a maʾsūm; all his opinions are right; therefore it is right. It is not a separate method called remembrance. What is inferred from a solitary report, however, produces presumption and has no authority outside fiqh unless it conforms to the Qur’an; presumption has no standing against contrary demonstrative proof.

Literalist traditionalists say that because God addressed people in familiar language, they need only cling to the apparent meaning of religious statements and have no need of logic, philosophy, or other learning associated with unbelievers. Al-Mizan replies that this argument itself employs logic. No one claims every Muslim must formally study logic, but logical thinking is as unavoidable in understanding as language is in speech. Rejecting logic because some non-Muslims developed it resembles rejecting Arabic because it was the language of the Age of Ignorance.

Such literalism also confuses meaning with application. Muslims must understand divine knowledge, power, life, hearing, sight, speech, volition, and will as opposed to ignorance, incapacity, death, deafness, blindness, and the like. But they may not infer that God possesses these attributes in the human manner. The Book, Sunnah, and reason do not permit this assimilation.

The objection that reason cannot establish its own authority without a vicious circle misunderstands what is meant by following reason. If it concerns practical obligation, condemnation, or punishment, it is a dictate of practical intellect. If it means the necessary acceptance of a conclusion produced by properly formed academic premises after full comprehension of the matter, then its validity is self-evident. A self-evident proposition is its own proof and needs no external proof. Similarly, the claim that modern research denies totality, generality, permanence, and stable quiddities defeats itself: it offers a supposedly general and enduring conclusion by using logic and established concepts.

The Qur’an guides intellect to do what it was created to do: arrange known premises in order to obtain unknown results. In questions of real truth, it uses authentic and indisputable premises to produce authentic conclusions; this is proof. In practical questions of felicity, misery, benefit, harm, good, and evil, it uses well-known or accepted, mentally posited premises; this is debate or disputation. In matters of presumed good or evil it uses premises that encourage presumed good or deter presumed evil; this is admonition. Thus wisdom, goodly exhortation, and the best disputation are distinct modes of Qur’anic guidance.

Piety is indeed indispensable to beneficial knowledge, but it is not an independent epistemic route separate from natural contemplation. If it were, Qur’anic and Sunnah arguments against unbelievers, polytheists, sinners, and deviant groups would be pointless, since they could not understand an argument before attaining piety. Rather, piety restores the intelligent soul to its natural uprightness.

Human beings possess conflicting animal and predatory powers connected with the body. Each naturally seeks its own satisfaction without regard to the proper measure or to other powers. Unrestrained appetite for food, sex, or other pleasures can divert a person from livelihood, family, society, and individual and collective obligations; unchecked anger produces a comparable imbalance. Human felicity in this world and the next requires gathering these powers under knowledge and perfection, giving each its due without allowing it to obstruct or extinguish another. The balanced middle state produces qualities such as wisdom, bravery, and chastity, collectively called justice or probity.

Human thought begins with elementary perceptions arising from the needs of internal faculties, and develops through generalizing, particularizing, combining, and separating. If a person gives one contrary power excessive obedience, his thought is distorted: its propositions become dominant and the claims of other powers are ignored. Those enslaved by appetites become unable to attend to the weightier obligations of humanity; oppressive and arrogant people become hard-hearted and incapable of compassion, mercy, or humility even when required. Both pursue knowledge through a distorted soul and remain unaware of beneficial knowledge and true cognition. Excellent character and complete human virtues are therefore necessary for sound cognition, and this is piety. Good deeds preserve good character, and good character preserves true cognition, beneficial knowledge, and correct thought; knowledge without practice has no good in it.

The Qur’an’s commands to follow the middle course, fear God, purify the soul, and avoid sensual desire and unjust pride express this relation between piety and understanding. Sensual desire leads to perdition, while pride and heedlessness turn people from the way of rectitude to error. Those whose hearts, eyes, and ears do not grasp what a blessed human being grasps remain at the level of cattle or below. Thus thought, remembrance, and understanding are made conditional upon piety, and knowledge is joined to practice so that thought may be freed from animal imaginations and Satanic insinuations.

Al-Mizan nevertheless affirms a further Qur’anic reality: one brought under divine guardianship and near heavenly sanctity may be shown the kingdoms of the heavens and earth, the great signs of God, and lights of His omnipotence that remain hidden from others. A report from al-Ṣādiq says that people would see these kingdoms if Satans did not hover around their hearts. A Sunnī report from the Prophet says that, without excessive talk and confused hearts, people would see what he saw and hear what he heard. Worship, striving for God, certainty, and the observation of the kingdom are presented as connected with this disclosure. Yet this does not displace natural reasoning: it is a divine gift reserved for God’s chosen servants, and the good end belongs to the pious.

Al-Mizan next surveys Islamic intellectual history in order to measure it against the Qur’an, rather than to defend or attack a school. The Qur’an governs every kind of person and every aspect of life—belief, ethics, and deeds—and urges the acquisition of knowledge concerning the heavens, earth, plants, animals, humanity, angels, devils, and social life, so that people may know God and order human affairs. It supports the natural, logical path of thought, itself employing proof, disputation, and admonition, and calls the community to do likewise.

During the Prophet’s Medinan life, Muslims were newly formed in Islamic teaching. Their discussions were simple and aimed at knowing divine commands; they concentrated on reciting and memorizing the Qur’an and on memorizing and transmitting hadith without writing them. Their disputes with Jews and Christians marked the beginnings of scholastic theology. Poetry remained part of Arab culture but received no significant Qur’anic or Sunnah praise.

After the Prophet’s death, the dispute over the caliphate deepened division. The Qur’an was collected after the battle of Yamāmah, during the first caliph’s reign. Under the first two caliphs, military expansion occupied Muslims and did not advance academic study. The victories also revived pre-Islamic pride and domination, visible in the division between Arabs and clients, in Muʾāwiyah’s Caesarian manner of rule, and in reports about the armies. This disposition harmed intellectual development, especially Qur’anic teaching.

Hadith spread extensively. Converts from the People of the Book supplied narratives from their scriptures, including stories of prophets and earlier nations, which were mixed with transmitted Prophetic reports. Forgery and unauthorized material thereby circulated, and many early reports conflict plainly with the Qur’an. The exalted status of companionship and hadith transmission, rivalry for prestige among narrators, and a concern with narration rather than testing reports or contemplating their meanings all contributed. The Prophet is reported to have commanded that reports be presented to the Qur’an: what conforms to it should be accepted and what conflicts with it rejected.

This environment allowed fabricated material about divine names, attributes, and acts; alleged lapses of prophets; slanders concerning the Prophet; myths of creation; stories of past peoples; and even claims of Qur’anic alteration. Qur’an became assigned an outward place while hadith was made the basis of practice, and the Qur’an was soon effectively forsaken. The continued failure to test hadith by the Qur’an, with only rare exceptions, helped preserve ancient myths and superstitions among Muslim peoples.

The caliphate also turned many Muslims from the Prophet’s family. Some remained devoted to Ahl al-Bayt, some neglected their Qur’anic knowledge, and others became hostile to them, despite reports whose authenticity and meaning Al-Mizan treats as unquestioned: the Prophet directed the community to learn from them rather than teach them, described them as more knowledgeable of the Book, and declared in the mutawātir report of the Two Precious Things that the Book of God and his descendants would not separate until they met him at the reservoir. A nearly mutawātir report also warns that one who interprets the Qur’an by personal opinion should prepare a place in hell.

This abandonment was a great loss for Qur’anic knowledge and its proper mode of thought. Al-Mizan points to the small number of reports transmitted from ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn—particularly in Qur’anic exegesis—despite the vast number recorded through Sunnī chains. It considers their historical isolation more supportive of abandonment of Ahl al-Bayt than of the suggestion that their reports had first been abundant and later suppressed. Their reports remained neglected until the time of al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq, when conflict between the Umayyads and ʿAbbāsids gave them some opportunity to revive the inherited teaching.

Even the reports of Ahl al-Bayt were not protected from forgery and interpolation. The two Imams named certain forgers, and the Imams rejected reports attributed to themselves and to the Prophet, commanding their followers to test narrated material by the Qur’an. Most people, especially outside fiqh, did not put this into practice. Some went so far as to deny all authority to the apparent meanings of the Qur’an while assigning authority to books such as Misbāh al-sharīʿah, Fiqh al-Riḍā, and Jāmiʿ al-akhbār; some held that hadith explains the Qur’an even against the Qur’an’s clear meaning. Al-Mizan cites a reported scholarly judgment that Sunnīs abandoned Ahl al-Bayt and consequently the Book, while Shīʿahs abandoned the Book and consequently Ahl al-Bayt, so that the community collectively forsook both.

This treatment of hadith severed the Islamic sciences from the Qur’an, although they should be its branches and fruits. A student can become proficient in grammar, rhetoric, language, hadith, rijāl, hadith criticism, jurisprudence, and its principles without reciting or consulting the Qur’an. The Book is consequently reduced to recitation for reward or use as an amulet.

Contact with other religions after the conquests increased theological debate in the period of ʿUmar, although it was not yet extensively systematized or written. Under ʿUthmān, the Qur’anic collections were united into one version. During ʿAlī’s caliphate, internal wars occupied him, but Al-Mizan credits him with laying down the broad lines of Arabic grammar for Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, as well as delivering sermons, hadith, and theological discussions containing extensive religious knowledge and Qur’anic mysteries.

The general condition of Qur’an and hadith continued through the Umayyad and early ʿAbbāsid periods. Muʾāwiyah is said to have systematically promoted hadith forgery to obliterate the name and traces of Ahl al-Bayt, while religious rule became autocratic and Byzantine in style. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz later ordered hadith committed to writing, whereas it had previously been preserved orally. Arabic poetry and literary transmission became highly profitable and influential under the Umayyads and ʿAbbāsids, who used them in their political struggles against the Hāshimites and Fāṭimids. Scholars increasingly argued from poetry, proverbs, and linguistic rules, a habit that deeply affected intellectual procedure.

Theological discussion expanded and became organized around the Ashʾarites and Muʾtazilites, though the roots of their main questions already existed in Prophetic reports and in ʿAlī’s discussions of compulsion, delegation, qadar, and ability. The Muʾtazilites gave rational dictates authority over religious appearances, holding that intellect recognizes good and evil, that preference without a reason is wrong, that imposing what is beyond capacity is repugnant, and that human beings possess independence in their acts. Ashʾarites gave religious appearances authority over rational dictates, denying that reason knows good and evil, allowing preference without reason, affirming compulsion rather than human independence, and holding divine speech eternal. The subsequent translation of Greek works led theologians to add questions drawn from philosophy, but it is incorrect to say that theology began, or split into Iʿtizāl and Ashʿariyyah, only after Greek philosophy entered Islam.

The Muʾtazilites rose until the early ʿAbbāsid period and then declined until the Ayyūbids extinguished them, amid massacres whose extent God knows best. Ashʿarites then became the prevailing Sunnī theological school, although their jurists had previously treated scholastic discussion as sinful. Shīʿites, according to Al-Mizan, entered theological debate soon after the Prophet’s death through companions such as Salmān, Abū Dharr, Miqdād, ʿAmmār, and ʿAmr b. al-Ḥamq, and later followers including Rushayd, Kumayl, and Maytham. Umayyad persecution devastated them, but they revived under al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq, received some respite under the Buwayhids, and later endured renewed suppression until the Safavids.

Shīʿite theological positions resembled Muʾtazilite positions more than Ashʿarite ones in matters such as rational good and evil and qadar, but this does not mean that Shīʿism derives its foundations from Muʿtazilism. Its authoritative principles are those narrated from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt and do not share the Muʿtazilite taste and method. Theology is in itself a noble discipline for defending true religious teachings, yet Muslim theologians erred by failing to distinguish types of intellectual proposition, mixing truth with what is merely accepted.

Translations from Greek, Latin, Sanskrit, Persian, and Syriac introduced logic, mathematics, physics, metaphysics, medicine, and practical hikmah. Religious scholars reacted against attacks on religion by atheists, Manichaeans, and certain philosophers, as well as against Muslim philosophers who disparaged religion and its adherents.
