Their strongest objection concerned propositions drawn from Greek astronomy and physics—such as the Ptolemaic heavens, the supposed incorruptibility and eternity of celestial bodies, and the eternity of elements and species—which were treated as demonstrated even though philosophy had not proven them. Some who claimed philosophy added false teachings such as transmigration and the rejection of bodily resurrection, using them to ridicule the apparent meanings of religion. Others depicted religion as a discipline for primitive minds which the philosophical knower no longer needed.

Jurists and theologians therefore opposed such people through debate, condemnation, exclusion from Islam, and destruction of books under al-Mutawakkil. Philosophy nearly disappeared until al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Miskawayh, Ibn Rushd, and others revived it. It continued thereafter with few students and varying strength, and eventually became concentrated in Iran. Theologians largely accepted logic because it conformed to natural argumentation, but often misused it: they applied real definitions to mentally posited concepts and demonstrative proof to subjective considerations, where dialectical argument was appropriate. They defined such matters as good and evil, reward and punishment, forfeiture and grace by genus and species; argued about subjective religious questions through necessity and impossibility; and made subjective considerations rule over realities by saying, for example, that something is obligatory or improper for God. Al-Mizan calls such supposed proof merely poetic analogy.

Sūfism arose from asceticism and publicly emerged in the early ʿAbbāsid period with figures such as Abū Yazīd, Junayd, al-Shiblī, and Maʿrūf. Sūfīs held that true human perfection and cognition are attained by entering a tarīqah of diligent shariah practice, and many, Sunnī and Shīʿite alike, traced their chain to ʿAlī. They claimed extraordinary acts and uttered statements that seemed to contradict clear religion and reason, while saying that these expressions had meanings beyond ordinary understanding. Jurists and ordinary Muslims consequently opposed them, sometimes declaring them unbelievers and subjecting them to imprisonment, flogging, execution, crucifixion, expulsion, or exile.

If their path were truly the kernel of religion and its outward teachings merely a shell, the Lawgiver would have been more entitled to make it public; if it were not true, it could only be error. Sūfīs initially transmitted their ideas orally, then wrote books after the third century, expanded their public influence, and reached their height in the sixth and seventh centuries. Their decline followed, first, because popular systems attract insincere people seeking worldly gain, thereby making the system hated; and, second, because some shaykhs called self-knowledge an unlegislated but God-pleasing innovation, analogous to Christian monasticism. This opened the way to invented rites that displaced shariah practices, separated tarīqah from shariah, permitted unlawful conduct, abandoned obligations, and reduced some groups to beggary and addiction to opium and bhang under the name of obliterating the self.

The Book and Sunnah affirm that the outward side of the shariah has hidden realities and that people have a path to them, but that path is nothing other than diligent obedience to the outward shariah. No esoteric truth lies beyond the guidance of outward practice, and no nearer path than that brought by the Prophet was neglected by him. The Qur’an explains everything clearly.

Thus three methods emerged for seeking reality: adherence to the apparent meanings of religion, intellectual research, and purification of the soul. Their followers continually dispute, usually imposing their own learned views on the Qur’an instead of letting the Qur’an shape their views. Yet the Book confirms every truth contained in these methods: no true inward reality can conflict with the outward religious sense, and no truth, inward or outward, can conflict with true proof. This led some scholars to seek harmony between religious appearances and ʿirfān, others between philosophy and ʿirfān, others between religion and philosophy, and still others among all three. Their efforts did not end the entrenched conflict. Scholars of each discipline accuse the others of ignorance, atheism, or stupidity, while the masses reject all of them. Al-Mizan attributes this enduring condition to the community’s initial failure to heed the Qur’an’s call to united reflection and unity upon the rope of Allah.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan holds that Moses’ command to enter the holy land came after the Exodus, as is indicated by “and made you kings,” and after such signs as manna and quails, water gushing from the rock, and cloud-shade. The later repeated description of the Israelites as “transgressors” shows that disobedience to Moses had become their settled habit, so the wilderness wandering occurred late in Moses’ life, after most Qur’anic events concerning them.

Moses’ reminder embraces God’s total favor—sending Moses, guidance and religion, deliverance from Pharaoh, the Torah, and the shariah—and prepares them to receive its completion: an independent holy land in which to live and rule. The favors are threefold. Raising prophets among them may mean prophets in their ancestral line, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and those after them, or Israelite prophets such as Joseph, the tribes, Moses, and Aaron.

“Made you kings” means liberation from Pharaoh’s humiliation and tyrannical domination: one is a king who independently manages himself, his family, and property. Their monotheistic order required obedience to God and His messenger, complete justice, and non-aggression; it excluded mastery by one group member over another and disruptive class distinctions. Moses alone stood above them, as a prophet rather than an unjust king or tribal chief. The view that the phrase foretells later kings beginning with Tālūt, David, and subsequent rulers is rejected because it would require “made among you kings,” like “raised prophets among you.” The alternative that it means authority concentrated in certain members, extending from Joseph and Moses to Joshua and later kings, faces the same objection.

Finally, the unprecedented gift denotes the sustained clear signs, miracles, and proofs surrounding them in Egypt and after their deliverance. These favors would set their lives right if they kept their covenant. Al-Mizan concludes that no nation before Moses’ time had received so many continuous favors; “the worlds” therefore need not be restricted to the worlds of that time.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses, knowing his people’s habitual transgression, emphasized the command to enter the holy land by forbidding retreat and warning that disobedience would make them losers. Their later designation as “transgressors” indicates repeated, settled disobedience, not a single offence.

The land is “holy” in the sense that it contains a great good, as a blessed land does; this includes establishment of religion and removal of polytheism. “Allah has prescribed for you” apparently decrees their dwelling there, yet leaves unspecified its time and which members of the ummah would enter. Thus the later forty-year prohibition does not contradict but confirms the prescription: even if the generation addressed died in the wilderness and their descendants entered under Joshua b. Nun, the prescribed settlement followed that period.

The prescription belongs to the divine promise to grant the oppressed inheritance and power in the land (28:5–6), but its fulfilment depended on seeking God’s help and patience. Their inheritance of the blessed land fulfilled the divine word because they bore suffering patiently (7:137). This patience includes obedience, avoidance of sin, and endurance of bitter events; their persistent disobedience accordingly brought increasingly difficult assignments.

The Qur’anic evidence makes the prescription conditional, not unrestricted or irrevocable: rule in the land was a test, gratitude brought increase, and ingratitude severe chastisement. The verses do not specify the prescription’s precise time or extent. Al-Mizan therefore sets aside an exegete’s appeal to Old Testament promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whether original or forged, because the Qur’an is not explained through the Torah.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Jabr originally concerns restoring something with force, though it can also mean restoration without that connotation; al-ijbār commonly means compulsion. Applied to a human being, al-jabbār denotes a tyrannical, insolent person who compensates for a deficiency by claiming an undeserved high rank, and the term can also convey towering over others. Thus the “strong race” means a people possessing authority and power by which they compel others to obey.

By making entry conditional on that people’s departure, the Israelites in fact rejected Moses’ command, even while promising to enter if their condition were fulfilled. Al-Mizan rejects traditions portraying the Amalekites as extraordinarily gigantic: their implausible descriptions are unsupported by archaeology or physical research and are forgeries inserted into Islamic literature.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan says that the two men were among those who feared God and avoided disobeying Him and His prophet. God’s unqualified “favor” upon them denotes divine wilāyah (friendship), confirming that their fear was of God alone, since God’s friends fear none but Him. It is also possible that the favor concerns God’s having bestowed fear upon them; the omitted object of “feared” is understood from the context, for they plainly did not fear the strong race.

The interpretation that they were two Amalekites whom the Israelites feared, guided to Islam and allied with Moses, rests on Ibn Jubayr’s passive reading yukhāfūn and explanatory traditions. Al-Mizan rejects it because these are solitary reports unsupported by the Qur’an.

“Enter upon them by the gate” may mean entering the nearest town of the strong race, reportedly Arihā’, or its town gate. Their certain promise of victory arose from complete faith in Moses’ truthful declaration that God had prescribed the land for them, or perhaps from knowledge granted through divine friendship. Most Shīʾah and Sunnī exegetes identify them as Joshua b. Nun and Caleb b. Yuqina, two of Israel’s twelve chiefs. Their call to rely on God was meant to reassure and encourage the Israelites, for God suffices one who relies on Him.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains that the Israelites repeated their absolute refusal in order to make Moses despair of persuading them. Their words are derisive, insulting, and contemptuous toward Moses and the divine command and promise he conveyed. They ignored the two advisers altogether; after earlier lengthy discussion, their abrupt brevity toward Moses signals that they were weary of him and unwilling to hear him. Their emphatic “never” and “at all” culminate in the folly of telling Moses and his Lord to fight while they remain seated.

The commentary holds that this plainly proves they conceived God bodily, like idol-worshippers. Their earlier request, “O Moses! Make for us a god as they have (their) gods,” confirms their ignorance (7:138); Al-Mizan further states that their books show their continuing belief in anthropomorphization and embodiment of God.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains Moses’ statement that he controlled only himself and his brother as an indirect declaration that, in this matter, he could compel no one to accept his call except their own obedience. It does not mean that no one had believed or listened to him, since the two God-fearing men and other believers had done so; nor does it concern his and Aaron’s families. Moses had diligently conveyed a legitimate divine responsibility, but the Israelite society answered with an ignominious total refusal, leaving the messengers’ path blocked.

His complaint therefore asks God to enforce His command and judge between the two messengers and the transgressors, so that the people might receive the completed favor of inheriting and succeeding in the land. Their former disobediences had been many, but this open and rude repudiation surpassed the limit; if left unanswered, it would destroy the authority of prophetic commands and dissolve the unity Moses had established.

Moses mentions himself and Aaron because they were the conveyors of the message, whereas other obedient believers were not charged with tablīgh and mission. The complaint itself is an appeal for divine help in enforcing the command. Grammatically, “and my brother” is joined to “I”: Aaron, like Moses, had control only over himself in obedience; it is not joined to “my own self,” as though Moses meant that he controlled both himself and Aaron, although that sense is true in itself. Moses does not pray for their final punishment, nor for the removal or death of himself and Aaron. The later instruction, “therefore do not grieve for the nation of transgressors” (5:26), shows instead that he feared punishment would overtake them and would grieve at their wilderness ordeal.
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains that “it” is the holy land: by a divine creative decree, entering and capturing it were forbidden to them for forty years. During al-Tīh they would wander in the land where they then were, belonging neither to settled town life nor to desert-dwelling life. Moses is told not to grieve at this chastisement, for God confirms that they are transgressors and that it is the retribution of their deeds.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that watlu, “relate,” derives from following something in succession, because a report is recounted stage by stage; al-qurbān is an offering intended to bring one near to God and, as a verbal noun, remains singular even when two offerings are meant. The pronoun “them” addresses the People of the Book.

The two sons are sons of Adam, the progenitor of mankind, not—as one exegete alleged—the sons of an Israelite. The Qur’an mentions no other Adam without a distinguishing indication. Moreover, the crow episode and the killer’s ignorance of burial fit early humanity’s rudimentary knowledge, not the civilized Children of Israel. Recasting the event as an Israelite incident also fails to explain why the maxim that killing one person is like killing all humanity would be stated only in connection with that incident or addressed to one nation. That maxim is not a legislative command restricted to Israel; it is a profound principle explained to them, whose benefit encompasses all people, just as Qur’anic admonitions addressed to Muḥammad’s community are not confined to it. Israel is singled out because the passage rebukes its envy and hostility, which led to mischief and warfare. The supposed Israelite story has no basis in tradition or history.

“Relate … with truth” declares that the story circulating among the audience had suffered distortion or omission. In particular, Genesis omits the crow and portrays God corporeally, whereas God is exalted above such a depiction. Each brother offered to God, and both knew that one offering had been accepted and the other rejected, although the verse does not state how they knew. Since offerings were sometimes known to be accepted when consumed by fire, as indicated in (3:183), this may have been the sign in this case; in any event, their knowledge is certain.

The brother whose offering was rejected threatened murder solely from envy, not because the accepted brother had committed any offence. The latter’s answer establishes both his innocence and the cause of rejection: acceptance belongs only to the pious, whereas the killer lacked fear of God. He refuses to intend his brother’s death even if threatened, because piety and fear of the Lord of the worlds prevent injustice. The murderer would consequently bear his own sin and that of his victim and enter the Fire.

Thus the episode sets out the condition for acceptance of worship, warns against envy, murder, and injustice, and affirms divine recompense. Perfect Lordship requires an ordered system in which deeds are justly evaluated: oppression either ceases or brings upon its author the punishment he has prepared for himself, namely the Fire.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan holds that the emphatic construction of “If you will stretch forth your hand … I am not one to stretch forth my hand” shows that the victim was utterly removed from any intention to kill his brother. Stretching forth the hand denotes preparing and arranging murder, while the oath, the strengthened negation, and the nominal expression all emphasize that such a thought had never entered his mind. His fear of Allah, the Lord of the worlds, confirms this innocence: one who remembers that the Lord recompenses every sin is restrained from the injustice that leads to perdition.

The victim faced two alternatives: either he would kill his brother and become the unjust aggressor, bearing both sins and entering the Fire, or his brother would murder him and incur those consequences. He chose the latter, preserving his own felicity without committing oppression. Accordingly, his later “wish” that his brother bear his sin denotes a choice between these alternatives, not a desire to make his brother wicked. The commentary compares this to the preference in the story of Moses’s companion for a death joined to felicity rather than a life that would culminate in oppression and disbelief.

The murdered son of Adam is presented as pious, God-fearing, and possessed of gnosis. His statement that God accepts only from the pious is an unrebutted claim to piety, and his expressed fear of God is likewise unrebutted. His discourse contains the roots of religious knowledge: humanity will include both pious and unjust people; all are governed by one Lord, who loves justice and beneficence and hates transgression; obedience founded on piety is accepted, while sin remains upon its perpetrator; and resurrection must follow so that deeds are recompensed, with the Fire as the recompense of oppressors.

The commentary stresses that he did not say that he would surrender without defending himself, nor that he wanted to be murdered in order to condemn his brother. He said only that he would not kill. Therefore, the objection that he failed in a duty of self-defence is baseless: the verse does not say he knowingly refrained from defence, and he may have been ambushed or killed while defending himself. Likewise, the ascetic view that a victim should submit to an oppressor so that the oppressor alone bears the sin is rejected as foolishness: helping a sinner to sin makes helper and sinner partners in it. Causing another’s disgrace and misguidance is itself injustice; the victim merely chose not to become a killer when confronted with the alternative.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that tabūa, rendered “bear,” literally conveys remaining or staying with something; explaining it as “return” concerns an inseparable implication. In “that you should bear my sin as well as your own sin,” the victim’s sin is transferred to his unjust killer. The killer therefore bears two sins, while the murdered person comes to God with no sin remaining in his account. The apparent wording, traditions, and reason support this meaning.

This does not violate the principle, “That no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another” (53:38). The question concerns practical wisdom and social order, not a theoretical impossibility. Society can transfer responsibility where injustice requires it: a killer may be made liable for rights owed by the person he killed, and a rebel who corrupts public order may have his good qualities treated as null. Once the victim’s sins are assigned to the oppressor as the consequence and compensation of his oppression, they are no longer another person’s burden; they have become the killer’s burden. The transfer resembles a sale: after ownership is transferred, the seller’s former rights cease without invalidating the rule that property is not lawful to another without its owner’s consent.

The commentary rejects reported alternative explanations: that “my sin” means only the sin of murdering the victim and “your sin” previous sins, as narrated from Ibn Masʾūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others; that it means the murder plus the prior sin for which the offering was rejected, attributed to al-Jubbāʾī and al-Zajjāj; or that it means murder plus the sin of killing all humanity. None is supported by the Qur’anic wording or reason. If both sins were already the killer’s own acts, there would be no reason to place them side by side while attributing one to the victim and the other to the killer.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan maintains that tawwaʾat in “his mind facilitated to him the slaying of his brother” does not itself mean both obedience and seduction. Unlike the simpler form denoting prompt compliance, its form indicates graduality: successive insinuations and temptations progressively brought his mind to submit to the plan to murder his brother. “The slaying of his brother” stands for the command or undertaking of slaying him.

Other proposed grammatical readings take tawwaʾat to mean that his mind made the murder attractive, or that it acceded to him in committing it. The commentary does not infer that the murder occurred at night from fa-asbaha. Although the word literally relates to morning, Arabic commonly uses it simply to mean “became,” without temporal force; it has that usage elsewhere in the Qur’an.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that the killer remained bewildered for a considerable time after the murder, fearing discovery but unable to devise a way to conceal his brother’s body. His cry of helplessness therefore came after God sent the crow, not immediately after the killing. The crow did more than dig: it buried something after digging, thereby demonstrating burial itself. Mere digging would not have taught so simple-minded a man how to cover a corpse. Crows characteristically store part of their prey in the earth, unlike birds that scratch the ground merely to find food.

The pronoun in “so that he might show him” most naturally refers to the crow, the nearest noun, though referring it to God is also possible in meaning. When the killer saw how easily the crow buried something, he recognized that he too could have done so and regretted overlooking the obvious connection between digging and burial. His question is a self-reproaching question that implies he did not lack the ability; he had no answer for why he remained oblivious and needlessly troubled for so long. Thus his regret principally concerns failing to hide and bury the corpse, although it may also include regret for the murder itself.

The commentary generalizes this remorse. An unjust person who seeks to conceal a socially unacceptable crime cannot compel society to accept it; its effects are bound to emerge, just as the body cannot digest poison. Even if a crime remains hidden in this world, the criminal must meet God, where he will recognize the defect in his plans and regret it. Further opportunities would only lead him to damage other matters until God disgraces him.

Al-Mizan regards the crow episode as uniquely portraying the human acquisition of knowledge through perception and thought. Human cognitions continually grow during life and, traced back to their beginning, diminish to nothing; hence God taught man what he did not know. Knowledge guides beings to their perfection, and every guidance is ultimately from God. Theoretical knowledge of the properties of things arises through the senses: the crow’s action outwardly taught burial, but God, who arranged the encounter within the system of creation, was the real teacher. Likewise, knowledge learned from teachers, acquired through personal discovery, or used in training animals and writing is attributed to God because all causal means and the knowledge that perfects human life belong to His governance.

This divine attribution does not abolish secondary causes. God creates through a chain of apparent causes, which function as instruments and conditions; denying all causes in the name of divine unity contradicts the very reasoning by which that denial is made. God has made what is in the heavens and earth serviceable to human beings and has given them senses and intellect so that they may understand and use these things to attain their appointed perfection.

The commentary distinguishes three forms of divine guidance in human knowledge. First, knowledge of external particulars and their properties comes through the five senses. Second, universal and comprehensive intellectual knowledge is given through God’s subjugation of creation and is indispensable to human beings, though it is not supplied by the senses themselves. Third, practical knowledge of what should and should not be done—good and evil—comes by divine inspiration or instinct cast into the heart. This practical inspiration works properly only when intellect is sound and upright; intellect in turn functions properly only where natural religion and piety are sound. A defective intellect cannot recognize truth and falsehood so as to follow or avoid them, while perverted natural religion disorders desire, anger, love, and hate and thereby impairs theoretical perception.

For this reason, the Qur’an teaches according to the proper route of each kind of knowledge. It appeals to the senses concerning perceptible particulars, to reason and understanding concerning universal matters such as creation and resurrection, and to the inward awareness of piety concerning practical good and evil. This refutes materialists who confine knowledge to sensation and experiment, since monotheism—the Qur’an’s fundamental teaching—is a purely rational matter far removed from sense experience. True cognition belongs to human nature; deviation does not erase nature but misuses it, like an archer who misses with a bow made for hitting the target or a tool incorrectly fitted into a machine.

Those who reject pure rational proof because it yields disputes nevertheless rely on rational premises to establish the supremacy of sense and experiment. Their experimental argument itself depends on rational judgments about repeated effects, fixed conditions, and the impossibility of permanent chance. Nature therefore cannot be negated, even though it may be misused.

Al-Mizan further rejects making or validating enacted laws through social experimentation, statistics, analogy, or discretionary preference. The Qur’an presents the fundamental law as natural and clear, general piety and impiety as known through inspiration, and the details of law as learned from revelation. Conjecture cannot yield truth, and one cannot attain truth through falsehood, justice through injustice, good through evil, or piety through impiety. The commentary likewise rejects a path of “remembrance” that dismisses thought and natural logic, and rejects contemplation detached from fear of God. Hence Qur’anic legislation is accompanied by moral instruction: moral virtues awaken the innate piety through which people properly understand and observe the law.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan takes “For this reason” to refer to the preceding story of Adam’s two sons: that grievous murder occasioned the explanation given to the Children of Israel. Though it is grammatically possible to connect the phrase with the killer’s regret, that reading would require an unmarked new sentence after it and is less consistent with Qur’anic style. The story exposes a human disposition to desire and jealousy over gifts beyond one’s control, a disposition that can blind a person into killing even his brother and opposing the purpose of creation.

Human beings share one reality, humanity. God multiplies individual persons, whose lives are brief, so that this reality endures through successive generations and the worship of God continues. To murder one person without right is therefore mischief in creation and an assault upon the divine aim of preserving humanity; it is, in this sense, war against God’s Lordship. Conversely, preserving one person preserves that same humanity. The verse addresses the Children of Israel especially because their jealousy, pride, desire, and rejection of truth made them particularly liable to such transgression. “We prescribed to the Children of Israel” is not the enactment of a new law, but an emphatic declaration of the gravity of murder and of what brings divine wrath in this world or the next.

The verse excepts killing in two cases: retributive punishment for manslaughter and punishment for mischief in the land. Otherwise, saying that one who kills a soul has killed all people is not a calculation that makes the punishment for one murder identical in quantity to that for every possible murder. Nor does it mean that one individual is literally equal to himself plus all others, or to all others excluding himself. Such readings wrongly treat the statement as an ordinary numerical simile.

Rather, it alludes to the single reality shared equally by all human beings: whoever attacks the humanity present in one person attacks the humanity present in all. Like water divided among many glasses, the same reality is present in each portion. This resolves the objections that further murders would have no additional significance or that the comparison is logically impossible. The converse, that one who keeps a soul alive has kept all people alive, rests on the same shared reality. Giving life includes rescue from drowning or captivity, and, because the Qur’an counts guidance as life, guiding a person to true faith is also giving life.

The messengers came to the Children of Israel with clear proofs, warning them against murder and related forms of corruption, yet many continued to act extravagantly in the land. The closing clause supplies the intended rebuke: despite the warning and proof, they persisted in arrogance and insolence. Extravagance means exceeding the proper boundary in one’s activities, though the term is often used particularly of spending.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that “waging war against Allah and His Messenger” cannot be literal. Although metaphorically it could cover every disobedience, joining the Messenger to God confines it to matters in which the Messenger was given authority, especially preserving public security. The accompanying phrase, “and strive to make mischief in the land,” specifies the intended offence: disturbing peace and security through such acts as highway robbery, rather than fighting Muslims. The Prophet did not impose these penalties on disbelievers defeated in battle, and the following verse’s exception for repentance further shows that the offence is this public mischief, not polytheism. Thus waging war and making mischief here are one reality: upsetting general law and order by creating fear and anxiety, ordinarily through armed violence and killing; the sunnah accordingly explains it as drawing the sword and the like.

The listed penalties—killing, crucifixion, cutting a hand and foot on opposite sides, or banishment—are alternatives, since aw (“or”) does not join them together. The verse itself does not decide whether they are a matter of sequence or choice. Traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-bayt explain that they correspond to degrees of mischief: one may draw the sword, kill, and take property; another may only kill; another only take property; and another only draw the sword, with differing penalties for each. Cutting on opposite sides means one hand and one foot, such as the right hand and left foot, not both hands and feet. al-nafy means banishment, explained in tradition as removal from one town to another.

These punishments are disgrace in this world, while the offender may still face grievous chastisement in the hereafter; undergoing the prescribed punishment does not necessarily remove the latter.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that the prescribed punishment is waived for those who repent before they are apprehended. Once they have been caught and proof is established, it is not waived. “So know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” alludes to this waiver and is among the verses in which forgiveness concerns an affair other than the next world.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Wasīlah, with s, means attaining something with longing and is more particular than al-waṣilah, “joining” or “attaining.” It is spiritual connection between the servant and his Lord. Since nothing connects man to God except worshipful submission and veneration, seeking this means of nearness is to realize veneration and turn to God in humility and poverty. Knowledge and good deeds are its instruments and concomitants, unless they are themselves taken in this sense.

The more evident meaning of al-jihād, “strive hard in His way,” is broad enough to include fighting unbelievers as well as struggling against base desire and anger. Its connection with seeking nearness to God, and the reason supplied by the following verses, support this breadth. Yet it is also possible to restrict it to fighting unbelievers, because “in His way” is the qualification used in verses urging combat, whereas general striving is expressed differently: And (as for) those who strive hard for Us, We will most certainly guide them onto Our ways; and Allah is most surely with the doers of good (29:69). On this reading, fighting is mentioned after the general command to seek nearness in order to emphasize its importance; likewise, seeking nearness may be mentioned after fearing God as a particular after a general.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses apparently provide the reason for the preceding commands to fear God, seek nearness to Him, and strive in His way. These are the effective means of warding off the painful, lasting punishment; nothing else can replace them. Even if the unbelievers possessed all that is in the earth and its like besides it, their ransom would not be accepted. They will wish to leave the Fire but cannot, because its punishment lasts.

The verses show, first, that punishment is the basic prospect nearest to man, and only īmān and piety avert it, as indicated by And there is not one of you but shall come down to it; this is a decided decree of your Lord. Then We shall deliver those who were pious, and We shall leave the unjust therein on their knees (19:71–72), and Most surely man is in loss, except those who believe and do good, and enjoin on each other truth, and enjoin on each other patience (103:2–3). Second, the original human nature that feels the pain of fire in this world does not cease in the next world; otherwise the people of the Fire would neither suffer its agony nor desire to escape it.

verses.38:
Al-Mizan notes that the opening “And” functions here as ammā, “as for,” which accounts for the ensuing predicate. Although aydi, “hands,” is plural, it refers to the two hands of the male and female thief; Arabic commonly uses the plural in such cases. “Hand” can denote the limb attached to the shoulder, but traditions specify the right hand here, and cutting means severing all or part of it with a sharp instrument.

The cutting is a punishment for what they have earned and an al-nakāl: an exemplary punishment intended to deter both the offender and others. This purpose explains the following promise concerning repentance. If a thief repents after the wrongdoing and reforms himself—shown by no longer intending theft—God accepts the repentance and turns to him in forgiveness and mercy. The verse thus joins deterrent punishment with acceptance of genuine reformation.

verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse gives the reason God accepts the repentance of the stealing man or woman when they repent and reform. Since the kingdom of the heavens and earth belongs to Him, He possesses full authority over His kingdom and subjects to punish or show mercy according to reason and wisdom: He punishes the unrepentant thief and forgives the repentant one.

“Allah has the power over all things” explains His kingdom. Ownership arises from creation and origination, or divine guardianship: God is the Creator and Originator of everything, and every thing and its effects belong to Him; He gives and withholds as He pleases. Kingdom and rulership, in turn, are the power to carry out whatever He wills, since everything begins from Him and His decree and will are effective. Thus He is Owner because all things subsist through Him, and King because His power is neither deficient nor obstructed.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet about hypocrites whose verbal profession of faith never reached their hearts, and about the Jews involved in this case. Their “hastening in unbelief” means rapidly advancing in it through successive words and acts; it is not merely a movement toward unbelief.

The descriptions of being “listeners for the sake of a lie” and “listeners for another people who have not come to you” apply to the Jews, not the hypocrites. The first denotes knowingly attending to lies, while the second denotes accepting reports and orders from others. Their scholars knowingly displaced a clear divine ruling in their Book, then sent delegates to seek the Prophet’s judgement, instructing them to accept it only if it agreed with the corrupted ruling. Their being subject to a divinely intended trial means that the Prophet cannot remove what God has decreed; their accumulating sins have left their hearts unpurified and in error. They are threatened with disgrace in this world and grievous punishment in the hereafter.

Al-Mizan takes “what is forbidden” in the next verse to mean bribe. The Jewish scholars who altered the divine law took bribes, while their followers listened to their lies; together the two descriptions characterize the community. Although suht includes every unlawfully acquired property, its contextual application here is bribery used to evade a ruling that endangered certain people.

The Prophet was left to his own justified judgement whether to decide their case or decline it. If he declined, they could not harm him; if he judged, he had to judge equitably. Thus God does not approve their being judged except by His law: if they would not accept that law, the Prophet should not involve himself, since no alternative law could be applied.

verses.43:
Al-Mizan finds the Jews’ conduct astonishing: though they possessed the Torah and its clear ruling on their case, while rejecting the Prophet’s prophethood, Book, and shariah, they nevertheless sought his judgement and then turned away from the Torah’s divine law. “Yet they turn back after that” most fittingly means that they abandoned the Torah’s ruling, and “these are not the believers” means that they had abandoned belief in the Torah and its law. It is possible to refer these phrases instead to their rejection of the Prophet’s judgement, or to disbelief in both the Torah and the Prophet, but the first explanation accords better with the context.

The commentary concludes that the Torah then held by the Jews, and still prevalent among them, contains parts of the original Torah sent down to Moses, including divine laws, while many parts have been corrupted by additions, omissions, changes of wording, and changes of context. It identifies this as the Qur’anic view, and says that extensive research supports it.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that God revealed books containing guidance and light so that communities might be guided, gain insight, and refer their disputes to them. Prophets and religious authorities were commanded to judge by these books, guard them from alteration, fear God rather than people, and refuse any worldly price for divine judgement. Different laws were appointed for different peoples and eras because their capacities differ, and because God tests them through what He gives them.

The Torah’s guidance and light gave the Israelites cognitions and laws suitable to their condition and capabilities. The prophets who judged by it are called those who submitted to God in order to show that the one divine religion is submission to Him; one who submits has no right to reject His commands. The “Divines” are scholars wholly devoted to God, or those who raise people through knowledge, while the ahbār are learned experts who judge by the divine order and preserve its shariah. They were witnesses of the Book because, having been charged to guard it, they preserved it through perfect memorization. This witnessing does not mean either testifying that stoning was in the Torah or merely testifying that the Book came from God, since neither interpretation suits the context.

The command not to fear people or barter God’s signs forbids concealing or changing the Torah through fear, greed, wealth, or worldly status. More appropriately, it follows from the covenant implicit in their charge to guard the Book: they were made its witnesses on the condition that they would disclose it without fearing anyone but God and would not sell its signs for a small price. The final warning against judging otherwise than what God revealed forcefully confirms this obligation.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse sets out retribution for felonies such as killing, cutting, and wounding: a life is taken for a life, and an eye, nose, ear, tooth, or wound is requited by its like from the offender. The word “for” indicates exchange, placing the person entitled to retaliation in relation to the felon. The law appears distinct from the particular issue for which the Jews had initially approached the Prophet, and it is found in the present Torah.

If the holder of the right of retaliation—the heir of the slain, the victim, or the wounded person—forgives the offender, that remission is an expiation, either for the remitter’s sins or for the offender in respect of that felony. If he does not forgive, he must decide according to God’s revealed law; otherwise he is among the unjust. The clause concerning one who does not judge by God’s revelation is connected to the clause concerning forgiveness, not an independent statement: it expresses the reason for the required judgement when remission is withheld.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains Jesus’ being sent in the footsteps of the earlier prophets as a metaphor for his proceeding on their path: the call to monotheism and submission to God. His verification of the Torah shows that his call was the same as Moses’ call. The Books concerning Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad thus accord with one another.

The Gospel was an actual book revealed to Jesus, not merely “good news,” even though the Qur’an does not describe the manner or details of its revelation as it does for the Torah and Qur’an. Its first “guidance” concerns cognition in faith and belief, such as God’s Oneness and resurrection; its “light” denotes shariah and laws, which illuminate the path of life; and its second “guidance,” explicated by “admonition,” is the guidance that leads to fear of God and piety. The repetition of “guidance” is therefore not redundant.

The Gospel’s verification of the Torah is not merely emphatic: it means that the Gospel followed the Torah’s shariah and called people to follow it, apart from the few things Jesus made lawful that had formerly been prohibited. The Gospel especially cared for piety in addition to belief and practical law. Although the Qur’an does not wholly verify the Torah now in Jewish hands, and the four Gospels attributed to Matthew, Marks, Luke, and John are not the Gospel revealed to Jesus, the commentary says that they confirm this special concern with piety.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that the Gospel confirmed the Torah’s laws except for rules abrogated and identified in the Book revealed to Jesus. Hence obeying the Torah’s law, apart from what the Gospel made lawful, was itself obedience to the Gospel. The verse therefore does not prove that the Gospel contained an elaborate independent shariah like the Torah.

The recurring formula concerning those who do not judge by God’s revelation emphasizes the respective charges recorded against Jews and Christians: unbelief, injustice, and transgression. Christians are called transgressors because they changed monotheism into trinity and abandoned the Torah’s laws, having been misled by Paul’s teaching that Jesus brought a religion independent of Moses and that his atonement abrogated all law. They consequently went outside the boundary of the true divine religion through mistaken interpretation. The Jews, by contrast, knowingly rejected laws and beliefs whose truth they fully knew, which was disbelief in God’s signs and injustice.

Nevertheless, these three verdicts are unrestricted, although applied here to the People of the Book. Al-Mizan distinguishes between knowingly rejecting an established religious rule, which is disbelief; violating it while knowing it is true but without rejecting it, which is transgression; and rejecting it without knowing that it is an established matter of religion, which is neither disbelief nor transgression because of excusable incapacity—unless one negligently failed to investigate the proofs.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains Haymanah as the Qur’an’s authority, protection, preservation, and management over the earlier divine Books. As their explanation and guardian, it retains their permanent, unchangeable fundamentals and abrogates or completes changeable subsidiary laws in accordance with humanity’s gradual development. Thus its verification of earlier Books does not mean that every previous law remains unchanged; it affirms that their laws and cognitions truly came from God, who may abrogate or complete them. The Qur’an preserves whatever earlier law and knowledge is suitable for this ummah, and additions, omissions, or abrogations do not contradict this verification, just as the Gospel verified the Torah while making some formerly forbidden things lawful.

Because the revealed shariah is truth whether it agrees with or differs from prior Books, the Prophet must judge by what God has revealed and not follow desires that diverge from the truth. “Judge between them” may refer either to the People of the Book, in which case it is conditional upon choosing to judge them, or to people generally. Al-Mizan considers the latter more appropriate, since hypocrites were mentioned with the Jews and no reason exists to restrict the pronoun to Jews alone.

Shariah is the divinely laid path for a particular prophet or ummah, whereas dīn is the one comprehensive divine religion, submission to God, embracing all nations. Shariah may be abrogated, but religion in this wider sense is unalterable. Shariah is attributed to God, a prophet, or an ummah, but not to an ordinary individual, because it implies a path specially laid down. Millah, though largely synonymous with shariah, denotes the system as transmitted and practised by a people generation after generation; it is ascribed to a prophet or community, not to God. Thus dīn is more general than shariah and millah.

The different laws given to different nations do not reflect differences of place, language, or race, nor simultaneous competing shariahs; they arose through successive eras as human intellectual and social capacities developed. If God had willed, He could have treated humanity as one people at one level and imposed one law. Instead, differing divine gifts and capacities required differing tests, and the laws are means by which human potential is brought to fulfilment in felicity or misery and the party of God is distinguished from that of Satan. The verse therefore calls the community to compete in virtuous deeds—namely, the prescribed laws and duties—rather than become entangled in differences, since all return to God, who will disclose and judge what they disputed.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse repeats the command to judge by God’s revelation and not follow low desires, but develops a different consequence from the preceding verse. The earlier command leads to competing in virtuous deeds under the shariah prescribed for the Prophet and his community; this one explains that those who turn away from revealed truth do so because of transgression, and that God desires to afflict them for sins that produced it. This affliction apparently consists in leaving them to error. The command is connected to the preceding mention of the Book: God revealed both the laws prescribed for them and the command to judge by what He revealed.

The warning that they might seduce the Prophet from part of revelation does not conflict with his ʿismah. ʿIsmah is an intellectual and cognitive aptitude; it does not abolish free will, choice, or the laws based upon them. As certain knowledge that food is poisoned makes eating it practically like impossible while the organs of eating still remain capable of acting, so infallibility does not remove the underlying power to act or refrain.

Their turning away should console rather than grieve the Prophet. God’s dominance cannot be weakened or escaped: because of their transgression, He leaves them in error, deviates their hearts after their deviation, removes His help, and lures them into evil. The wording teaches that their refusal occurs under divine subjugation, so it does not represent failure in the religious call. The purpose of messengers’ warning and good news is not that every person must enter true religion, but that people be tested and it become known who is best in deed. Many people are transgressors, and this explains why God desires to afflict them for some of their sins.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan treats the verse as flowing from their turning away from the revealed judgement of God which they knew to be true, and possibly as the conclusion of the preceding discussion. Since these revealed laws are truth and no other true shariah exists, turning away from them can only mean desiring the judgement of the Days of Ignorance, a system arising from low desires.

The first question is therefore a rebuke, and the second has the implied negative answer that none judges better than God. The phrase “for a people who are sure” insinuates that those truthful in their claim to believe in God are certain of His signs and cannot hold that anyone judges better than Him.

The shifts between the divine names and pronouns are also significant. Use of the proper Divine Name in the third person emphasizes the gravity of the subject. The first-person singular shows that affairs belong to God alone, without intervention by any friend or intercessor: He alone fulfils promises, and His warnings cannot be averted by any intermediary or cause.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that al-wilāyah is a proximity that removes barriers for a particular purpose. Thus a waliyy may be a helper, beloved, heir, or one exercising authority, according to whether the proximity concerns help, love, kinship, or obedience. Although the prohibition of taking Jews and Christians as awliyāʾ is unrestricted, the following excuse—fear that a calamity may befall—shows that the intended wilāyah is nearness through love and friendship, which also brings expectations of help and a spiritual blending. It does not mean merely a pact of mutual assistance.

The commentary rejects an exegete’s attempt to confine the verse to alliances and covenants. The reported occasions of revelation are mutually contradictory, do not account for Christians, and are generally weak attempts to apply historical events to verses. Even if accepted as historical applications, they cannot restrict the unrestricted wording of the Qur’an; otherwise its verses would expire with the events in which they were revealed. The verse itself is therefore an authority in its general sense.

Its wording supports friendship and affection, not covenants: “they are friends of each other” denotes love, unity, and religious affinity, not a treaty among Jews or among Christians; and “whoever amongst you takes them for a friend, then surely he is one of them” is intelligible because love joins souls, perceptions, character, and conduct until lovers become like one person. Treating the clause as a prohibition of subsequent mutual-help pacts would be strained and would require unstated conditions. The Qur’an had already allowed the Prophet to make pacts and truces, and when it prohibits something previously lawful it normally indicates that change.

Thus the verse forbids love and affection because they produce reciprocal moral influence: Muslims affected by un-Islamic conduct would depart from the religious path founded on following truth for the path of unbelief, founded on low desire and worship of Satan. The verse calls them Jews and Christians rather than People of the Book because the latter designation suggests a nearness that can invite the affection being prohibited. Their having been given a Book becomes a greater condemnation when they mock the true religion.

“they are friends of each other” means that, despite their internal discord, Jews and Christians are united by mutual attraction, the pursuit of low desires, rejection of truth, and opposition to the Prophet and Muslims; they therefore form one force against Muslims. The clause both explains why believers must not seek their affection and may also mean that a group befriended for support against another will not help against its own people.

Whoever befriends them is counted by revelation as one of them, even if outwardly a believer. This indicates that faith has degrees and can be blemished or pure; such blemish is the disease of the heart. The person is no longer travelling the path of divine guidance but their path, and is unjust like them; Allah does not guide the unjust. The verse establishes this fundamental reality, but does not itself specify all its subsidiary legal consequences; those must be sought in the sunnah and examined by fiqh.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan takes this verse as consequent upon “surely Allah does not guide the unjust people.” Since those people lack divine guidance, they err by hastening “in” the Jews and Christians—not merely towards them—thereby occupying their place in error. Their claim that they fear a calamity is a contrived excuse to escape the Prophet’s and believers’ blame; their real motive is friendship with and love for God’s enemies.

Their hypocrisy lies in displaying a motive different from what they conceal, not in being unbelievers who merely pretend to believe. The commentary rejects the interpretation, based on reported occasions of revelation, that they were technical hypocrites such as ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy, maintaining alliances with both sides as a prudent safeguard for personal advantage. Such precaution would not explain why victory or a divine act should make them regret, nor why their deeds should be forfeited and they should become losers. Their condemnation could in principle be explained by disobeying the prohibition or distrusting God’s promise of victory, but the verse’s wording does not support that explanation.

In divine speech, ʿasā, “may be,” expresses an expectation related to the listener or the situation; here its connection with the preceding assertion makes the promised event certain. The reference to “the victory,” set beside an unspecified “thing from Himself,” probably makes victory generic rather than a particular conquest such as Mecca. Although Qur’anic usage often refers by this word to the conquest of Mecca, it can also denote a judgement at which later faith no longer profits disbelievers. Faith or repentance is unprofitable either when this world passes into the next and free choice ends, or when a heart has become so hardened that return to God is no longer possible.

If the victory is understood as Islam’s victory over unbelief and a clear judgement between the Messenger and his people, the verse is an apocalyptic Qur’anic text concerning future events for this ummah. By contrast, interpreting it as a particular military conquest leaves the regret and the following statement of believers obscure.

Their regret arises from what they hid: probably their love for Jews and Christians and their haste to serve what those enemies of Islam sought—to extinguish God’s light and gain worldly objects of desire free from religious restraint. When God grants victory to truth, these concealed aims and their efforts will fail, exposing their falsehood and pretence.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan notes that yaqūlu, “will say,” is also recited yaqūla. The latter is preferable because it joins the believers’ speech to the diseased-hearted people’s regret: while they regret what they concealed, believers rebuke them for loving and hastening among Jews and Christians. Although the pronouns could be assigned in more than one way, the context indicates that “Are these they” refers to the Jews and Christians, while “with you” addresses those whose hearts are diseased. The believers then ask the weak in faith whether these are the people who swore most forcefully that they stood with them, and why they do not now help them. “Their deeds shall go for nothing” answers the implied question about the result of loving them: their deeds are forfeited and they are losers.

The commentary explains that calling a heart diseased implies that it can also be healthy. In Qur’anic usage, disease of the heart is suspicion and doubt about God and His signs that pollutes faith, removes reliance on the signs, and mingles faith with polytheism. It produces conditions and actions akin to unbelief and rejection of divine communications. A sound heart, by contrast, remains upon the straight nature and right path, sincerely affirms divine unity, relies on God, and discards objects of low desire.

Those “in whose hearts is a disease” are therefore not identical with hypocrites in the strict sense. The Qur’an frequently distinguishes “the hypocrites” from “those in whose hearts is a disease.” Strict hypocrites profess belief verbally while their hearts do not believe at all; complete unbelief is the heart’s death, not its disease. The diseased-hearted are persons of weak faith, overwhelmed by doubt and readily turned by every loud voice, unable to remain firm in religious belief. They may sometimes be called hypocrites analytically, since both groups lack true inward faith, but the phrase itself does not mean people who conceal disbelief while feigning belief for worldly gain.

The commentary reads the description in the chapter of “The Cow” as portraying a progression: people initially claim belief while remaining doubtful, then their disease increases until they reject and mock the truth and perish as unbelievers. Like bodily illness, heart-disease becomes deep-rooted and fatal through disobedience. Its cure is repentance and return to God: faith, good thought, and good deed. This entails steadfast adherence to belief, holding fast to Allah, the Book and the Sunnah, and sincerity in religion.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan observes that al-irtidād literally means turning back, while Muslim terminology uses it for apostasy: a convert who apostatizes is called murtadd millī, and one born Muslim who does so murtadd fitrī. Yet the context shows that the verse is not detached from the preceding verses and does not refer only to apostasy in this technical sense. It reminds believers that God does not need their belief and will bring a community that remains faithful to His religion.

Here, turning back from religion includes befriending Jews and Christians in preference to believers. Such friendship gives the heart an attachment incompatible with love of God; it makes one lowly before unbelievers and proud before believers, seeks honour from God’s enemies rather than from God, and brings laxity in jihād and unwillingness to bear hardship or sever social connections for God’s cause. In this literal and analytical sense it is irtidād, for the preceding verse has said that whoever befriends them is one of them. God’s religion has no need of people whose religion is polluted by love of His enemies, who sell it for worldly advantage and transient honour, and whose community contains diseased hearts.

The verse therefore foretells a future upheaval: if weak believers prefer love of others to God’s love, seek honour with His enemies, slacken in His way, and fear their reproach, God will soon bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, who are gentle with believers, mighty against unbelievers, strive in His way, and do not fear any censurer. The promised “people” are a community, not isolated individuals appearing in every age. God’s bringing them is not creation, since He creates everything; it means that He will arouse them to aid the religion, honour them through reciprocal love, and help them act with these qualities. Their aid to religion is thus God’s aid through them, whether the promise is fulfilled soon or later.

The commentary insists that the unrestricted divine attributes must not be weakened by unstated qualifications. Unlike human speech, which is affected by limited knowledge, analogy, exaggeration, and neglect of exceptions, God’s speech is decisive and not a jest. Thus, when God says that He loves these people, He does not dislike them in any respect; and when He calls them lowly before believers, this lowliness holds in every circumstance in relation to their belief. An attribute may be truly ascribed to a whole community although it is realized in a select group within it, where the relation between part and whole justifies the attribution; this is not imprecision.

Their love of God is unconditional preference for Him over wealth, honour, family, and all else. They love none of God’s enemies; any love they have is for His friends because of Him. God’s love for them shows that they are free from every injustice and spiritual impurity, whether unbelief or sin, either through divine protection or divine forgiveness following repentance. Since God loves no evil, the removal of evils entails the corresponding virtues. They are consequently true believers whose faith is not mixed with injustice, are protected from straying, follow the Messenger, and submit wholly to him. Following the Messenger and being loved by God are inseparable; through it they acquire piety, justice, magnanimity, patience, trust in God, repentance, purity, and other virtues. Such people are the heirs of the earth and have the good end of the abode.

Their being “lowly before the believers” means gentleness toward them for God’s sake, while being “mighty against the unbelievers” means disregarding the false honour displayed by unbelievers. Fighting in Allah’s way is singled out because God raises this community to help His religion. “They shall not fear the censure of any censurer” apparently qualifies all the preceding qualities, not striving alone: censurers may warn of the loss and hardship of jihād, and may similarly reproach believers for forsaking the worldly attractions and apparent power of unbelievers. The true believers do not fear this. The verse thus contains a prophecy of undesirable unseen events to come.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that reads (5:55-56) together with the surrounding prohibitions on taking Jews, Christians, and unbelievers as guardians, and consequently takes wilāyah here to mean mutual help. On that reading, God, the Messenger, and the sincere believers are the believers’ helpers, while “while they bow” is made metaphorical: either they submit completely to God or give charity despite poverty. The commentary argues that this interpretation fails both contextually and linguistically.

The chapter’s verses were not necessarily revealed at one time merely because they stand together; some were certainly revealed earlier, as their meanings and reported occasions of revelation show. Nor do the surrounding passages have one purpose. The preceding verses forbid friendship with Jews and Christians and shame hypocrites who seek their interests, whereas the following verses prohibit taking mockers of religion as guardians and command an address exposing their transgression. Further, the language that Jews and Christians “are friends of each other” and that whoever befriends them “is one of them” concerns wilāyah of love, which produces an inward affinity and reciprocal influence capable of joining two communities in character and activity; it does not fit a mere alliance of assistance.

More decisively, the Messenger cannot properly be described as the believers’ helper in the sense intended by those exegetes. Qur’anic help concerns religion: religion may be ascribed to God, who instituted its sharīʾah, so that prophets and believers are summoned to help God’s religion; it may be ascribed to the Messenger, who conveyed it, so that believers help him; and believers may be helped by God because they follow the religion. But religion cannot be ascribed primarily to believers while the Messenger is made their helper, since he has the foremost share in every religious dignity. The Qur’an nowhere calls the Messenger a helper of the believers. Therefore, when it calls him their waliyy, it signifies Guardianship and authority, or love and affection, as in The Prophet has a greater claim on the believers than they have on themselves, … (33:6), not assistance. The promise that Allah’s party will triumph does not determine the meaning as help, since triumph may arise through authority, love, or help alike.

The commentary maintains that the many traditions reporting that the verses were revealed when ʿAlī gave his ring in charity while praying establish that the verses concern him and are not a general declaration merely of believers’ friendship with one another. To disregard such numerous accumulated reports of the occasion of revelation would undermine reliance on reported occasions throughout Qur’anic exegesis. Opponents object that the reports conflict with the supposed context of help, improperly use plurals for one person, and call the gift of a ring zakāt. Al-Mizan considers none of these objections sound.

First, the surrounding verses do not establish the alleged context of help, and even if they did, this verse would not accord with it. Second, Arabic rejects using a plural merely to mean one particular singular entity, but it commonly states a general proposition in the plural so that it applies to every qualified instance, even where only one such instance exists at the time. The Qur’an frequently employs plurals when an occasion concerns one person, including passages concerning Ḥāṭib b. Abī Baltaʾah, ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy b. Salūl, and a single questioner or spender. The objectors themselves accept that the plural in (they say), “We fear lest a calamity should befall us;” … (5:52) refers to Ibn Ubayy. The plural here can encompass ʿAlī together with those who share or approve the relevant quality, and indicates that such religious dignities depend on precedence in sincerity and deeds rather than an arbitrary exclusion of all others. The early transmitters, being Arabic-speaking Companions and their disciples, did not regard this usage as linguistically objectionable.

Third, zakāt in its literal Qur’anic usage includes general alms and spending for God’s sake, not only the later technical obligation of wealth-zakāt. Its use in connection with earlier prophets and in Meccan passages revealed before the later legal form of zakāt was legislated shows this broader sense. The verse commanding the taking of alms likewise presents zakāt as charity that cleanses and purifies. Thus a ring given as alms may be called zakāt. There is consequently no need to make rukūʾ metaphorical: it is the bodily posture of bowing, especially the prescribed posture of prayer, though it can at times allude symbolically to humility or need. In this verse, “while they bow” qualifies the subject implicit in “pay,” specifying the manner of their giving.

Al-Mizan explains wilāyah from the basic idea of nearness: al-Walāʾ and al-Tawālī denote a position in which nothing extraneous intervenes between things, and are extended from physical proximity to affinity, friendship, help, belief, and management of affairs. Such nearness in non-material affairs gives the waliyy a right of management over the mawlā that others do not possess except through him. Hence an heir administers a deceased person’s estate, a guardian manages a minor’s property, a helper manages the assisted person’s affairs in strengthening his defence, and a ruler or judge has authority within his jurisdiction. Across its uses, wilāyah signifies a proximity that entails authority to manage and plan.

In “Only Allah is your Guardian and His Messenger and those who believe,” the same singular term, “your Guardian,” governs God, the Messenger, and the believers; their wilāyah must therefore have one meaning. The conclusion that those who take them as guardians belong to Allah’s triumphant party further shows that the Messenger’s and believers’ guardianship grows out of Allah’s guardianship. Allah possesses authority over creation, by which He disposes of all creatures’ affairs, and authority over legislation, by which He legislates, guides, advises, and assists believers in their religious affairs. The Prophet’s particular wilāyah is the latter: he legislates, calls, trains the ummah, rules, judges, and decides its affairs. His unconditional obedience is incumbent because obedience to him is obedience to God; his precedence over believers is thus derived from God’s legislative authority, not from a role as their helper.

The verse gives this same wilāyah, directly belonging to God and indirectly belonging, by His permission, to the Messenger and those believers described by prayer, charity, and bowing. Had the word borne one meaning for God and another for the believers, the wording would have repeated it to prevent confusion, as the Qur’an repeats a word when its two applications differ. The singular “your Guardian” with the plural “those who believe” likewise indicates one unified guardianship, directly Allah’s and derivatively the Messenger’s and believers’. “Only” confines this wilāyah to those named, and may also negate it for everyone else.

The final verse means that whoever takes God, His Messenger, and these believing guardians shall be triumphant because he belongs to Allah’s party, and Allah’s party is triumphant. It substitutes this major premise for the explicit conclusion in order to state the reason for the result. al-Falāḥ is victory and attainment of what is sought. The promised success is unrestricted: felicity, adherence to truth, and the defeat of unhappiness and falsehood in this world and the hereafter—here through a good life in a virtuous, pious society of God’s friends, free from Satan’s friends, and there through nearness to the Lord of the worlds.

verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that treating religion as mockery, play, or a joke means refusing to treat it seriously or as directed to a sound purpose, thereby portraying it as unreal and fit only for false motives. Had such people recognized religion as true, and respected its Legislator, its caller, and its believers, they would not have treated it in this way.

The description of those forbidden as friends supplies the reason for the prohibition. Friendship, or walāyah, entails spiritual association and involvement in one’s personal and social affairs; a waliyy (friend) does not mock what his friend holds more precious than himself. Believers must therefore not admit such people into their spiritual or worldly affairs.

The address, “you who believe,” corresponds to “those who take your religion for a mockery and a joke,” while “your religion” emphasizes the believers’ close bond with Islam and warns them against their enemies’ manipulation. “And fear God if you are believers” reinforces the prohibition: genuine faith prevents satisfaction with the mockery of what one believes and requires fearing God by not taking such hostile people as friends. It may alternatively allude to the earlier warning that whoever takes them as a friend is one of them, but the first meaning is more apparent.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse confirms that the unbelievers mocked the believers’ religion. The call to prayer is the adhān, and the pronoun in “they take it” may refer either to the prayer or to the act of calling to it.

Their mockery of the prayer or adhān arises from their lack of understanding: they cannot grasp the spiritual realities in worship, including servitude to God, nearness to Him, and the convergence of human happiness in this world and the hereafter.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as asking the People of the Book whether they resent the believers for anything except their faith in God and in revelation, while most of the People of the Book are transgressors. The question has the force of censuring those who find fault with a virtue while they themselves possess the contrary vice. Another possible reading is that their own transgression is the reason for their hostility.

“What has been revealed before” means revelation sent to both Muslims and the People of the Book. It is not expressly ascribed to the latter because they failed to fulfil their covenant with God and to follow their books’ commandments, as though those books had not been sent to them and they were unfit to receive them. The believers do not differentiate among revealed books or God’s messengers; this implicitly reproaches the People of the Book for believing in some messengers and rejecting others.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse meets those who mock religion on their own terms in order to complete the proof against them. If they despise believers for faith in God and His revealed books, then, were such faith an evil—which it never is—they ought more properly to despise themselves for divine curse and wrath, transmutation into apes and swine, and service of Satan. Since they do not hate themselves despite these grounds for hatred, they have no basis for hating believers who remain firm in faith.

Al-mathūbah, literally “reward,” here means recompense or retribution, probably as an expression for the final, inseparable outcome. Its being “near Allah” shows its permanence and unchangeability as something divinely decreed. The verse reverses the expected formulation: rather than directly saying that curse, transmutation, and Satan’s worship are worse than belief, it substitutes the persons bearing those traits for the traits themselves and says that they are worse in place and further astray.

The commentary also reports two readings of “this.” It may refer to the community of believers, making the sense straightforward: the addressed people themselves are worse than the believers whom they fault. Or it may refer to their very fault-finding and hatred: what they have incurred of curse and transmutation is a worse retribution than that conduct.
verses.61: Al-Mizan says that the verse exposes their concealed hypocrisy. They profess faith when they meet the believers, but enter with disbelief and depart with the same disbelief; their condition never changes, and their treachery and perfidy remain hidden only from people, not from God. The emphatic pronoun indicates that disbelief is firmly rooted in their hearts. A reported alternative takes the clause to mean that they move from one state of disbelief to another.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan takes “sin” here to mean their reckless intrusion into the religious verses revealed to believers and their sinful speech about religious knowledge, speech that leads to disbelief and transgression. Sin, exceeding the limits, and consuming unlawful gain thus cover transgression in word and deed: verbal wrongdoing; aggression against other believers; and wrongdoing against themselves, such as consuming interest, bribes, and similar unlawful gains.

The verses condemn these acts and strongly rebuke the learned men and doctors of law for failing, despite their knowledge of their gravity, to forbid sinful speech and unlawful consumption. The omission of “exceeding the limits” in the second verse indicates that verbal sin itself is exceeding the divine limits, corresponding to practical transgression, of which consuming unlawful things is an example. The passage therefore exposes one fundamental fault of speech and another of action.
