verses.64:
Al-Mizan notes that the Jews rejected the abrogation of religious laws and al-badā’ in creation, but holds that the saying, “The hand of Allah is tied up,” is not referring to those doctrines, because its reply concerns God’s expenditure. It is more likely that, after hearing Qur’anic invitations to lend God a goodly loan, they uttered it mockingly, as though God could not obtain what He needed to propagate His religion and revive His mission. The suggestions that it mocked the poverty of believers or arose from their own famine do not fit the context: the Muslims then enjoyed prosperity, and the verses concern their hostility and treachery toward Muslims. The commentary adds that ascribing incapacity to God was not alien to aspects of their beliefs or to depictions in the present Torah, which describe matters in which God’s will was allegedly obstructed.

“Their hands shall be shackled and they shall be cursed” is primarily an invocation against them corresponding to their impious attribution to God. Their shackling manifests the divine curse, since God curses through punishment in this world or the next; the curse is therefore punishment equal to, or more comprehensive than, the shackling. The alternative view that the clause merely reports a punishment already inflicted is less understandable.

“Both His hands are spread out” refutes their claim by alluding to God’s complete and firmly established power, while “He expends as He pleases” explains that power in respect of expenditure. The dual expression intensifies the meaning of perfect power. Although “hand” originally denotes the bodily organ, when scripture applies it to God its meaning is determined by context: here, and in the creation of Adam, it denotes power and its perfection; elsewhere it may denote kingdom and authority, or simply presence.

The revelation’s increasing many of them in inordinacy and unbelief explains why such contemptuous speech is unsurprising from people long immersed in transgression and disbelief. Their oppression and envy were stirred when they saw a revealed Book, containing truth, elevated teaching, and complete guidance, given to a people formerly subject to their knowledge and book. Their pride in being the People of the Book and in their learning made them resent a Book that would overcome them in the very field of their boast.

The Qur’an is said to increase them in these qualities because their unjust and envious souls react to its truth by rising in transgression and disbelief. Such attribution of leading astray to God is not blameworthy when it is retribution for a person’s prior moral corruption, rather than an initial act without cause. Here it means deprivation of divine help: God does not bring them from their inordinacy and disbelief to submission and acceptance of the true call. Inordinacy is mentioned before disbelief because disbelief is among its effects.

The enmity and hatred placed among “them” refer particularly to the Jews, and to the discord and divisions among their sects and schools. Enmity apparently denotes hatred expressed in unjust action, while hatred may remain inward; together they include both. Their continuance until the Day of Resurrection indicates that their ummah will remain until the end of the world.

Their kindling of war means efforts against the divine religion and Muslims on account of faith in God and His signs; God’s decree is that these efforts will fail. It may also explain the preceding internal enmity: when they ignite war, God extinguishes it by reviving their divisions. The statement does not extend to wars they may wage for political motives or racial or national superiority rather than religion. Their striving is directed toward mischief in the land, but because God does not love mischief-makers, He does not leave them free to attain that aim. This explains how their hands are tied and how the curse takes effect: their repeated efforts to wage war against the Prophet and Muslims and to spread mischief will not succeed.
verses.65: Al-Mizan says that the discussion returns to the People of the Book generally and describes the blessings they forfeited in this world and the next. Their promised entry into gardens of bliss is conditioned on belief and taqwā. Here taqwā means abstaining from prohibitions and guarding against sins that bring divine wrath and the punishment of the Fire, especially associating partners with God and major sins threatened with the Fire. The evil deeds which God promises to cover are therefore minor misdeeds.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains that the Torah and Gospel here are the divine books revealed to Moses and Jesus, not the Old and New Testaments possessed by Jews and Christians, which have reportedly been extensively manipulated and altered. “That which was revealed to them from their Lord” apparently means the other scriptures and revelations sent through Israelite prophets, such as the Zabūr of David.

The commentary rejects the view that this latter phrase means the Qur’an. The Qur’an’s sharīʾah abrogated the laws of the Torah and Gospel, and the command to “keep up” those books means firmly preserving something upon its foundations, an expression unsuitable for abrogated laws as such. The Torah and Gospel could be kept up before their abrogation, and the Gospel had abrogated the Torah only in minor respects. Moreover, the Qur’an is not described as having been revealed to Jews and Christians. Keeping these books up meant diligently obeying their divine laws and affirming their teachings concerning genesis and return, rather than altering, concealing, or abandoning their truths.

Their eating “from above them and from beneath their feet” signifies an easy, comfortable life and unrestricted enjoyment of blessings from heaven and earth. The verse shows that human belief and good deeds affect the well-being of the created order insofar as it is connected with humankind: if people act rightly, the world’s system remains conducive to their happy life by repelling misfortune and providing abundant blessings; corruption and affliction, conversely, arise through human deeds.

The moderate party among them is one that follows the middle course in religious affairs and submits to God’s commands. The passage begins afresh to clarify that the transgression, disbelief, divine wrath, and curse attributed to them characterize their majority, not every individual. By recognizing the moderate group, the divine speech gives each person his due and acknowledges the revival of truth even when it is slight.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse plainly commands the Messenger, in the form of a threat, to convey a revealed matter and promises him protection from the people. Although it stands among verses concerning the People of the Book, it is wholly disconnected from their context and was revealed as an independent verse. If it concerned the immediately surrounding address to the Jews and Christians, its severe warning and the promise of protection would be inexplicable: they did not then possess power sufficient to endanger the Prophet or the religion, and he had already conveyed to them, as well as to the more violent Quraysh and Arabian idolaters, teachings far harsher and more offensive than this. By the time this Medinan chapter was revealed, Jewish power had been broken, and Jews and Christians had entered the Islamic domain through treaties and the payment of jizyah.

The verse indicates that the Prophet had delayed announcing an exceptionally consequential command until suitable circumstances arose. Yet his fear was not fear of losing his life in God’s cause; his life and the Qur’anic description of messengers disprove that. Nor could he have feared that his death would terminate the mission, since the matter belongs to God, who could revive His mission by whatever means He willed. Rather, he may have feared that the announcement would lead people to accuse him of a selfish purpose, thereby causing an irreparable injury to the effectiveness of the whole conveyance. His postponement was thus an exercise of discretion concerning the success of the delivery, not personal cowardice. This also rules out the view that the verse was revealed in the earliest days of prophethood, when interpreting the protection as protection against being killed, or against the failure of tablīgh, would be untenable.

The commentary rejects interpreting “what has been revealed to you from your Lord” as the entire religion or its basic message. Such a reading would make the statement, “and if you do it not, then you have not delivered His message,” an empty tautology: if he did not convey the religion, then he did not convey the religion. The kind of rhetorical expression illustrated by Abu al-Najm’s saying, “I’m Abu al-Najm, and my poem is poem,” works where a particular and a general, or a restricted and unrestricted thing, are related in a meaningful way; it cannot make this interpretation coherent, especially if the early basic message was a single, unaltered body of religious knowledge.

The revealed matter must therefore have been a particular command, while “His message,” whether read in the singular or, in another reading, the plural, denotes the totality of divine messages brought by the Messenger. The meaning is that failure to convey this particular command would amount to failure to convey the religion as a whole. This is not because every religious rule is equally central, but because this command occupied a position in the religious structure comparable to the soul in a body: without it, what remained would be lifeless. It was an order by which religion would be completed and firmly established. The threat is consequently not doubt that the Prophet would obey—God knows where He places His message—but an emphatic disclosure to him and others of the command’s decisive importance and of his lack of authority to defer it further.

The subsequent clauses show that people opposed, or were expected to oppose, this particular order with extreme efforts to nullify the mission. Thus the matter cannot be any ordinary revealed command. The Prophet understood the people’s disposition and delayed the announcement in hope of a peaceful setting in which it would succeed, but God commanded him to announce it promptly and guaranteed that their schemes would not prevail. Such a danger is more intelligible after the hijrah, when Islam had become established and the Muslim society included sincere believers, powerful hypocrites, and those with diseased hearts. Some treated the Prophet as kings are treated and regarded the sharīʾah as merely human political law. A command that appeared to give the Prophet a personal advantage could then lead them to imagine that he was pursuing kingship under the guise of prophethood; such a misconception could corrupt religion beyond repair.

The command in question must therefore have seemed to grant the Prophet a desired privilege and to deprive others of something they wished to enjoy. Rules specially concerning him, which did not affect ordinary Muslims, would not in themselves have created this danger. His conduct in preferring Muslims to himself in the distribution of wealth also excludes imputing personal desire to him in such matters. The commentary concludes that this analysis supports traditions transmitted by both sects: the verse concerned the guardianship of ʿAlī; the Prophet delayed declaring it because people might accuse him of favouring his cousin; and at Ghadīr Khumm he announced, “He whose mawlā (Guardian) am I, this ʿAlī is his mawlā.”

Al-Mizan further argues that guardianship over the affairs of the ummah is indispensable to religion. Islam provides fundamental knowledge, ethical principles, and practical rules for every aspect of individual and collective human life, so it cannot reasonably be thought not to require a guardian to preserve and administer it. The Prophet appointed deputies whenever he left Medina, appointed ʿAlī in his place for the expedition of Tabūk, installed governors in Muslim towns, and appointed commanders for expeditions. The need for such governance is still more pressing after his death than during his life.

The address, “O Messenger,” itself suits the obligation to convey, because messengership consists in delivering what one has been entrusted with. The command is left unspecified, which indicates its greatness and makes clear that it came entirely from God: the Messenger had neither a hand in its formulation nor discretion to conceal or postpone it. Its vagueness also gave him a justification before the people for announcing it, while requiring him to announce it in his own words.

The protection promised in “and Allah will protect you from the people” is not the general prophetic ‘iṣmah described by al-Rāghib, although that description of ‘iṣmah is accepted in its proper place. Here ya’ṣim denotes protection from the people’s evil directed against the Prophet’s person, the aims of his Call, or the success of his religious work. Its original sense is holding fast, and its sense of protection is allusive, since protection entails holding fast. The statement is unrestricted as to the means of harm—physical attack, abusive speech, slander, treachery, deception, or disruption of affairs—but its context confines it to the evil capable of destroying the religious structure he had raised.

“The people” is a broad expression, probably referring here to the undifferentiated multitude, including believers, hypocrites, and those whose hearts were diseased. Correspondingly, “the unbelieving people” may denote people within that public whose hearts had acquired the characteristic of disbelief, rather than persons publicly identified as unbelievers. Their disbelief is apparently rejection of this particular divine command, not rejection of the two testimonies. To take it as total disbelief would depend on the already rejected assumption that the command concerned the sum of all revelation.

God’s statement that He will not guide them does not mean that He will not guide them to faith, for this would contradict the purpose of the divine Call and the manifest fact that God guides many unbelievers. It means that He will not guide them to the success of their treachery and machinations: He will not allow the ordinary causes at their disposal to serve their aim of extinguishing the truth and negating the revealed command. Their powers come from God and cannot overcome Him. They may obtain a temporary result, but their plotting ultimately turns back upon them, while truth remains and falsehood passes away.

Thus the promise of protection specifies that the people will not be permitted to harm the Prophet before he delivers and announces this command to the ummah. They cannot kill him before that delivery, overturn his affairs, produce accusations that drive believers from the religion, or devise a means of annihilating the sharīʾah. God will make the word of truth victorious and establish religion as He wills. The promise does not, however, grant the Prophet immunity from every affliction: Qur’an, ḥadīth, and accepted history show that he suffered many injuries from believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, as expressed in the well-known ḥadīth, “No prophet was ever harmed like I have been.”
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains “you have no ground to stand upon” as an image of one who cannot undertake a heavy task without firm support. Just as bodily exertion requires a stable foothold, keeping God’s religion requires a spiritual foundation: patience, firmness, high resolve, true piety, and abstention from what is forbidden. Religion is a weighty burden, which cannot be maintained merely by wishing to do so.

The People of the Book lack the support needed to uphold the Torah, the Gospel, and their Lord’s revelations because they turn arrogantly from worship and exceed God’s limits. That support is acquired through piety, repeated repentance, holding fast to God’s cord, and reliance on His pillar. Keeping religion also depends on God’s guidance, granted to one who continually returns to Him and does not break this bond.

The commentary connects failure to uphold religion with division, rivalry, envy, and transgression of the middle course. Returning to God, guarding one’s duty, and preserving unity are the means of maintaining the natural religion; sectarian division severs the connection to God. The Jews and Christians are said to have consequently fallen into enduring division, enmity, and hatred, and Muslims are warned not to follow their course. The revelation’s increasing many of them in inordinacy and unbelief has been explained elsewhere; the final prohibition against grief consoles the Prophet over the unbelievers.
verses.69: Al-Mizan takes al-ṣābiūn, though nominative, as coordinated with “those who believe,” and holds that the verse disproves the grammatical rule forbidding such coordination before the predicate of inna is stated. Its chief point is that names such as believers, Jews, Sabaeans, and Christians do not determine ultimate happiness. Before God, only belief in Allah and the Last Day together with good deeds brings freedom from fear and grief.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan presents the conduct of the Children of Israel as proof that their sins severed their connection with God, leaving them unable to uphold or rely on His Books. It may also confirm that religious titles do not secure true felicity: if they did, they would have restrained them from rejecting and killing prophets. The verses may, in turn, elaborate both this point and the preceding statement that the People of the Book have no ground to stand upon.

Whenever a messenger brought what their souls disliked, they arrogantly opposed him: they called some messengers liars and killed others. The fronting of “some” emphasizes these objects and completes the clause concerning every messenger who came to them. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains the shift from past to future tense as showing an established and continuing habit—having called prophets liars and killed them, they would do so again—and perhaps also as serving the verse’s rhyme.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains their blindness as failure to perceive truth and distinguish good from evil, and their deafness as refusal to hear admonition. Their delusion that no affliction would befall them apparently arose from conceit over Jewish descent and their supposed status as God’s sons and beloveds. Imagining themselves immune from trial, they became unable to hear their prophets or see the truth; thus titles and communal prestige brought them no benefit and led them to reject and kill prophets.

God’s merciful turning to them means that He accepted their repentance after they had been removed from His mercy and care. They were thereby released from the delusion, recognized themselves as servants whose only distinction is piety, and again saw truth and heard prophetic counsel. Yet many again became blind and deaf.

The first attribution of blindness and deafness to the whole group uses the majority’s quality for the whole, while indicating that the affliction initially spread throughout it. The later attribution to many shows that God’s mercy was effective: a minority repented and remained immune when the majority relapsed. God’s being well seeing of what they do means that no outward honor or appearance can conceal their realities from Him.
verses.72: Al-Mizan holds that all Christians fall under the verse’s verdict of disbelief, because every Christian account of Christ’s divinity exceeds proper bounds: some describe his person as branching from the Lord’s, others say the Lord transformed into Christ, and others posit incarnation. Calling him “the Messiah, son of Mary” proves—or at least indicates—that the error lies in deifying a man born of a woman, both created from dust. The Messiah’s quoted words, “Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord,” identify him as a created servant needing the Lord who manages his affairs. His warning that associating others with God bars the Garden, leads to the Fire, and leaves the unjust without helpers also refutes atonement: the claim that Christ’s crucifixion redeemed Christians cannot grant advance forgiveness, exemption from divine law, guaranteed entry to the Garden, or immunity from the Fire.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains “Allah is the third of the three” as the claim that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are each God, while God is at once three and one. The proposed analogy of one person described as Zayd, son of ʿAmr, and man fails: if the plurality is real, the persons must really be plural; if the person is really one, the plurality is only conceptual. Real singularity and real plurality cannot coexist in one thing. The commentary notes that some Christian missionaries reportedly acknowledge that the Trinity is inherited from early Church fathers and cannot be rationally demonstrated, while every claim requires proof.

“And there is no god but one God” refutes this doctrine by affirming a unity from which no plurality can arise. God is one in His Person, without division or multiplicity in reality, imagination, reason, names, or attributes. His unity is not numerical unity, since numerical oneness and the plurality associated with it are themselves created effects. The emphatic Qur’anic wording negates every god and affirms the species of an absolutely one God; merely saying “the One God” would not answer those who call Him one while maintaining three real Persons.

The threatened painful chastisement apparently belongs to the hereafter. Al-Mizan holds that most ordinary Christians accept the verbal formula of the Trinity without understanding its meaning and are not thereby actual trinitarians. Real disbelief that rejects divine unity and communications applies only to some, especially those who knowingly uphold the doctrine; this may explain why the threat concerns “those among them who disbelieve.” Alternatively, it may indicate Christians who did not believe in the Trinity and regarded Jesus only as God’s servant and messenger, as history reportedly records of Ethiopian Christians. The commentary rejects as unsupported the claim that “those among them who disbelieve” merely replaces a pronoun, or means simply “those who disbelieve, namely these.”
verses.74: Al-Mizan says that the verse exhorts them to repent and seek Allah’s forgiveness by recalling that He is Forgiving and Merciful. The interrogative may alternatively be admonitory or negative, meaning that they do not turn to God or ask His forgiveness.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan refutes the claims that Allah is the Messiah or the third of three by showing that the Messiah is like earlier messengers who passed away: a mortal human being sent by God for mankind’s guidance, not a lord. Mary was a truthful woman who affirmed divine signs and was likewise mortal. Their eating food proves their need, and need is the first sign of transience and createdness. Jesus, born of a transient mother, and Mary were dependent servants who worshipped God, not lords.

The commentary says that the Gospels themselves attest Mary’s belief and worship, Jesus’ human birth and mission as a messenger, and the fact that both ate food; these facts establish his servitude and messengership. The verse may also rebut those who held Mary to be divine beside Jesus, as suggested by (5:116); alternatively, taking Mary as a god may mean submitting to her as people submit to religious authorities in a manner reason and sharīʿah do not approve.

The passing away of preceding messengers reinforces Jesus’ humanity and mortality. The address to the Prophet—“See how We make the signs clear to them, then behold, how they are turned away”—expresses wonder at their refusal to grasp such clear proof against Christ’s divinity.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that people ordinarily worship a lord in order to repel harm and obtain benefit. Since nothing besides God owns or controls harm or profit, and all things are owned and empowered by Him, no creature can be joined with Him in worship. God alone hears and answers His servants and knows their needs; others possess only what He gives them and can do only what He enables them to do.

This proof differs from the preceding proof concerning the Messiah and Mary. That proof establishes that, as mortal, needy, obedient servants, they cannot be lords; this one establishes that the Messiah, being owned by God and unable to control harm or benefit, cannot be worshipped. The argument applies to every object of worship other than God, including insensate things. The use of mā, ordinarily for non-rational beings, therefore does not exclude the Messiah, whose rationality has no bearing on the proof; even perceptive creatures do not possess their perception or being independently.

Harm precedes profit because present affliction and the loss of blessings more readily drive human nature to seek refuge in a lord than does the acquisition of profit. Thus the verse contains two proofs for exclusive worship: the worshipped must control harm and benefit, which only God does; and the worshipped must hear the distressed and know his true need, which only God does.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan understands the command as forbidding the People of the Book, especially Christians, from excess in religion by associating partners with the one God. Jews and Christians placed prophets, scholars, and monks in a position of lordship and submitted to them in a manner reserved for God. The Qur’anic qualification that their excess is “without truth” intensifies the prohibition, since excess can never be true.

The commentary apparently takes the Jews’ calling Ezra God’s son as an honorific in recognition of his services, like the Christians’ use of “father” for religious authorities; Ezra is thus included among their doctors of law and monks. Reason does not reject using “father” or “son” for God if stripped of material implications—father meaning the One who controls creation and upbringing—but the sharīʿah strictly forbids such self-invented divine names, requiring the names God has approved because unauthorized titles lead to corruption.

Those whose desires must not be followed are apparently the leaders who clung to their own opinions, went astray, and led many astray; their error is compounded by both their own deviation and their misleading of others. The context further identifies them as earlier idol-worshippers, not merely the forefathers of the People of the Book. The commentary holds that the beliefs in divine fatherhood and sonship entered the People of the Book from such earlier idolatry, later being given a religious dress by Christian leaders: the name remained monotheistic while its meaning became idolatrous.
verses.78: Al-Mizan says that David and Jesus, son of Mary, cursed the disbelievers among the Children of Israel because they disobeyed and repeatedly exceeded the limits. Their failure to forbid one another’s hateful deeds explains this continuing transgression.
verses.79: Al-Mizan says that David and Jesus, son of Mary, cursed the disbelievers among the Children of Israel because they disobeyed and repeatedly exceeded the limits. Their failure to forbid one another’s hateful deeds explains this continuing transgression.
verses.80: Al-Mizan treats their friendship with disbelievers as visible proof that they had exceeded religion’s limits. Had they respected what they held sacred, they would have befriended believers in one God and avoided those hostile to that faith; friendship with an enemy means abandoning what one formerly regarded as sacred. Their souls’ sending evil ahead for them refers to this friendship arising from low desire, while the verse expresses its recompense in place of the act itself: God’s displeasure and abiding chastisement.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that if the People of the Book had believed in Allah, the Prophet Muḥammad, and his revelation—or in their own prophet, such as Moses, and the Torah—they would not have befriended the disbelievers, for Islam cuts worldly ties. Most of them are transgressors who refuse belief.

A proposed alternative makes both pronouns refer to the disbelievers: if those whom the People of the Book befriended had believed in Allah, Muḥammad, and the Qur’an, they would not have been taken as friends. The commentary finds no inherent difficulty in this reading, but judges that the concluding statement, “but most of them are transgressors,” does not fit it.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as a general principle describing non-Muslim communities’ dispositions toward Islam: Jews and polytheists are the most violent in enmity toward believers, while those who call themselves Christians are nearest in friendship and more ready to hear the truth. Their nearness is shown by Christians who recognized the revealed truth and believed. The distinctive point is not simply that some of them entered Islam, since Jews and many Arab polytheists also did, but that Christians are said to have accepted sincerely despite having alternatives—remaining on their religion under jizyah or fighting. Polytheists had no alternative except Islam or fighting, while Jews, though they had the same alternatives as Christians, persisted in pride, bigotry, covenant-breaking, and deception. The commentary says these respective characteristics continued after the Prophet, with many Christians accepting Islam and few Jews or polytheists doing so.

Their relative nearness is attributed to priests, monks and ascetics, and their lack of pride. Religious felicity requires knowledge of the true religion, removal of arrogance, bigotry, and prejudice that obstruct submission to truth, and a social environment where good actions are practised and become habitual. Knowledgeable teachers instruct people in religious truth, ascetics practically remind them of their Lord and of felicity in this world and the next, and humility enables acceptance of what is recognized as true. Thus Christians are described as more prepared to accept the call: their scholars teach verbally, their ascetics teach by practice, and pride does not prevent submission. Jews had scholars but their pride and stubbornness obstructed them; polytheists lacked religious scholars and ascetics and were also arrogant.
verses.83: Al-Mizan explains that their eyes overflow with abundant tears because of the truth they recognize. In the wording, min in min al-damʿ denotes the beginning, mimmā ʿarafū indicates emergence, and mina ’l-ḥaqq gives the explanation.
verses.84: Al-Mizan explains “cause us to enter” as placing them with and including them among the good people, which accounts for its use with maʿ. Their declaration of faith and desire to join the good confirm that Christians are nearest in friendship to believers: they possess beneficial knowledge and good action, surrender to truth, and are prepared for it by priests, monks, and lack of pride.
verses.85: Al-Mizan says that the first verse gives the believers’ reward—everlasting gardens beneath which rivers flow—as the recompense for what they said and for doing good; the second gives the opposing disbelievers who reject God’s signs their recompense as companions of the Flame. Together, the two verses deal with all the groups.
verses.86: Al-Mizan says that the first verse gives the believers’ reward—everlasting gardens beneath which rivers flow—as the recompense for what they said and for doing good; the second gives the opposing disbelievers who reject God’s signs their recompense as companions of the Flame. Together, the two verses deal with all the groups.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains that ḥill, lawfulness, is metaphorically derived from untying a knot, while ḥurmah, unlawfulness, evokes its tying; these terms were already generally used in those senses before Islam.

The verse forbids believers to prohibit what God has made lawful, whether by legislating against God’s law, forbidding it to others, or abstaining from it and imposing that abstinence on oneself or others. Such conduct is a usurpation of God’s legislative authority and conflicts with belief in Him and submission to His commands. The description of these things as good further shows that self-denial opposes both divine law and the natural recognition that these lawful things are good and free of impurity. “Lawful” here includes permissible, commendable, and obligatory things.

“Do not exceed the limits” therefore refers, in its context, to this very act of self-imposed prohibition: revolting against obedience to God and transgressing His limits. It reinforces the preceding prohibition, and God does not love those who do so. The interpretations that take exceeding the limits to mean either immoderate indulgence in lawful enjoyments or crossing from lawful things into unlawful ones are sound themes elsewhere in the Qur’an, but they do not fit this verse and its context.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan holds that the conjunction “And” joins “eat” to the preceding prohibition against forbidding what God has made lawful. The verse thus repeats and emphasizes that command: “the lawful and good (things)” parallels the preceding reference to the good things God has made lawful, and “fear Allah in Whom you believe” corresponds to its address to believers.

Coming after the prohibition, “eat” conveys permission to use God’s good bounties without self-imposed restriction. Although it may refer broadly to usufruct and disposal, as “eating” commonly does, it may possibly be literal eating; on that reading, the verses would address believers who had forbidden themselves good food. The preceding verse would nevertheless remain comprehensive, covering both food and other lawful uses.

The preferred grammatical analysis makes “that God has given you” the object of “eat,” while “the lawful and good (things)” describes it, preserving the correspondence between the two verses. Other parses are possible. The phrase “lawful and good” is not a restrictive qualification implying that sustenance may itself include unlawful and bad things; rather, it explains the sustenance mentioned. Its purpose is to remove any excuse for avoiding what God has bestowed, since it is lawful and good.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains that al-laghw is an inconsequential act and that an oath, al-yamīn, is allusively connected with the right hand used in concluding agreements. Since “what is vain in your oaths” is set against “the making of deliberate oaths,” a vain oath is one uttered without serious intention or inward deliberation, such as habitual expressions, especially in trade, like “No, by God!” or “Certainly, by God!” It differs from a deliberate undertaking to do or not do something.

The sharīʿah also treats as vain an oath to commit an unlawful act or to omit an obligatory one, because the Supreme Legislator has rendered an oath concerning something without standing in the sharīʿah ineffectual. This additional rule comes through the sunnah, not from the apparent wording of the Qur’an. The deliberate oath for which one is accountable is consequently an oath endorsed by the sharīʿah, as the command to guard oaths confirms; an oath God has declared vain cannot be one that must be guarded.

Al-kaffārah is that which covers the evil of disobedience. The expiation in the verse concerns breaking a deliberate oath, not making it: otherwise there would be no sense in commanding people to guard their oaths. Thus accountability for deliberate oaths likewise concerns their breach, and “when you swear” means when you swear and then break the oath.

The expiation offers a choice among feeding ten poor persons from the average food given to one’s family, clothing them, or freeing a neck; the use of “or” means that these are alternatives, not cumulative requirements. Fasting three days applies only to one unable to obtain the means for any of those options. The verse contains further legal details belonging to jurisprudence.

The shift from singular demonstratives to plural pronouns probably reflects that God’s clarification reaches believers through the Prophet. God makes His commandments clear so that they may show gratitude by learning them and acting upon them.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains al-khamr as every fermented liquid that intoxicates and covers reason, al-maysir as gambling of every kind, al-anṣāb as venerated idols or stones upon which sacrifices were slaughtered, and al-azlām as the arrows used to divide a camel’s shares. Although al-azlām can also denote arrows used for oracle-seeking, its use in verse 3—where division of an animal’s meat by arrows is prohibited among unlawful foods—shows that it here means the gambling practice of dividing shares by arrows.

An objection holds that, since gambling already includes this kind of division by arrows, al-azlām must instead mean oracle-arrows, by which one drew a piece marked “Do,” “Don’t do,” or blank in order to decide an undertaking. That practice would be unlawful as a claim to know the future, and, on this interpretation, similar practices such as istikhārah by rosary would also be prohibited. The commentary replies that verse 3 establishes the relevant meaning as gambling. Even if the two verses were not connected, the intended meaning would depend on traditions; numerous traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt permit seeking divine guidance by rosary and the like when one is genuinely perplexed.

Istikhārah is not an attempt to know the unseen or to share in God’s governance. A person should first use thought and consult those able to distinguish right from wrong. If still unable to decide, he turns to God for help and uses istikhārah only to make a practical positive or negative choice and escape hesitation. It neither makes an act obligatory or unlawful nor discloses the hidden good or evil of its eventual outcome; that outcome may be good or evil, just as it may after one acts on one’s own judgment or advice. Correct ḥadīth through both sects report that the Prophet sought and commanded good omens, forbade belief in ill omens, and commanded reliance on God. Thus one may seek an omen from the Qur’an and proceed with reliance on God if its result is not good. Such seeking chiefly gives peace of mind, and exegetes are wholly mistaken to make the verse’s “arrows” oracle-arrows and thereby declare istikhārah unlawful.

The things listed are called al-Rijs, an abomination or defiling thing from which nature recoils, because they lack the elements of true human happiness. Even where intoxicants and gambling bring some profit, their sin dominates that profit without exception. They are attributed exclusively to Satan’s handiwork because Satan is humanity’s enemy, cut off from all good, whose action upon people consists in seducing, tempting, and casting ideas into their hearts. He has no authority over them beyond calling them, and those who answer his call follow error. Thus these practices are Satanic not necessarily because Satan physically produced them, but because their use ultimately arises from his whispering and invitation to error; error itself is called uncleanness.

Reports that Satan appeared to people, made liquor, or taught its manufacture are solitary reports and need not be accepted, although other diverse reports and the Qur’an lend some support to the possibility of Satanic and angelic appearances and of things and deeds taking forms. In any case, a report cannot alter a Qur’anic verse’s apparent meaning when that meaning is supported by other verses. Even a physical appearance or instruction from Satan would amount only to temptation, seduction, or imparting information, not to authority beyond the whispering described by the Qur’an.

“Shun it therefore that you may be successful” is an unambiguous prohibition, issued after the practices’ evil has been shown. The promise of success for shunning them intensifies the command and implies that those who do not refrain have no hope of success.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan states that the verse explains why intoxicants, gambling, sacrificial stones, and division by arrows are Satan’s handiwork and an abomination of it: Satan’s sole purpose is to create enmity and intense hatred and to turn people from the remembrance of God and from prayer. Enmity signifies transgression, disharmony, and unjust overstepping; hatred is the opposite of love and entails turning away; and desisting means obeying a prohibition.

The verse singles out intoxicants and gambling as the special causes of enmity and hatred because those effects are most apparent in them, while all the listed practices turn people from God’s remembrance and prayer. Intoxicants overpower reason, stir bigotry, and, when they arouse anger, can lead to extreme crimes; when they arouse desire, they make every kind of indecency seem fair, including violations concerning oneself, property, honour, and religious or social sanctities. They lead to such acts as theft, embezzlement, betrayal of secrets, and disregard for prohibitions, and they have a predominant share in crime and debauchery where drinking is prevalent.

Gambling rapidly destroys the wealth, property, status, honour, life, and prestige for which a person laboured. Winning induces extravagance, debauchery, and indifference to earning lawfully; losing produces bitterness, grief, irritation, and hatred of the winner. Though these consequences may not be conspicuous in an occasional first instance, the rare becomes habitual and the small becomes widespread, until corruption permeates society and unruly passions and destructive desires prevail.

The exclusive “only” covers all the previously enumerated things: each prevents remembrance and prayer, whereas enmity and hatred arise especially by the nature of intoxicants and gambling. Prayer, though itself a form of remembrance, is mentioned separately to show its exceptional rank in the sharīʾah as the complete expression of remembrance; a correct ḥadīth reports the Prophet’s saying, “The prayer is the pillar of religion.” Remembrance is placed before prayer because it is the purpose of the Divine Mission, the life of servitude, and the foundation of happiness in this world and the next. In Qur’anic usage, it opposes forgetfulness of Lordship, which produces forgetfulness of one’s own servitude; humble servitude is the religious conduct through which the soul attains felicity.

“Will you then desist?” is a reproving question, indicating that Muslims had not fully desisted from the earlier prohibitions. The verse also explains that the profit mentioned alongside the great sin of intoxicants and gambling cannot ever be separated from their sin, unlike a lie whose benefit may on occasion be separable from its sin, such as a lie intended to reconcile two people. Since Satan’s only aim in these practices is enmity, hatred, and diversion from remembrance and prayer, no circumstance can make their supposed profit separable from their sin, and they can never be lawful.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse reinforces the command to shun these abominations by ordering obedience first to God, who legislates the law, then to the Messenger, who implements it, and finally by issuing a clear warning. “But if you turn back, then know that only a clear deliverance (of the message) is (incumbent) on Our Messenger” is an especially grave warning: one who opposes the Prophet may suppose that he is merely defying or overcoming the Prophet, but the Messenger’s task is only to deliver God’s revealed message. Such opposition is therefore a dispute with God in His Lordship.

The verse completes a sequence of emphases: the address to believers; innamā; the description of these things as an abomination and Satan’s handiwork; the explicit command to shun them; the hope of success; the disclosure that they cause enmity and hatred and turn people from God’s remembrance and prayer; the rebuke for not desisting; the command to obey God and the Messenger; and the final warning against turning away after the message has been clearly delivered.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse is connected to the preceding prohibition and answers the implicit question about Muslims who had consumed liquor, used gambling proceeds, or used what was sacrificed to idols before the prohibition was revealed, reached them, or was understood by them. “What they have eaten” does not mean lawful food in general; “eating” can include drinking or tasting, and here refers to intoxicants or, more broadly, to all the previously named forbidden practices and their uses.

The interpretation that the verse merely removes blame for eating lawful provisions is untenable. If it implies that all food is forbidden to those outside the qualified group, it conflicts with the Qur’anic affirmation of good provisions and with the religion’s recognition of lawful human enjoyments. If it does not imply this, it makes the lawfulness of food dependent on belief, good deeds, and a threefold, onerous condition of piety, though lawful food is not restricted in this way even among believers, much less among humanity generally. Every interpretation built on the proposition that believers who avoid unlawful things are blameless for eating lawful things faces one of these two difficulties.

The commentary likewise rejects the proposal that words about abstaining from other unlawful things have been omitted, since this assumes an omission without evidence and does not remove the original problem. It rejects the claim that belief and good deeds are mentioned only to stress the obligation of avoiding what is unlawful, since the verse manifestly concerns removal of blame for what was eaten. It also rejects restricting blamelessness to believers on the ground that unbelievers deserve punishment or have barred themselves from knowing lawful and unlawful things: there is no evidence for such a restriction, and it does not resolve the difficulty created by the repeated condition of fearing God.

The verse instead absolves Muslims who had previously used these things, provided that they were believers who did good deeds and proceeded in piety. Its stages explain the necessary character of that piety. The initial phrase, “when they fear God and believe and do good deeds,” repeats the qualities already mentioned and shows that they contribute to removing blame. “Then they fear Allah and believe” means a detailed belief in every law brought by the Messenger, without rejecting any of them, and therefore submission to every command and prohibition. “Then they fear God and do good” adds the importance of al-Iḥsān: performing an act for its goodness, without false or hypocritical intention. In this context, it means acting out of nearness to God and complete submission, rather than doing good to other people.

Piety is not fully realised by general belief in God and affirmation of His religion. It requires detailed belief in every law of the sharīʾah, because rejecting even one law is rejection of the religion; and it further requires good action in accordance with those laws, by fulfilling obligations and abstaining from prohibitions in sincere obedience. The threefold repetition of piety emphatically requires real piety, free of every irreligious motive, throughout all these stages. Piety is not one particular spiritual station, but a spiritual condition that accompanies every station, each of which has its own piety.

Accordingly, there is no blame on believers who did good deeds for their earlier use of intoxicants and the other Satanic abominations if they adhered to piety, believed in God and His Messenger, and obeyed all subsequently known obligations and prohibitions. Their prior conduct causes no harm when it occurred before the prohibiting verse was revealed, before it reached them, or before they understood it. The case resembles the earlier assurance that prayers offered toward the former qiblah would not be rendered fruitless.

The context further indicates that the verse was revealed with the preceding final verses on intoxicants and that some Muslims had retained the habit of drinking between the earlier revelations and these verses. Their circumstances differed: some had acted before prohibition, some before learning it, and some without excuse. Blamelessness belongs only to those believers who drank before prohibition or through ignorance of its unlawfulness; the ruling for the others differs.

Al-Mizan records several alternative explanations of the three repetitions: that they refer successively to avoidance of unlawful things, belief in their prohibition, and continued avoidance; to duties toward oneself, other people, and God; to beginning, middle, and end; to avoiding forbidden, doubtful, and some permissible things; to abstaining from liquor, continuing in faith, obligatory acts, and supererogatory acts; or to rationally known sins, sharīʾah-based sins, and the rights of other people. It concludes that neither the wording nor any other evidence supports applying the verse to any of these schemes; their weakness becomes clear from its context and the preceding explanation.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan explains that the emphatic promise of trial concerns even an insignificant amount of game, making compliance with the coming prohibition easier. Game reachable by hands includes such things as young birds, cubs, and eggs; game reachable by lances includes larger animals normally hunted with weapons.

The verse apparently prepares for the severe prohibitory law that follows. God’s “knowing” is not the removal of ignorance, but apparently means His foreordination of the test in order to distinguish those who fear Him in secret from those who do not. Secret fear is fear of the unseen punishment and sufferings of the Hereafter, of which human senses perceive nothing. Whoever thereafter transgresses the limit God has fixed faces a painful punishment.
verses.95:
Al-Mizan explains that al-ḥurum denotes one in pilgrim garb, in a state of sanctity. The verse prohibits killing game in that condition; the following verse specifies that the prohibition concerns land game. “Intentionally” apparently contrasts with an unintended killing, such as when an arrow aimed elsewhere strikes game. Compensation is due when one intended to kill the game, whether or not one remembered being in pilgrim garb.

The compensation is cattle resembling the game killed, its likeness being determined by two just religious persons. It is an offering brought to the Ka’bah and slaughtered in the sanctuary at Mecca or Minā, as explained by the Prophetic sunnah. Alternatively, there are the expiations of feeding the poor or its equivalent in fasting. “Or” establishes alternatives, whose detailed ordering comes from the sunnah, though the verse’s mention first of feeding and then of equivalent fasting suggests a sequence. These measures are retribution, so that the offender tastes the unwholesome result of the deed.

“What is gone by” means game killed before this law was revealed; it removes any idea that compensation applies retroactively. The verse also shows that pardon may apply to acts not yet sinful when they contain an evil apt to be prohibited by legislation. Apparently, “whoever returns” means one who repeats the sin after committing the deed that incurred compensation, while God’s retribution for the recurrence is something other than that compensation.

Thus, in accordance with most traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, the first post-legislation offence requires compensation by a like animal, whereas one who repeats the sin is subject to God’s retribution and owes no compensation. Without those traditions, the wording might have been understood as making the repeated killing subject to the general retribution of compensation or expiation, but this is far from the verse’s wording.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses regulate intentional hunting while in iḥrām. This verse permits both hunting sea game and eating it: ṭa’āmuhu here means its food, not the act of eating. Although seafood in general could include both hunted animals and what the sea casts up, traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt explain it as the wholesome flesh of game, salted or otherwise.

“A provision for you and for the travellers” describes sea game and its food as a gracious boon, and may mean provision for those in iḥrām and for others. The passage adds that the verses contain further juristic questions treated in works of fiqh.
verses.97:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse is founded on sanctity: the Ka’bah is the Sacred House; the month is sacred; and the offerings and garlanded animals are connected with the House’s sanctity. Qiyām means that by which something stands firm; thus the Ka’bah is a means of support for people in this world and the Hereafter. God made the House sacred, made certain months sacred, and prescribed related rites, including ḥajj in Dhi ‘l-Ḥijjah and sacrificial animals, as supports for a flourishing social life.

The Sacred House is the qiblah for prayer, for the dead and slaughtered animals, and an object of respect even in shameful conditions. It unites the community, strengthens its ties, revives and preserves religion, draws pilgrims from distant places to witness benefits and pursue servitude, and guides people through its name, remembrance, and sight, by which they seek nearness to God. Likewise, the sacred month is a sanctuary: the prohibition of fighting provides security for lives, honour, and property, enabling people to repair their affairs, like a resting station for a weary traveller.

Together, the House, sacred month, and connected sacrificial animals support people’s worldly and otherworldly life. Their benefits include strengthened kinship and friendship, voluntary spending on the needy, flourishing markets, recognition among strangers, closer hearts, purified souls, renewed powers, mutual social support, revival of religion, and the raising of truth and monotheism.

The commentary says that this follows the hunting laws in order to dispel the idea that restrictions on hunting and rules concerning sacrificial animals are useless remnants of superstition. Their sanctity and rules rest on a serious reality: they support human life. “This is that you may know” may refer either to the preceding legislation, whose rationale is then given by the Ka’bah’s being a sanctuary, or to this explanation itself. In either case, obedience leads people to recognize that God knows all that is in heaven and earth and knows what benefits them; these laws are therefore neither useless nor superstitious.
verses.98: Al-Mizan explains that these verses reinforce and establish the preceding laws: they threaten the disobedient and promise good to the obedient. Both clauses retain a threatening tone, which is why God’s severity in punishment is mentioned before His forgiveness and mercy, and why the passage concludes that the Messenger’s duty is only delivery while God knows what people disclose and conceal.

verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that the inequality of the bad and the good in (5:100) is not merely the obvious claim that good is better. Good intrinsically stands above bad; thus denying that they are equal more forcefully denies that bad could surpass good. Were bad to become better, even through an accidental development, it would first have to rise to the good’s rank and then go beyond it. This also explains why the verse places “the bad” before “the good”: it refutes the impression that the bad becomes better through its abundance. Had the order been reversed, the point would instead have been that good could not be more lowly than bad, and the relevant contrast would have been the smallness of good rather than the abundance of bad.

The commentary holds that goodness and badness here are real attributes of things outside imagination, as with good or bad food and land. When these terms are applied to subjective matters such as judgments or conduct, they rest on a kind of consideration. The command, “so fear Allah, O men of understanding, that you may be successful,” is derived from the preceding statement and concerns action and inaction, whose goodness and badness are considered in this latter sense. Since “The bad and the good are not equal” is treated as an accepted principle from which that command follows, this is strongest proof that the verse means the real good and bad of things; otherwise the argument would be unclear, for every community regards its own system as good and what opposes its desires as bad.

Al-Mizan therefore connects the verse to the Qur’anic teaching that religion rests on nature and creation. Religion calls to the good life and prohibits the bad; God makes lawful only good things and forbids only bad things. The verse is consequently a parable showing that religious laws, grounded in the inherent good or bad of things, affect human bliss and misery without changing according to whether good or bad is scarce or abundant. Good remains good when little of it exists, and bad remains bad when it is widespread.

A person of understanding must distinguish bad from good, choose the good in seeking a blissful life, fear God, and follow His path. He must not be deceived by the multitude devoted to ruinous deeds and conditions, nor be diverted from truth by base desire, fear, or favor. He will probably then attain human bliss. Piety is tied to the divine sharīʾah, which is founded on the creative good and bad that secure human success; therefore, no rational person can doubt that one must fear God by acting according to His sharīʾah in order to be successful.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan explains that the prohibition in (5:101–102) is addressed to those who would question the Prophet about matters whose disclosure would trouble them. Its stated rationale also extends beyond questioning the Prophet: people should not seek realities that God has deliberately left veiled and that cannot ordinarily be uncovered. Learning such matters as the time or manner of one’s death, the fate of loved ones, or the loss of rank and dominion may itself bring misery or ruin.

God has ordered life through both disclosure and concealment, each for a reason. To uncover what He has hidden, or to hide what He has made manifest, would disturb this universal order, just as adding to or removing from the organs and powers of a body may destroy a principal function or life itself. The clause “which if declared to you may trouble you” qualifies “things”: if those matters were disclosed, their troubling consequence would certainly follow. Thus, asking about them amounts to seeking trouble.

The commentary notes an objection: a rational person does not deliberately seek what will hurt him, so why prohibit questions about matters certainly harmful if disclosed? It rejects the reply that the use of in (“if”), rather than idhā, makes the harm merely possible. A conditional introduced by in does not make its consequence uncertain once its condition occurs; hence this grammatical argument cannot answer the objection. The verse concerns matters that would definitely trouble the questioners if disclosed.

Al-Mizan also rejects an interpretation, supported by some traditions, that confines the questions to hidden personal matters—such as one’s lifespan, manner of death, final end, or true father. Though such disclosures may cause grief and may lead an arrogant person to deny the Prophet, this reading does not fit the words, “and if you question about them while the Qur’an is being revealed, they shall be declared to you.” If the clause permits such questions during revelation, the scandal inherent in them remains; if it reinforces the prohibition because the Prophet otherwise might withhold an answer for the questioner’s welfare, revelation concerns matters requiring disclosure—religious knowledge and laws—not such personal facts as Zayd’s age, how ʿAmr will die, or a man’s parentage.

The more suitable interpretation is that the questions concern unmentioned particulars and conditions of revealed laws. The clause about revelation and the warning that earlier people asked and then disbelieved show that believers are forbidden to press for minute legal details. Excessive questioning brings stricter rulings and greater hardship, as in the Israelites’ repeated inquiries about the cow they were commanded to slaughter, which progressively narrowed their choices.

“God has pardoned of this” is, apparently, an independent sentence giving the reason for the prohibition, not an adjective qualifying “things.” The use of ‘afā with ‘an indicates that what is pardoned concerns sharīʾah and laws; if the subject were created realities, the expression would almost certainly have been “God has pardoned this.” The Qur’an’s silence over these legal particulars is therefore not forgetfulness or neglect, but a divine concession intended to ease people’s lives. By demanding details, they expose themselves to added restrictions and distress, rejecting the pardon through which God has made life easier. “And God is Forgiving, Forbearing” consequently relates to this pardon, not to the prohibition itself.

Thus, “and if you question about them while the Qur’an is being revealed, they shall be declared to you” completes the prohibition; it does not suspend or cancel it during the period of revelation. The commentary adds that sa’alahu and sa’ala ‘anhu may both mean asking about someone, and thumma denotes a delay in expression rather than time. Bihā is apparently connected with “disbelievers”: those before them became disbelievers in the laws because the laws’ detailed conditions burdened their souls and constricted their hearts against accepting them. Reading bi as causal, meaning “on account of them,” is possible but farfetched. Although the verse does not name those people, it may apply to Qur’anic accounts such as the table among the Christians and episodes involving Moses’ community.
