verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse does not deny that these animals, or their attributes as such, were created by Allah. It denies that Allah ordained the rules which the Arabs attached to the attributes called baḥīrah, sāibah, waṣīlah, and ḥāmi—rules of special freedom, respect, and protection for particular cattle. Thus, the disbelievers’ attribution of such laws to Allah was a fabrication.

The precise meanings of these names and the rules connected with them are variously reported. It is nevertheless agreed that baḥīrah, sāibah, and ḥāmi concerned camels, while waṣīlah concerned goats, and that all received some privileged treatment, such as exemption from riding, slaughter, shearing, or exclusion from water and pasture. Reports describe baḥīrah as, among other things, an ear-slit she-camel after a specified birth, whose use or milk could be restricted; sāibah as a camel released through a vow, dedicated to idols, or freed after successive female births; waṣīlah as a goat whose male offspring was spared or whose offspring and benefits could be reserved for men when a male and female were born together; and ḥāmi as a male camel whose back was declared protected after it had sired a specified number of pregnancies or when its descendant reproduced. The differences probably reflect differing tribal usages and customs, since such superstitions were widespread among ancient barbaric nations.

In any case, the verse refutes the fabricated laws themselves and their false ascription to Allah. The clause, “but those who disbelieve fabricate a lie against Allah,” answers the implied question of what status their claims possess. “And most of them do not understand” distinguishes most fabricators, who act without understanding, from a small group who know the truth but knowingly fabricate against Allah. These are the listened-to leaders who direct the masses, and they are obstinate and stubborn.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan says that the call to what Allah revealed and to the Messenger, whose task is to convey the message, is a call to truth free from fabrication and to knowledge free from ignorance. Their refusal of it in favor of what they found their fathers doing is therefore blind imitation.

al-Taqlīd, or following, is not invariably blameworthy. It is proper, and necessary for the progress of human society in matters in which people cannot acquire the required knowledge, when an ignorant person follows one who knows. But an ignorant person’s following another ignorant person is severely condemned; likewise, a learned person should not abandon his own conclusions merely to follow another learned person’s findings.

The fathers’ lack of knowledge alone would not complete the proof against following them, since an ignorant person may still travel rightly under the direction of a knowledgeable guide. Probably for this reason the verse adds, “and did not follow the right way”: their fathers neither knew nor followed knowledgeable guidance. Reason does not permit one to follow a person who lacks knowledge and is not on the right path, just as one should not take an unsafe path whose condition is unknown either directly or through an expert. There was consequently no excuse for imitating them.

The commentary further reads the verse’s indirect wording as significant. The preceding verse had shown that most of these people lacked understanding, while their misleading leaders were stubborn and arrogant; such people did not deserve direct divine address or argument. Finally, referring to the Book of Allah and His Messenger—that is, to the sunnah—is not among the condemned forms of blind imitation.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains that ‘alaykum anfusakum is literally an injunction to “adhere to your souls.” Guidance and error presuppose a path: one who remains on it reaches the intended destination, while one who deviates misses it. All people, guided and misguided alike, are unavoidably travelling to God, with Whom alone lies the reward they seek. Yet their paths differ: the guided traveller reaches success and nearness, whereas the misguided traveller’s long course ends in ruin and perdition.

The verse therefore directs believers to attend to their own guidance rather than become preoccupied with those who go astray. The misguided are accountable to their Lord, not to believers, and truth remains truth even if few follow it, just as falsehood remains false even if it becomes widespread. “He who errs cannot hurt you when you are on the right way” warns believers not to let prevailing misguidance discourage them from religion or persuade them that worldly conditions make spiritual life impossible. Nor should fear for others’ misguidance make them neglect themselves and thereby become like those they seek to rescue.

This does not excuse believers from calling to God, enjoining good, and forbidding evil. These duties belong to a believer’s own path of guidance. He must arrange the normal means and discharge the duty imposed on him, then leave the result to God; he is neither required to destroy himself with grief over those who refuse guidance nor charged with accounting for their deeds. Thus the verse does not conflict with, qualify, or abrogate the verses commanding the Call and enjoining right and forbidding wrong. A believer invites with clear sight solely to fulfil his duty, without exceeding its limits in an attempt to compel the misguided to change.

The command to adhere to one’s souls further shows that the believer’s own soul is the path by which he travels to his Lord. Man’s beliefs and bodily actions, good or evil, become his provision for the coming stages of existence: from embryonic life through youth, age, barzakh, Resurrection, and finally the Garden or the Fire. God is the destination, while the soul is the compulsory path to Him. Every person travels it, believer or unbeliever, attentive or heedless. The verse does not place a person on this path; it awakens believers to a reality which they already traverse.

To remember God is to remember the destination and therefore the path and the soul; to forget God is to forget one’s own soul, fail to prepare provision for tomorrow, and perish. This is the sense in which both sects have narrated from the Prophet: “Whoever knew his soul knew his Lord.” A person’s apparent concern even for others ultimately returns to the good or evil of his own soul. Success and failure are determined by the soul’s purification or corruption through piety and impiety, good and evil deeds. Since divine rearing encompasses every creature and proceeds without incongruity to God, actions that accord with the reality and purpose of creation nurture the soul toward felicity, whereas contrary actions lead to loss.

One who is mindful of this inescapable journey cannot be like one who forgets it. When a person attends to his true position before God, he finds that his soul is cut off from all else: none encompasses or governs it except its Lord, Who directs it by His power and guidance. He discovers that it is alone with God and has no guardian or master besides Him. This recognition changes perception from polytheism to servitude and monotheism, from imagined self-sufficiency to dependence, from satanic arrogance to divine humility—if divine care takes the soul by the hand. Al-Mizan adds that people are generally too entangled in worldly life to comprehend these realities in their detail, though sound reflection can confirm their broad outlines.

The verse may also address the believers as a community. On this reading, “take care of your souls” commands the Islamic society to reform itself through divine guidance, preserving religious knowledge, virtuous deeds, and Islamic symbols by collective adherence to the Book and Sunnah. Misguided non-Islamic societies then cannot harm it, and Muslims are not bound to exert themselves beyond normal limits in spreading Islam. The clause may also warn Muslims not to lose their own guidance by envying misguided societies’ indulgence in desires and forbidden enjoyments, since all will return to God for judgment. Alternatively, it may deny that disbelievers can forcibly transform the Islamic society into a non-Islamic one.

Al-Mizan reports that some ancient exegetes understood the verse as permitting the abandonment of the Call and of enjoining good and forbidding evil when the believer lacks security from harm. This interpretation treats the clause about the misguided not harming believers as removing responsibility for their misguidance. The commentary considers it far-fetched and contrary to the context: the wording is not that of an exception to the general obligation, and the verses commanding the Call and enjoining and forbidding cannot be abrogated by it.

In the narrations, al-Āmidī reports from ʿAlī: “He who knew his soul knew his Lord.” Al-Mizan notes that both sects also report it from the Prophet and calls it a well-known ḥadīth. It rejects the view that the saying joins two impossibilities, so that neither the soul nor God can be known: another Prophetic report says that greater knowledge of one’s soul brings greater knowledge of one’s Lord, and the saying stands in contrast to the verse stating that those who forget Allah are made to forget their souls. Another saying from ʿAlī declares that the astute person knows his soul and purifies his deeds, connecting self-knowledge with purification.

ʿAlī is also reported in al-Ghurar wa al-durar to have said, “Gnosis through the soul is the more beneficial of the two gnosis.” Al-Mizan takes the two forms to be knowledge through the signs in souls and through the signs in the universe. Both lead to knowledge of God, His names and attributes, the Hereafter, human duties, and adherence to true religion and the divine sharīʾah. Knowledge through the soul is more beneficial because it is ordinarily joined to reform of character and action: a person can inspect his own powers, instruments, moderation or excess, virtues and vices, diagnose his illness from near at hand, correct defects, and preserve what is sound. Knowledge through the universe also summons one to reform, but its summons comes from afar.

The commentary gives this saying a deeper sense. Knowledge drawn from cosmic signs is acquired, reasoned knowledge, dependent on retaining its premises and proofs; when attention leaves those premises, doubts and controversies can arise. The soul’s knowledge of itself, its powers, and its existential stages is witnessing and immediate. When a person observes his soul’s poverty and need before its Lord, he sees that its existence, life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, will, love, attributes, and acts are attached to divine perfection. He then sees that the soul never leaves its own compulsory course and is separated from everything except its Lord, Who encompasses its inward and outward reality. When it turns from all else to God alone, no veil conceals Him from it; this is the highest gnosis ordained for man and deserves to be called knowledge of God through God. By contrast, rational knowledge of God through mental images cannot encompass Him.

Biḥār al-anwār reports from the Leader of the Faithful that God is too great either to be hidden from anything or for anything to be hidden from Him. Mūsá b. Jaʾfar is reported in al-Tawḥīd to have said that the only veil between God and creation is creation itself; God is hidden without a covering and concealed without a veil. Al-Ṣadūq reports from al-Ṣādiq that one who thinks he knows God through a curtain, form, or image is an idolater, for these are other than Him; only one who knows God through God knows Him, while one who does not know Him through Him knows something other than Him. Al-Mizan states that traditions from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt on this subject are numerous.

Although observation of the soul’s signs is the most precious and complete route to real gnosis, ʿAlī called it the more beneficial of two ways, not the sole way, because the general public cannot attain that level. The Book, the Sunnah, and the practice of the Prophet and his Ahl al-Bayt accept the belief of one who knows God through reflection on His creation. Thus both paths are beneficial, though the path through the soul is more comprehensive.

ʿAlī is further reported to have said that the gnostic knows his soul, frees it, and purifies it from what takes it far away; Al-Mizan explains this liberation as release from the captivity of desire and slavery to lust. The commentary also cites numerous sayings attributed to him: the greatest ignorance is neglect of the soul, and the greatest wisdom and best understanding are knowledge of it; one who knows his soul fears his Lord most, fights his soul rather than leaving it unfettered, is freer from worldly entanglement, rises in rank, knows others better, and reaches the end of knowledge. Conversely, ignorance of the soul is ignorance of everything and leads one away from deliverance into error.

In a ḥadīth in Tuḥaf al-’uqūl, al-Ṣādiq rejects knowing God through mental imagination, a mere name, an attribute apart from perception, or an imagined joining of the characterized entity and its attribute; all such notions compromise divine oneness. Asked about the path of monotheism, he says that knowledge of a present person precedes knowledge of his attributes, whereas an absent person is known first by his attributes. He explains that one knows God, knows His knowledge, and knows oneself through Him rather than through oneself; what is found in Him is His and through Him. Al-Mizan relates this to direct gnosis: exclusive attachment to God removes veils, overwhelms the person before divine majesty, and reveals the soul as wholly dependent on and owned by God, with no independence in any affair.

A sermon attributed through al-Masʿūdī to the Leader of the Faithful describes eyes from which veils have been removed, whose spirits rise to contemplate divine majesty. A report quoted by al-Majlisī from Irshād al-qulūb of al-Daylamī describes divine gifts to one who acts according to God’s pleasure: unmixed thankfulness, unforgetting remembrance, and love preferring God to creatures; then divine love, the opening of the heart’s eye, hidden knowledge, forgiveness, awareness of the Garden, Fire, Resurrection, and reckoning, and a direct reckoning without an interpreter. The report ends by commanding Aḥmad to keep his concern single, his tongue single, and his body alive through continual attentiveness. Al-Mizan says that these last reports are not directly about uprightness, but are cited to show that true gnosis is not fully gained by reflective knowledge and includes divine gifts unattainable through rational process. It calls them upright and correct traditions whose soundness is witnessed by the Divine Book.

Al-Qummī narrates in his al-Tafsīr that the Imam said: keep your souls good; do not pursue or reproach people for their shortcomings, for their misguidance will not harm you if you are good. Al-Mizan says this supports the view that the verse forbids excessive involvement in social reform, not negligence of the Call or of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Al-Ṣādiq is reported in Nahj al-bayān to have said that the verse was revealed concerning taqiyyah (dissimulation). The commentary explains that this applies it to a situation of fear in calling to truth or enjoining and forbidding, since the duty is conditional in sharīʾah upon absence of danger; nevertheless, the apparent meaning of the verse itself does not support this restriction. Al-Suyūṭī reports similar views from several early exegetes, but Al-Mizan says Prophetic reports on the subject do not support them.

A report transmitted by al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, and others from Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khashanī has the Prophet instruct believers to continue enjoining good and forbidding evil until they see niggardliness obeyed, desire followed, worldly attraction preferred, and every opinion-holder admiring his own opinion; then they should attend especially to themselves and leave the affairs of the general people. The coming days will be days of patience, in which the patient person resembles one holding live coal, and one doing good will receive the reward of fifty such persons. Al-Mizan notes a similar report from Maʿādh b. Jabal and concludes that the verse did not eliminate enjoining good and forbidding evil.

Al-Suyūṭī also reports from Abū ʿĀmir al-Ashʿarī that the Prophet explained the verse as meaning that one who errs from among the disbelievers cannot harm believers when they are rightly guided. Al-Mizan observes that this report restricts the verse to abandoning the call of disbelievers, not to abandoning enjoining and forbidding in matters of sharīʾah; in any event, verses establishing the obligation of the Call and related jihād show that the verse does not oppose those duties. Al-Suyūṭī further reports from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Prophet said the verse’s interpretation would not come until Jesus son of Mary descends; Al-Mizan applies the preceding comments to this report as well. Finally, al-Suyūṭī reports from Ḥudhayfah that the verse applies “when you have enjoined the good and forbidden the evil.” Al-Mizan calls this a moderate interpretation returning to its own explanation and notes that Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab reported similarly.

In its academic discourse, Al-Mizan argues first that human beings have always referred to “I” and “my soul,” thereby indicating a real created reality which they understand in general, even if they err about its nature. Immersion in bodily life has led some to identify the soul with the body, breath, blood, or the enduring elements gathered in semen. Such theories do not invalidate the immediate awareness of the self; people may correctly grasp a reality generally while disputing its detailed quiddity.

Every person is aware at every stage of existence of an inward reality to which he refers as “I” or “my soul.” With deeper understanding he finds that it differs from physical things, which are divisible, changing, spatial, and temporal, and differs from the material body governed by matter’s laws. A person may forget a limb or become unaware of his body but never literally forgets his soul. Expressions such as “I forgot myself” are metaphorical, since it is the soul to which one attributes the forgetting. Nor does unconsciousness prove that one ceases to perceive the self: after regaining consciousness one remembers only that one does not remember having perceived it, not that one remembers failing to perceive it; some also remember dreams and other experiences from unconsciousness. If a person turns from bodily functions and material desires to what he observes of his soul, he will recognize its difference from matter. Daily preoccupation and physical desire, however, lead many to neglect this reality and settle for primitive explanations.

Intense fear, joy, grief, love, or emergency can turn a person away from everything else and concentrate him upon his soul. In such states people may experience things not reached by ordinary sense or empty thought: terror in isolation may produce visions or voices attributed to ghoul, jinn, or an unseen caller; overpowering love or grief may yield, in sleep or between sleep and wakefulness, perceptions of past or future events or other hidden matters; and strengthened will joined to certainty and firm belief may accomplish feats beyond usual causes. Al-Mizan does not investigate the immediate causes of these occurrences, but holds that they depend on the soul’s withdrawal from external affairs, especially bodily enjoyments, and its turning toward itself. Hence the foundation of all psychological regimes is opposition to the soul’s desires: enslavement to desire divides its attention, binds it to external objects, and makes it forget itself.

Such effects occur briefly for some and more enduringly for others, such as ascetics who abstain from worldly objects and train the soul. This inward occupation is not new, but has existed since ancient humanity. Investigation of peoples, customs, and religions shows that pursuit of knowledge of the soul and its extraordinary effects has long been prized. Remnants of witchcraft and oracular claims among primitive peoples, and the beliefs and disciplines of Hinduism, Buddhism, Sabiism, Manichaeism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, all testify to this concern, although they differ in their explanations, teachings, and methods.

Al-Mizan presents al-Bīrūnī’s account of Brahmin life as an example: after childhood, a Brahmin undergoes a disciplined stage of study, service to a teacher, fasting, sacrifice, and abstention; then may marry and live socially; later returns to severe asceticism outside civilization; and finally lives in solitude, detachment, and contemplation until death. Hindu Yogis, spiritualists, and philosophers likewise use demanding regimens involving seclusion and deprivation. Buddhism is said to rest upon cleansing the soul and opposing its desires; Buddha is reported to have relinquished princely life for solitude and self-training until true cognition was cast into his heart, after which he called others to the same discipline. Sabians seek purification from desire and anger in order to gain affinity with spiritual powers and seek their intercession through worship, supplication, fasting, sacrifice, incense, and spells. Manichaeans regard the soul as belonging to a luminous world and the body as a dark prison, so that perfection lies in release through spiritual discipline or death. The scriptures of Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians call to redemption of the soul and opposition to its desires, while monastic and ascetic communities testify to this tendency. Other practitioners of magic, talismans, spirits, jinn, letters, and stars also employ particular disciplines that yield a degree of control over affairs of souls. Thus, despite their divergences, the religions seek purification of the soul through rejection of its desires and cleansing from evil traits.

An objection remains: religious asceticism and strenuous exercises are often pursued for reward, power, or a promised state, not consciously for knowledge of an immaterial soul; some practitioners even hold the soul to be bodily matter, blood, vapour mingled with blood, material elements, or a subtle body. Al-Mizan answers that, whether consciously or not, all such disciplines detach the soul from external and material causes, turn it to itself, and seek results unavailable through ordinary physical means. The religious ascetic seeks real happiness—either the good life of the Hereafter or, for those who deny it, a worldly life gathering good and repelling evil—and recognizes that animal enjoyment cannot secure it. He therefore abandons desire, submits to causes above material causes, and preserves this inward attachment through bodily acts and omissions such as prayer and ḥajj.

Religious practices and extraordinary exercises consequently concern the soul through its inward affairs. Human beings always act for what they perceive as their own benefit, and are never wholly unaware of themselves, though they may misinterpret that awareness intellectually. Exercises do not have a merely physical causal connection to their promised results; rather, their connection is immaterial and proceeds through the exerciser’s perception and will. Correct exercise strengthens and perfects the soul’s perception and will until it knows the desired result to be within its power, whether unconditionally or under specified conditions. The reported saying of the Prophet that a disciple of Jesus with stronger certainty could have walked on air rather than water indicates that effects depend on conviction concerning God, once created causes are stripped of independent efficacy: the greater one’s reliance on absolute divine power, the more worldly things submit to one’s will. Al-Ṣādiq’s saying, “The body does not feel weak from doing what the intention is strong about,” and the Prophetic saying, “The actions are only according to intentions,” express the same principle. It is self-deception to suppose that outward acts by themselves produce either otherworldly rewards or unusual worldly effects without a real inner connection.

Al-Mizan warns, however, against equating religion with cognition or Sufism, as materialist writers who divide human ways into materialism and religion-as-cognition have done. Religion teaches that human happiness requires submission to what is above the material world and refusal to concentrate on material enjoyments. It uses reform and purification of the soul to train people for the happiness it promises, but knowledge of the soul is not religion itself. Religion calls people to worship God, directly or through intercessors and partners according to its particular form, because it locates happiness in that worship; purification is included because a soul entangled in material and animal desires cannot receive the promised good and blessing. Thus religion and self-knowledge are distinct, though religion cannot be wholly separated from it. Likewise, systems of exercises for unusual ends are distinct from self-knowledge, although connected with it.

The commentary holds that knowledge of the soul, by whatever route reached, is derived from religion. Independent inquiry shows that religions in all their differences spring from a deep-rooted natural religion: monotheism. When inherited and environmental prejudices are set aside, the unity-in-plurality and interconnection of the universe establish one Cause above all causes, the Truth to Whom one must submit and according to Whose governance life must be ordered. Even idolatry and dualism retain something of this living spirit, though they err in applying it. Some worship God alone because He is near and no guardian or intercessor exists beside Him; others, believing human lowliness bars direct access to God, seek nearness through exalted servants, spiritual powers, or images and idols representing them. Their disagreement lies in striking or missing the monotheistic foundation.

Accordingly, monotheism is the father of all religions, whose later forms are its good or evil offspring. Natural religion treats knowledge of the soul as a means to the true human blessing—knowledge of God—not as an end. Religion seeks servitude, so it cannot approve self-knowledge as an independently pursued goal. Nor does human nature itself call directly to self-knowledge in the way it calls to natural religion. Civil, tribal, monarchical, and democratic systems may organize human society, but no report shows that non-religious founders called people to self-knowledge and moral reform. Practitioners of witchcraft or spiritualism may arrive at it through accidentally observing unusual effects and then seeking powers capable of extraordinary manipulation, but not through nature’s direct summons.

Al-Mizan next notes reports that some righteous religious people receive extraordinary occurrences through their disciplines: they may perceive what others do not, have prayers answered, heal otherwise hopeless illness, or rescue people from danger by unusual means. Similar phenomena may even occur through an immoral person whose intention is true and whose soul is detached from worldly involvement. Such persons may ascribe what occurs directly to God without recognizing an intermediate cause. The direct attribution to God is true, but denial of intermediate causes is not desirable.

The commentary describes reported spiritualist phenomena in which a child is made to see a spirit in a mirror or water while others cannot; alleged spirits sometimes lie, supposedly disclose the secrets of a living and unaware person, or a hypnotized person later performs actions commanded during trance without recollecting the instruction. Some infer from visible apparitions that spirits are material or have a material source, even attempting to devise instruments to capture them. Others infer from dreams and visions of one’s own form outside the body that the spirit is a subtle body inhabiting the physical body until death. Al-Mizan rejects both explanations. These forms are perceptual forms, like forms of one’s body and external things; they may multiply, change shape, or appear as another person’s soul, and therefore cannot simply be identified with the soul’s form.

Such practitioners have acquired some knowledge of the soul’s effects but have missed its true nature and consequently misdirected their explanations. Proof and experience, according to Al-Mizan, establish that the true reality denoted by “I” is essentially separate from material things. Its perceived feelings, thoughts, and understandings belong to their own world and receptacle, unlike bodily organs and their material motions, which have no life or perception in themselves. Extraordinary perceptions available to righteous people and those undertaking exercises remain within the soul’s grasp; the question concerns how and where that knowledge settles in it. The soul possesses a sublime sign corresponding to events and affairs connected with it, and unusual effects obey will and intention, while intention issues from perception. Human perception thus intervenes in events related to the person.

People concerned with knowledge of the soul may be divided first into those who seek unusual effects beyond material causation—such as practitioners of magic, talismans, invocations, or subjugation of stellar spirits, jinn, and human spirits—and those who turn from external things to examine the soul’s essence and states, such as Sufis. Sufism was not invented by Muslims; it appears among Christians, Hindus, Buddhists, and earlier peoples. Yet it is not merely a custom inherited through imitation. Since natural religion leads to asceticism and asceticism to knowledge of the soul, an enduring religious life prepares a people for the inevitable emergence of such a path, whether sound or unsound, even without contact with other religious communities.

The second group divides again. One pursues knowledge of the soul for the soul’s own sake, gains only partial information about it, and fails to know it comprehensively because it neglects its Maker, God, the true Cause Who governs the soul’s being and effects. To claim complete knowledge of the soul while ignoring its ultimate Cause resembles claiming knowledge of a bed while knowing nothing of its carpenter, tools, purpose, or other causes. This kind of self-knowledge is properly called sooth-saying, since it yields only limited information about the soul and its effects.

The other group seeks knowledge of the soul because it leads to knowledge of the Lord. This is the path with which religion is to some extent pleased: the soul is the nearest sign of the Lord, the path travelled, while God is the destination. Muslims have many such paths; the basic chains are counted as twenty-five, branching into smaller chains, and all but one ultimately reach ʿAlī. Some unattached people call themselves al-Uwaysiyyah after Uways al-Qarnī, while others bear no name or slogan. Their books describe their chains, paths, rules, ethics, narrated disclosures, proofs, and aims; Al-Mizan declines here to judge their correctness or error.

Finally, Al-Mizan concludes that knowledge of the soul has a practical aim and cannot be fully attained through theoretical study alone. The ancient written science of the soul is declared wholly useless, while the practical psychology devised by later scholars is merely a branch of ethics according to the older classification. And God is the Guide.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that the rule addresses believers and concerns a will made when the signs of death—normally serious illness—make a will necessary. Two just Muslims are to witness it at the time it is made. Here justice means probity and rectitude in religious affairs, and “from among you” means Muslims, not the testator’s relatives or clan.

“Or two others from among others than you” is a sequential alternative: non-Muslim witnesses are used only when Muslims cannot be found. The restriction, “if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death befalls you,” applies to this alternative, because travel may leave a Muslim unable to find Muslim witnesses. The non-Muslims intended are, apparently, the People of the Book, since the divine speech does not accord such standing to polytheists.

If the heirs doubt the account of the will, its property, or its conditions, the two witnesses are detained after the prayer and swear by God. Their oath means that they will not sell their testimony for any worldly gain—wealth, status, or kinship—even for a relative’s sake, and will not conceal or alter the truth. The pronoun in “We will not take for it a price” refers to testimony, not to the oath; otherwise the wording would imply a second oath without indication. “The testimony of Allah” is either God’s testimony to reality, of which human testimony is secondary, or a testimony that God has made obligatory upon His servants and which they must offer truthfully without concealment.

If it is discovered that the first witnesses committed sin through false testimony and perfidy, two others take their place and swear that their testimony concerning the will is truer and that they have not exceeded the limit against the first two. “Those who have a claim against them” denotes those against whom the original witnesses committed their wrong; in the relevant reading, they are the deceased’s two nearest relatives. Thus, when the first two are exposed as perjurers against the relatives, two of those relatives replace them and swear against their false testimony.

Al-Mizan notes an alternative recital, al-awwalīn, which apparently means the nearest relatives having the first claim to the estate. It considers its contextual explanation clearer than the numerous grammatical possibilities proposed by exegetes, which only multiply obscurity. The replacement oath is specifically the oath of the two nearest relatives: they attest that their evidence exposing the first witnesses’ falsity is truer, and that they have not wronged them by testifying otherwise.
