verses.108:
Al-Mizan explains that the prescribed sequence of oaths is the safest means of reaching the truth about an unknown will and of restraining the first two witnesses from injustice. Desire impels a person to take what he wants, whether rightfully or by violating another’s right; he is restrained either by external punishment or by an inner deterrent. The strongest inner deterrent is faith in God, to Whom people return, Who reckons their deeds, judges justly, and recompenses fully.

Where the deceased’s appointed witnesses are the only means of knowing the will, requiring them to swear by God, and then transferring the oath to the nearest relatives if the witnesses are found to have perjured themselves, most effectively keeps their testimony close to truth. They fear disgrace, exposure, and the refutation of their oaths. The verse therefore closes with the warning to fear Allah, heed the command, and remember that Allah does not guide transgressing people.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan connects this verse with the preceding warning against deviating from truthful testimony and treating an oath by God lightly. On the Day God assembles the messengers, who are witnesses over their nations, He will ask what answer their peoples gave them. Their reply, “We have no knowledge, surely Thou art the great Knower of the unseen things,” teaches witnesses to fear divine majesty, to testify only to the truth God has made known to them, and not to conceal God’s testimony. The reference to assembling the messengers particularly suits the preceding discussion of gathering witnesses for testimony.

The messengers do not deny all knowledge. Their answer denies independent, inward, and comprehensive knowledge—the knowledge that embraces an affair in all its causes, concomitants, and interconnections, and ultimately in relation to its Maker. Such complete knowledge is impossible for a limited creature, while human beings receive only a small, measured portion of knowledge needed for life. True knowledge belongs to God alone, and on the Day of Resurrection, when realities appear as they truly are, only true speech has place. The messengers therefore disclaim knowledge before God in humility, confessing their essential neediness and affirming that He alone possesses knowledge by Himself.

This is not their final answer, nor does it prevent their later testimony. God has made the messengers witnesses over their peoples, and they must testify as He has ordained. Their initial answer establishes that whatever knowledge creatures have is bestowed by God, after which they may disclose what they know of their peoples’ condition. Their witnessing is not ordinary human witnessing, but a kind of knowledge and testimony belonging especially to God and granted to chosen servants. Moreover, the Qur’an confirms that some of God’s close servants will possess knowledge on the Day of Resurrection, including those who bear witness to the truth, and it records the Messenger’s complaint that his people abandoned the Qur’ān. Finally, since both messengers and their peoples will be questioned, and even the guilty will answer with knowledge after their veils are removed, the messengers cannot be devoid of such knowledge.

Al-Mizan then explains that social life naturally produces disputes over possessions and rights, making judgment necessary. Judgment requires the facts to be preserved as they occurred. This may be done through a person who observes an event and undertakes to report it truthfully, or through recording. Witnessing is more generally available than writing and other forms of recording, and oral testimony based on the witness’s undertaking and memory is presented as less exposed to defects than such methods. All nations therefore give testimony some credence, though they only recognize testimony from those counted as members of their society; this explains why the testimony of an undiscerning child or an insane person is disregarded, and why some earlier societies excluded women when they did not count them as members.

Islam, as the natural religion, recognizes testimony as the definite proof; other corroborating means have no value unless they produce knowledge. It ordinarily fixes two witnesses so that each supports the other, except in fornication, where four are required. Islam counts women among the members of society and grants them the right to testify, but, because it founds society on understanding rather than emotion and regards women as more emotional, it gives two women’s testimony the weight of one man’s, so that one may remind the other if she forgets. Detailed rules of testimony belong to jurisprudence.

Al-Mizan defines al-’Adālah, in the present Qur’anic setting, as moderation between excess and deficiency. Society chiefly rests not on rare persons of exceptional virtue or on corrupt persons who violate social rights, but on the middle rank whose reliable conduct sustains its structure. This is the quality Islam seeks in a witness. Justice here concerns a person’s position within the religious society, not national or political standing: a just witness is one whose religiosity is relied upon and who does not commit major sins. Likewise, being “among those whom you are pleased with to be witnesses” means being acceptable to the religious community because of one’s trustworthiness in religious matters.

The fiqh faculty of ‘adālah differs from ethical ‘adālah. The former is the psychological condition which, in common estimation, restrains a person from major sins; the latter is a deeply rooted moral trait in reality. A report in Man lā yaḥḍuruh al-faqīh from Ibn Abī Ya’fūr relates that Abū ʿAbdillāh identified accepted justice with publicly known restraint, avoidance of major sins, concealment of one’s faults, and regular observance of the five prayers with the Muslims’ congregations except for a genuine excuse. Al-Mizan takes this report to show that the inward faculty is known through avoidance of prohibited desires and a good appearance among Muslims. A report from Abu al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā allows the testimony of one born on fiṭrah and known for goodness; a report from Abū ʿAbdillāh accepts that of an old or weak person who is righteous and chaste; and a report in al-Kāfī from Abū Jaʿfar directs one to pray only behind a person whose religion one trusts. These reports support the stated standard.

An oath joins a statement, command, prohibition, or intended act to something the speaker holds in honor, so that falsifying the statement or breaking the resolve would entail dishonoring that thing. It thereby intensifies assurance and creates a deterrent. Oaths are a universal social practice, used to repel accusation, remove suspicion, assure oneself, and strengthen information; civil laws later formalized them. Islam especially venerates oaths in God’s name, prescribes expiation for deliberately broken oaths, discourages frequent swearing, and recognizes an oath in litigation where no proof exists: proof belongs to the claimant and the oath to the denier.

In a religious society, the oath can serve as proof because the swearer ties his denial to his faith in God. If his oath proves false, his faith is no longer trustworthy: he has, as it were, pawned his faith, and loses his reliability and social standing among believers. Al-Mizan says this worked when religion governed desires, but maintains that in its contemporary condition religion has lost its social authority, material civilization predominates, and both religious safeguards and modern laws have lost people’s confidence. In such a condition, oaths and even stronger means cannot protect rights effectively.

Yet divine rules and the sharī’ah are not abrogated because people abandon them. Islam’s laws form an interdependent whole animated by monotheism; injury to one part harms the whole, as illness in a limb harms the body. The proper response is to preserve what is sound and treat what is diseased, not to neglect both. Islam’s obligations also have broad degrees suited to human capacity, extending from secure social conditions to individual emergencies; descent to a lesser level is conditional upon an emergency that removes responsibility or grants respite. Those who reject religious requirements merely because they conflict with prevailing materialistic customs follow materialistic rather than religious reasoning.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that every oath by other than God is polytheism. Such an oath involves honoring what is sworn by, but honoring something becomes polytheistic only if one attributes to it independent lordship and self-sufficiency. God Himself swears by many created things and has declared the greatness and dignity of the Qur’ān, the Throne, the Prophet’s character, the messengers, and believers. It is therefore permissible in general to honor what God has honored and to adjure Him by what He has sworn by or by rights He has established for His friends. This does not mean that a juridical oath carrying legal consequences is valid by a name other than God; fiqh restricts that oath to God’s name.

Likewise, swearing by the right of the Prophet and God’s friends, seeking nearness to them, or hoping for their intercession is not worship or an attribution of forbidden unseen authority unless it assigns them independent authority, which no Muslim who believes in the Qur’an gives to another besides God. If “unseen authority” instead means non-material agency by God’s permission, there is no proof that chosen servants cannot possess it. The Qur’an attributes unseen actions to angels, speaks of Satan’s unseen influence, and affirms prophetic and other intercession and miraculous signs. If effects may be attributed to creatures by God’s permission in the material realm, no principled distinction excludes non-material effects.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse enumerates Jesus’s clear signs as favors bestowed jointly upon him and his mother: his strengthening by the Holy Spirit, speech in the cradle and maturity, knowledge of the Book, Wisdom, Torah, and Injīl, creating a bird from clay, healing the blind and lepers, raising the dead, and God’s protection from the Children of Israel. Although these signs seem peculiar to Jesus, they were equally miraculous signs for Mary, just as his fatherless birth was; thus mother and son were together granted the favors and made one sign for mankind.

The strengthening by the Holy Spirit apparently enabled Jesus to speak to people: the wording joins cause and effect without a conjunction. It therefore does not mean merely receiving revelation through the Spirit, since all messengers shared that and the context does not support such an interpretation. The single temporal word “when,” governing the listed acts, may indicate that he was taught the Book, Wisdom, Torah, and Injīl at once by one divine command, without gradual acquisition.

Because “when” is not repeated between making the bird and healing the blind and lepers, these acts appear to have occurred at the same time. The explicit proviso “by My leave” is especially repeated in connection with making the bird because creation entails giving life; the Qur’an does not leave room for anyone to suppose that another independently bestows life. And God knows better. Raising the dead means restoring life to bodies buried in graves and bringing them back into worldly life; the wording indicates that this miracle occurred repeatedly. Finally, God’s holding back the Children of Israel shows that they intended to harm Jesus, but God prevented them, even though their unbelievers called his clear signs manifest sorcery.
verses.111: Al-Mizan holds that the disciples’ professed belief was not their first faith in Jesus, for they had been his earliest adherents and the parallel account shows this occurred later in his mission. The call sought their covenant to aid God’s religion, not an initial belief in God. Their witness that they were Muslims signifies readiness to submit to the divine command by establishing God’s call and enduring affliction for His sake—a stage subsequent to basic faith. The verse therefore recounts the taking of the covenant from the disciples.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan takes “When” as connected to an implied command such as “Remember.” It rejects the view that the verse is syntactically joined to the disciples’ preceding profession of belief so as to expose that profession as false: God had inspired them to believe, counted this as a favor to Jesus, and the wording “When the disciples said” does not fit such a connection.

The disciples’ apparent question about whether God is able to send down food is difficult to ascribe to companions of Christ, since even elementary faith recognizes God’s unrestricted power. Al-Kasā’ī’s reading, “Are you able (to ask) your Lord?”, reflects this difficulty. The best interpretation, however, is that “ability” alludes not to literal power but to whether the underlying reason requires and permits the act, as one may say that a ruler or wealthy person “cannot” do something that remains within his power.

The commentary rejects several other explanations. The claim that they merely sought tranquillity like Abraham lacks proof: unlike Abraham, whose sinlessness is established, they explicitly made eating an independent purpose—“eat of it and that our hearts should be at rest”—rather than seeking it solely for tranquillity. Moreover, Abraham’s request concerned seeing how the dead are raised, not requesting a further sign after direct observation. The suggestion that the disciples asked only about the act, rather than God’s power, is unsupported and still leaves their speech unbecoming to servitude. Nor can the question be supplied with an omitted meaning, “Are you able to ask your Lord?” The two readings use different grammatical persons, which omission cannot alter; and attributing to God the human concomitants of Jesus’s lack of power, need, eating, or drinking would be improper.

It is still less acceptable to make al-istiṭā‘ah mean al-iṭā‘ah, so that the question would mean whether God would obey Jesus or willingly grant the request; this is more offensive than asking about divine capability. The linguistic argument based on their common root ṭ-w-‘ and an analogy with ajāba and istajāba is invalid: language cannot be established by such analogy, conjugated forms need not preserve a root’s original sense, and prevailing Qur’anic usage gives istiṭā‘ah the meaning of ability and aṭā‘ah that of obedience. Ajāba and istajāba may share a meaning, but this does not justify equating aṭā‘a with istaṭā‘a; moreover, istif‘āl denotes seeking the sense of fa‘ala, not af‘ala. The context also refutes the benign interpretation, for neither Jesus’s rebuke nor the unprecedented threatened chastisement would suit a wholly proper request.

Thus Jesus’s “Fear Allah if you are believers” responds to the disciples’ demand for an unneeded sign after they had already seen clear signs. Their request risked treating divine signs lightly, while its crude wording also suggested an absence of firm certainty about God’s power.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan holds that the disciples offered these reasons to escape Jesus’s censure for requesting an unnecessary sign, not to deny that God has unrestricted power. Their explanation therefore confirms that the rebuke concerned demanding a sign after they had already witnessed many signs.

They give four purposes. First, they wished to eat from the food, showing that they were not merely playing with God’s signs; yet this reasonable purpose also acknowledges the force of the censure and threat. Claims that “eating” means either extreme hunger or seeking blessing cannot be inferred from the word, and would have required explicit mention if intended. Second, they sought tranquillity of heart through removal of notions inconsistent with sincerity and presence. Third, they sought settled certainty that Jesus had truly conveyed God’s message, after freedom from devilish doubt and insinuation. Some interpret this instead as certainty about Jesus’s promises concerning such matters as answered prayers, but this is less likely: the food was to descend through Jesus’s invocation, and they were already familiar with his signs and with the acceptance of his prayers. If this interpretation concerns the acceptance of Jesus’s prayer, it can fit; if it concerns their own prayers, it conflicts with the context.

Fourth, they wanted to be witnesses to the event, both against disbelievers and before God on the Day of Resurrection; the witnessing is broad, though it may specifically mean witness before God. In sum, they added attractive justifications to their central aim of eating heavenly food, seeking to soften the impropriety of asking for a further sign. Jesus ultimately consented after their persistence.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan explains that Jesus joins himself to the disciples in the request and replaces their expression “Is your Lord able …” with the fitting address, “O Allah, our Lord!” This opening is unique among the Qur’anic prayers of prophets, which otherwise begin “My Lord” or “Our Lord,” and reflects the delicacy of the situation and fear of appraisal.

Jesus recasts their request as one that can properly be presented to God. Rather than leave it as a demand for a sign despite the many signs already witnessed, he asks that the food be an ever-recurring happiness, an ‘īd, for himself and his followers. An ‘īd is so called because it returns repeatedly; “to the first of us and to the last of us” refers to the first members of his community and those who join them later, through descendants without limit. This festival, and this kind of sign, is exclusive to Jesus’s ummah.

He then makes its being “a sign from Thee” an additional benefit, not its sole intended object; if it had been sought merely as a sign, the good it could provide was already available through Jesus’s daily miracles. Likewise, “grant us sustenance” is treated as a resulting benefit rather than the central purpose. The disciples had put eating first as an end in itself, whereas Jesus places sustenance last, attributes provision to God as “the best of providers,” and makes the ‘īd the first request for himself and the whole ummah. The sign and sustenance thereby appear as benefits reserved to some rather than all.

Through omission, rearrangement, preservation, and refinement of their words, Jesus transforms a request unsuitable for the Divine Majesty into a prayer expressing the proper etiquette of servitude.
verses.115:
Al-Mizan notes two readings: munazziluhā, read by the people of Medina and Syria and by ʿĀṣim, and munziluha, read by others. It prefers munziluha, because inzāl denotes sending down all at once, as the food was sent down, whereas tanzīl generally denotes gradual descent.

“Surely I will send it down to you” is an unequivocal promise that the food did descend. Its original wording uses the nomen agentis—“I am its sender down”—rather than a verb, strengthening this indication. Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid are reported in al-Durr al-manthūr and Majmaʿ al-bayān to have said that it did not descend because the disciples withdrew their request after hearing the condition. The commentary rejects this: God would not make such an explicit promise while knowing it would be nullified by a withdrawal. The promise to send it down is unconditional, while the threatened punishment is a separate condition for whoever disbelieves after its descent; it is not a condition whose refusal would prevent the descent.

The promise, accompanied by the warning, therefore accepts rather than rejects Jesus’s prayer. Yet the acceptance is restricted: although the requested festival was specially granted to them, it was not an unrestricted mercy for every member of the community. It benefits those who remain believers and harms those who disbelieve. In this respect, the passage resembles a general prayer followed by a restricted acceptance.

The distinctive punishment corresponds to their request for a sign uniquely reserved to them: disbelief after receiving that exclusive privilege incurs a punishment likewise exclusive to them. Al-ʿālamīn consequently means all nations, not merely those living in Jesus’s time. The warning does not necessarily mean a punishment greater in pain or severity than every other punishment; it means one distinctively inflicted on them and on no other nation.
verses.116:
Al-Mizan explains that “when” refers to the Day of Resurrection, as indicated by the surrounding divine speech and Jesus’s later statement that he witnessed his people while among them and that God watched over them after his death. The wording, “me and my mother,” rather than “Jesus and Mary,” alludes to the proof thought most important for Jesus’s divinity: his birth from Mary without a father. Sonship and motherhood are therefore the basic elements of this claim. Dūn here ultimately means “besides,” as al-Rāghib also explains.

The expression “gods besides God” in the Qur’an generally means partners associated with God in divinity, not gods affirmed while God’s own divinity is denied. Such a denial would be senseless: whoever takes Christ, idols, or their lords as gods still affirms a god for the universe, but attributes to Him Christ’s human qualities or the qualities of plurality and multiplicity; this is partnership. Likewise, one who calls time or nature the origin of the world still affirms a maker, but ascribes defect and transience to Him. Even one who rejects a beginning and causality must posit a world with essential existence; its permanence cannot be secured by itself, since its parts change and cease, but requires another possessing perfection—God. Thus God cannot truly be negated; apparent wording that negates Him has no intelligible meaning.

The underlying reason is that man establishes God because the world needs one who supplies its requirements and governs its order. Whatever fulfils that need is God. If someone then affirms further gods, he has either erred regarding God’s attributes and names or assigned Him partners; to deny Him while affirming another is meaningless. Therefore, “two gods besides God” denotes two beings taken as partners apart from Him. Even if it were understood merely as two gods distinct in essence from God, that wording itself would neither affirm nor deny God’s divinity; the further conclusion would be external to the verse. Christians, in any case, do not deny God’s divinity while taking Christ and his mother as two gods besides Him.

The commentary answers the objection that Christians do not profess Mary’s divinity by distinguishing taking someone as a god from believing that person to be a god, although the latter may follow from the former. Taking someone as a god consists in humble submission, as in: Have you then considered him who takes his base desire for his god? (45:23). This manner of taking Mary as a god is reported from earlier Christians and seen among their descendants. Al-Ālūsī, in Rūḥu al-ma‘ānī, reports from Abū Jaʿfar al-Imāmī that an earlier Christian sect, the Maryiyyah, believed Mary to be a goddess. Rashīd Riḍā, in Tafsīr al-Manār, states that worship of Mary was accepted in Eastern and Western Churches after Constantine, while the much later Protestant denomination rejected it.

Al-Mizan describes this worship as including a form of ṣalāt containing praise, requests for help, and intercession; fasts in Mary’s name; humility and devotion toward her memory, images, and icons; and belief in an unseen authority to bring benefit and harm in this world and the next, either independently or through her son. It states that their doctrines explicitly make worship of her obligatory. Although most sects do not call her a “goddess,” but call her the “Mother of God,” some insist that this title is literal rather than metaphorical. The verse concerns taking Jesus and Mary as gods, not merely naming them so; worship constitutes such taking. This differs from their saying, Surely God, He is the Messiah son of Mary; … (5:72). The Prophet likewise explained They have taken their doctors of law and their monks for Lords besides God, … (9:31) as obedience to them in what they permitted and prohibited, not as calling them Lords.

The commentary says that it found an explicit Greek Orthodox declaration of Mary’s worship in al-Sawā‘ī, and that Catholics openly profess and take pride in it. It cites al-Mashriq, published by al-Jazwīt in Beirut, as confirming the worship of Mary in both Eastern and Western Churches. It also quotes Father Luis Shaykhū’s statements that the Armenian Church’s worship of the Virgin, Mother of God, is well known and that the Coptic Church is distinguished by worship of the Blessed Virgin. Shaykhū further quotes Father Inistas al-Karamli’s article on the antiquity of this worship. Al-Karamli interprets the woman in Genesis and Elijah’s servant’s sighting of a small cloud rising from the sea as images of Mary, traces worship of the Virgin in the East to Elijah in the tenth century B.C., and says the ancestors of the Karmalites first believed in Jesus after the apostles and disciples and first established a place of worship for the Virgin after her assumption with body and soul. The commentary reproduces this at length so that the reader may see the kind of reasoning by which her worship is affirmed and their recklessness in religion.

Jesus begins his answer by glorifying God when confronted with the attribution that he and his mother were taken as God’s partners. This is the etiquette of servitude: a servant should glorify his Lord upon hearing what is unfit to be ascribed to Him, as the Qur’an teaches in response to claims that the Beneficent God has taken a son or that daughters are ascribed to Allah. Jesus then does more than deny that he told people to take them as gods: “it did not befit me that I should say what I had no right to (say)” negates the cause and basic possibility of such speech. A bare statement, “I did not say it,” would only deny its occurrence while leaving it possible; denying any right to say it refutes its foundation, and therefore more decisively refutes its occurrence.

The nearer grammatical interpretation of mā yakūn is that “that I should say” is its subject and “what I had no right to” its predicate, with the lām denoting possession: Jesus does not possess what he has not been given possession of and cannot speak without a right. If the verb is taken as complete, the sense is that it does not occur to him to speak without a right. Either way, the deed is denied through denial of its cause.

His words, “if I had said it, Thou wouldst indeed have known it,” form a second rejection through its necessary consequence: nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from God, who watches every soul’s earning and encompasses all things. Jesus thereby substantiates his denial and shows that his words and deeds were directed to God’s knowledge, whether or not anyone else knew them. The divine question is not asked because of ignorance; questions may be asked either to inform the questioner or to inform others, and here it serves the latter purpose.

“Thou knowest what is in my mind, and I do not know what is in Thy mind” establishes that divine knowledge is unmixed with ignorance. Though phrased as praise, it is not praise in this setting, but a disavowal of the improper attribution. God’s knowledge of deeds is not like rulers’ partial knowledge of their subjects, gathered through reports while much remains unknown; He knows subtleties and all things, including Jesus’s soul. Yet Jesus cannot adequately describe this knowledge: God knows by encompassing what He knows, while nothing encompasses Him and none can comprehend anything of His knowledge. God is unlimited, whereas everything besides Him is limited and determined, unable to pass beyond the boundary of its own soul.

By calling God “the great Knower of the unseen things,” Jesus explains that this knowledge is not confined to what lies between himself and his Lord. Complete knowledge of every unseen thing belongs to God: whatever is hidden from one thing but known by another is nevertheless known and encompassed by Him. Since all else is created and limited, nothing besides God knows any unseen thing, wholly or partly. If something encompasses an aspect of the unseen by God’s will, it is itself encompassed by God and remains under His ownership; this is the meaning of: … and they cannot comprehend any thing out of His knowledge except what He pleases; … (2:255). Were God not to encompass what He knows, He would be limited and therefore created; far exalted is He from that.
verses.117:
Al-Mizan explains that Jesus completes his refutation of the claim that he and his mother commanded worship by defining the limits of his divinely assigned responsibility. His statement, “I did not say to them aught save what Thou didst enjoin me with,” combines negation and affirmation: he taught only, “That worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.” By calling Allah both his own Lord and theirs, he explicitly establishes himself as a servant and messenger calling to the worship of the one Lord without partners.

Jesus then states his second charge: besides conveying the message clearly, he was to witness his people’s deeds while he remained among them. Having neither exceeded these two duties nor instructed them to take himself and his mother as two gods besides Allah, he is free of responsibility for their deviation.

Al-Raqūb and al-riqābah mean protection and preservation; here, “watcher” denotes preservation of deeds. The substitution of “watcher” for “witness” also avoids repeating the latter word immediately before “and Thou art witness of all things.” More importantly, “Thou wert the watcher over them” restricts the ultimate witnessing to God. God witnessed them while Jesus witnessed them and continued after Jesus was taken away; Jesus’s witnessing was therefore a mediated, not independent, witnessing. This resembles other functions entrusted to servants—such as sustenance, giving life and death, preservation, call, and guidance—while God remains their real manager.

By adding “and Thou art witness of all things,” Jesus shows that his witnessing over his people was only a small part of God’s universal witnessing of every thing and deed: God is witness with other witnesses and without them. The restriction remains true even though God has other witnesses among His servants and messengers after Jesus. Jesus knew this, for he foretold a messenger after him named Aḥmad (61:6), and the Qur’an identifies the Prophet as a witness: … and bring you as a witness over these? (4:41).

Since God reports Jesus’s restriction without rejecting it, the reality of witnessing belongs to God alone despite the existence of subordinate witnesses. As with every perfection, goodness, and beauty bestowed on others, their witnessing derives from God’s granting them possession; this neither divests Him of it nor negates His ownership. Thus Jesus is innocent of what was attributed to him and bears no responsibility for his people’s deeds, which leads into his final words concerning whether God chastises or forgives them.
verses.118:
Al-Mizan explains that, having established that his duty was only to convey the message and bear witness, and that he neither exceeded this duty nor caused their unbelief, Jesus disclaims all responsibility for God’s judgement of them. This begins a new, independent point: their polytheism is theirs to face, and Jesus has not intervened in the decision concerning them.

If God punishes them, they are still His servants—that is, He is their true Master, to whom the management of servants belongs and who may be displeased with them. If He forgives their grave injustice, He is the Mighty, the Wise: power and wisdom belong to Him, His acts are appropriate and just, and none can oppose or question His decision. “Thou art the Mighty, the Wise” is not restrictive; the detached pronoun and the definite predicate emphatically affirm His power and wisdom.

The commentary adds that this direct dialogue takes place before a divine Majesty that requires complete servile humility. Jesus therefore neither intercedes nor questions God’s action, and does not say, “Thou art the Forgiving, the Merciful”; before such overpowering authority, the servant can only acknowledge God’s sovereignty and his own helplessness. Abraham’s saying, “then whoever follows me, he is surely of me, and whoever disobeys me, Thou surely art Forgiving, Merciful,” differs because it is an invocation, in which a servant may seek to stir divine mercy.
verses.119:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as an indirect confirmation of Jesus son of Mary’s truthfulness: although he is not named, the context identifies him. The truth that benefits the truthful on this Day is their truth in this world, for the gardens and abiding reward that follow are recompense for earthly conduct. There is no taklīf (religious responsibility) in the next world, and reward is consequent upon taklīf; the hereafter is the abode of reckoning, reward, and punishment, whereas this world is the abode of action and responsibility.

Because Jesus’ testimony concerning his earthly life comprised both speech and action, God’s confirmation embraces truthfulness in both. Thus, the truthful whose words and deeds are true in this world receive the Gardens, God’s pleasure, their pleasure in Him, and the mighty achievement. Truthful speech itself requires truthful action: deeds must be free of hypocrisy, and truthfulness leads to goodness. A report relates that, when a Bedouin asked the Prophet for advice, he was told not to lie; he later said this prevented him from sins, since committing one would oblige him to confess it if questioned.

God is pleased with the truthful because of the truth they sent ahead, and they are pleased with Him because of His reward. The verse speaks of God’s pleasure with their selves, not merely with their deeds. Pleasure with an act only means not rejecting it in dislike: one may approve an enemy’s act while disliking him, or dislike an act of a beloved friend. God’s pleasure with them therefore means that He loves their selves; this can occur only when the end for which they were created has appeared in them: “And I have not created the jinn and the men except that they should worship Me” (51:56).

Accordingly, God is pleased with the servant’s soul when it has become the soul of an exemplary worshipper: a servant submissive to God’s Lordship, who does not regard himself or anything else independently, turns only to God, and returns only to Him. This is also their being pleased with God. It is a station of servitude whose concomitant is purity of the soul from every rank of disbelief and from transgression; God does not like ungratefulness in His servants or the transgressing people.

A sign of this station is that, seeing all things as owned by God and subject to His command, the servant is pleased with God. He recognizes that whatever God gives is grace, generosity, and bounty, and that whatever He withholds is withheld for a reason. In the Garden they shall have what they please, and one who receives all that he wishes is naturally pleased. This is the highest human bliss and felicity in servitude, which is why the verse concludes: “this is the mighty achievement.”
verses.120:
Al-Mizan explains that al-milk, ownership, is a special authority over particular things, through which the owner’s will operates in what he administers; al-mulk, kingdom, is the corresponding authority over an ordered whole. Kingdom operates according to power; therefore, complete and unrestricted power entails an all-embracing kingdom, unrestricted by any thing or circumstance. This is why the verse joins God’s kingdom over the heavens, the earth, and all within them to His power over all things. It concludes the chapter by grounding its commands to fulfill covenants in God’s absolute rule: servants are wholly owned by their Lord, and their proper response to His commands, prohibitions, and covenants is hearing and obeying without breach.

A narration from Tha‘labah b. Maymūn, through some companions, reports Abū Jaʿfar’s explanation that God’s future question to Jesus—whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods—is phrased as an accomplished event because what God knows will occur is spoken of as already done. Al-ʿAyyāshī also reports a similar narration from Sulaymān b. Khālid from Abū ʿAbdillāh; the commentary says that the past tense is used because the future event is certain, a common linguistic usage.

Jābir al-Ju‘fī reports from Abū Jaʿfar that the Great Name consists of seventy-three letters, one of which God has concealed; Adam received seventy-two, inherited by the prophets until Jesus. On this report, Jesus’ statement that God knows what is in his mind refers to the seventy-two letters taught to him, while Jesus does not know what is in God’s mind because of the concealed letter. Al-Mizan says that the Great Name is not literally composed of letters: in this usage, “name” means God Himself considered through an attribute or aspect, while the spoken name is the name of that name. Reports assigning a number of letters to the Great Name, or locating them in particular sūrahs or verses, are symbolic parables that convey what can be understood of realities that cannot be stated directly.

God’s beautiful names are the means through which the kinds and occurrences of the universe are manifested. Creation proceeds through names appropriate to it: God creates as Creator, Magnanimous, and Originator; sustains as Sustainer and Bestower; and gives life as Living and Life-giving, not through names such as Avenger, Holder, or Forbidding. Qur’anic verses themselves commonly end with the name, or names, that illuminate the reality discussed. Were someone granted knowledge of these names, their relations to things, and what they require singly and together, he would know the universal order and its laws as they apply to particulars.

The Qur’an states general laws of origination, return, felicity, and wretchedness, and says, “... and We have revealed the Book to you explaining clearly everything, ...” (16:89). Yet these laws are necessary only through the necessity God bestows upon them, not by their own independent demand. Intellect and the realities whose laws and effects exist by God’s will therefore cannot compel or govern Him. Any demand or decision found in things belongs to an authority God has conferred upon them; He remains the absolute Owner and cannot be owned.

Thus, in itself, neither reason nor anything extraneous could prevent God from rewarding a sinner, punishing a good-doer, or doing whatever He wills. But He has promised and threatened, informed people of felicity and wretchedness, reward and recompense, and declared that He does not break His promise or speak except truth. Hence hearts are at rest concerning what He has taught, as in “surely Allah fails not in (His) promise. (3:9; 13:31)” and “and the truth do I speak. (38:84).” Such disclosures express what His names demand, but beyond all disclosed names remains His absolute ownership: He has the right and power to do and decide as He wishes, and “He is not questioned concerning what He does and they shall be questioned. (21:23).” This points to a divine name whose essence creatures cannot know. Known names are grasped through concepts and effects; effects which cannot be identified point inviolably to a name beyond conceptual capture, indicated only by absolute ownership. This is the hidden name to which no creature has access.

Al-Mizan defines al-adab, manners, as the good form in which a lawful voluntary act should be performed, whether in religion or among rational people in society. It belongs neither to forbidden acts such as injustice, treachery, and falsehood nor to ugly and ignominious deeds; it presupposes an act that may be done in more than one way, of which some forms are fitting and others are not. Communities disagree over particular manners and over what they identify as good or evil, but rational people agree in principle that manners are the good form of action and are good.

Manners differ from ethics. Ethics are ingrained traits of the soul, whereas manners are the various fitting forms taken by actions arising from such traits. A society’s manners reflect the ethical dispositions formed by its aims, social conditions, and other influences. Since a person’s intended end in life determines the forms of his acts and the limits he observes, manners grow from ethics, and ethics are shaped by the particular aim of a society.

Divine or prophetic manners are the fitting forms of religious action corresponding to religion’s aim: servitude, in degrees that differ with the completeness of true religions. Islam encompasses all human affairs and provides every deed with a form suited to its purpose. Its comprehensive aim is belief in one God both in faith and action: God is the source and return of all things and possesses the beautiful names and sublime parables. When this monotheism permeates inward and outward life, a person’s speech, deeds, and whole existence manifest pure servitude. Divine manners are therefore monotheism in action.

Practical knowledge does not fully produce its effect when presented merely as abstract principles; it must be joined with practice. The soul is occupied with sensible particulars and finds universal intellectual principles difficult to retain when sensory feeling opposes them, as fear may oppose one’s intellectual affirmation of courage. Training through action makes principles credible, removes opposing inclinations, and roots conviction, because actual occurrence is the strongest proof of possibility. What the soul has never experienced appears impossible or extraordinarily difficult; repetition makes it familiar. Good and evil alike become habits.

For this reason religious training begins with deeds before verbal explanation, so that the believer reaches religious understanding and law equipped with piety and good action. Teachers must act upon what they know: action guides just as speech does, while conduct contrary to one’s preaching shows that the speaker himself does not regard his words as true, though it does not prove that the words are false in themselves. A coward cannot practically form a courageous person, nor can a balanced scholar emerge from a school of prejudice and obstinacy. A teacher must possess the traits he seeks to cultivate and truly believe his teaching. Even a hypocrite whose speech outwardly conveys good carries in it the nature of his own soul, which an unsophisticated learner receives without separating the verbal meaning from its other aspects. Effective formation thus requires a teacher who believes what he teaches and whose deeds accord with it; no good should be expected from one who lacks belief or practice.

The Qur’an presents prophets’ worship, invocations, dealings, and speech as practical instruction in divine manners. Their guidance was guidance to monotheism, as shown by the warning that associating others with God would forfeit their deeds. Monotheism flows into their actions: their actions are forms that represent it as an image in a mirror, just as deeds reveal a soul’s pride or humility. The command to the Prophet to follow the earlier prophets’ guidance means following their monotheistic actions, not merely their persons or beliefs. The revelation to them of “the doing of good,” prayer, and zakāt is understood as guidance and training in their actual performance, not revelation of prophecy and legislation: God bestows a holy spirit that strengthens good deeds and caution against evil.

The prophets’ prostration and weeping when God’s signs are recited show outward submission and inward humility, the dominance of servitude when alone with God and when among people. By contrast, the generation that neglects prayer and follows desire displays corruption in its relation to God and to people. The prophets’ lives rest on knowing that they have a Lord who owns and governs them, from whom they come and to whom they return. Their repentance too is a divine manner, beginning with Adam.

God trained the prophets not to be distressed by what life assigns them or to affect what lies beyond their nature and capacity. Affectation exceeds nature and is a form of following desire, from which prophets are protected. They were taught to use wholesome provisions without crossing into what sound nature rejects, to do good, and to unite as one community under one Lord in piety rather than division. Individual and collective manners together establish a society protected from discord, worshipping one Lord, and settled in felicity. Their manner with God is monotheistic worship; their manner with people is to mingle with them rather than isolate themselves or claim distinction.

Adam and his wife, after eating from the tree, said, “Our Lord! We have been unjust to ourselves, and if Thou forgive us not, and have (not) mercy on us, we shall certainly be of the losers.” (7:23). Al-Mizan holds that the prohibition was advisory, not a legislative command whose violation entailed juridical sin; their act harmed the well-being and felicity of their life in the Garden. Faced with loss, they neither despaired nor occupied themselves with their own condition, but fled to the Lord who owned their affairs and held the good they sought. They confessed their injustice and described the loss threatening them without directly asking for forgiveness and mercy. Their need itself was the most eloquent plea. Feeling abasement and having no claim upon God, they surrendered to His judgment; calling Him their Lord indicated their hope as wards under their Guardian.

Noah’s words concerning his son—“My Lord! Surely my son is of my family, and Thy promise is surely true, and Thou art the justest of the judges”—were not a clear prayer for his son’s rescue. God had promised safety to Noah’s family except those against whom the word had gone forth. His wife’s unbelief was known, but his son had not openly manifested unbelief; his behavior showed disobedience to his father, so Noah could apparently suppose him included in the promise. Yet Noah had also been told not to speak to God concerning the unjust, and the scope of that description left him uncertain about his son. As one of the Ulu al-‘Azm messengers, he could not have forgotten revelation or sought safety for a son whom he knew to be an unbeliever. He therefore raised the matter as an inquiry grounded in God’s true promise and just judgment, expressing parental feeling without making a request.

God then explained that “family” in the promise meant the good-doers among his family and that his son was not one. Noah’s subsequent words, “My Lord! I seek refuge in Thee from asking Thee that of which I have no knowledge,” seek refuge from the request he was on the verge of making, not from one already made. His reply is outwardly repentance but is in reality thanksgiving for God’s teaching him this manner. Had he already asked, the response would have plainly rejected the request. Noah’s later prayer for forgiveness includes himself first as the leader of those on God’s path, then his believing parents, believers entering his house, and all believing men and women. After enduring his people’s rejection and praying for the destruction of unbelievers who had already misled many and would beget only immoral, ungrateful offspring—a matter known by prophetic foresight and revelation—he did not forget the believers. His parents’ inclusion proves that they were believers; those who entered his house were his contemporary believers; and all believers belong to his people because he first raised the call of religion with a book and sharīʿah and upheld monotheism.

Abraham’s praise of the Lord of the worlds, who created, guides, feeds, gives drink, restores health, causes death, gives life, and from whom he hopes forgiveness on the Day of Judgment, is comprehensive praise of God’s care from creation to return. It places Abraham in total poverty and God in absolute self-sufficiency and bounty. He attributes sickness to himself and healing to God because, in a context of praise, the purpose is to show the Lord’s mercy in restoring health, although sickness too is an event attributable to God. He asks for enduring realities rather than worldly adornment: wisdom, understood as sharīʿah; companionship with the good; a goodly mention among posterity, meaning a continuing call and sharīʿah carried by later prophets or messengers; inheritance of Paradise; forgiveness for his father; and protection from disgrace on the Day of Resurrection. God’s speech shows the acceptance of his requests other than the prayer for his father, concerning which it is silent; the commentary maintains that a prayer of God’s honored servant is not mentioned in vain.

Abraham sought a good offspring by attaching his worldly request to the quality of doing good, thereby directing it toward God’s pleasure. When he asked that Mecca become a secure town and its believing people receive fruits, he sought a divinely sacred center through which religion would be preserved: an enduring sign of God, a place of worship, ritual orientation, settlement, refuge, and pilgrimage. Its security is legislative, secured through its sanctity and people’s reverence rather than a created immunity from war, murder, or disturbance. Since the barren valley needed provisions in order to remain inhabited, he asked for fruits. He restricted the prayer to believers in God and the Last Day when he saw that its honor could include unbelievers. He did not attempt to instruct God how believers and unbelievers could coexist or how fruits would arrive in uncultivated land; a supplicant does not teach the All-Knowing, Wise, and All-Powerful Lord how to fulfill a request. God completed the prayer by declaring temporary enjoyment for the disbeliever followed by the Fire, since ordinary causality supplies believers and unbelievers alike.

In his later prayer, when Mecca was already a city, Abraham distinguishes private from shared requests by saying “My Lord” for the former and “Our Lord” for the latter. Whenever he asks for something that might be used lawfully or unlawfully, he states its rightful end: preservation from idols because they have led many astray; settlement near the Sacred House so that prayer may be maintained; and provision and people’s yearning so that they may be grateful. He ends needs with suitable names—Forgiving, Merciful, Hearer of prayer—and repeatedly invokes Lordship because it links servant and Lord and opens prayer. Even regarding those who disobey him, he does not curse, but invokes God as Forgiving and Merciful, seeking their rescue and the spread of divine bounty. Abraham and Ishmael’s prayer while raising the House’s foundations likewise embodies these manners: acceptance of their work, submission for themselves and their offspring, instruction in rites, repentance, and a messenger who will recite God’s signs, teach the Book and Wisdom, and purify the people.

Ishmael’s answer to Abraham’s vision of sacrifice—“O my father! Do what you are commanded; if Allah please, you will find me of the patient ones”—shows humility before his father and before God. He does not put forward a personal opinion, addresses Abraham as father, affirms that the dream is a divine command, and seeks to comfort him. By saying “if Allah please,” he refuses to assert independent efficacy or a definite decision apart from God’s will.

Jacob’s statement, “I only complain of my grief and sorrow to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know,” means that his grief for Joseph is directed to God rather than to those who possess neither benefit nor harm, and that he has not despaired of God’s mercy. Prophets do not follow desire; their love, anger, joy, sorrow, and dealings with worldly causes all remain in God’s way. This does not deny causes or their causal role, which would oppose human nature. Rather, they see no independence in anything besides God and put each cause where God has placed it. They adhere to God before, with, and after every cause, and seek nothing except Him.

Joseph’s preference for prison over the women’s invitation was not a prayer to be imprisoned, but an expression of his abhorrence of indecency if the two alternatives were assumed. He did not explicitly prescribe his own need, since judgment belongs to God; he alluded instead to the danger that their device might make him inclined to them and thus ignorant, and surrendered the affair to God. God removed their device, understood to include both temptation and imprisonment; his subsequent imprisonment resulted from their later decision, not from a prayer of Joseph’s. When reunited with his family, Joseph says, “Enter safe into Egypt, if Allah please,” immediately joining even his declaration of safety to God’s will so that no independence be imagined. He attributes the realization of his vision, release from prison, reunion with his family, kingdom, and knowledge of the interpretation of sayings to divine beneficence. He gently attributes his brothers’ wrongdoing to Satan’s sowing dissension rather than reproaching them. From praise of these gifts he rises to praise God as Originator of the heavens and earth and therefore Guardian in this world and the hereafter, then asks to die a Muslim and be joined with the good. This is a request for death in the submission granted to his fathers and for reunion with righteous servants.

Moses’ prayer after striking the Coptic—“My Lord! Surely I have done harm to myself, so do forgive me”—concerns harm done to himself and the removal of its evil consequences, not forgiveness for violating a legislative prohibition. The killing preceded his sharīʿah, the slain man was an unbeliever whose life was not inviolable, and no proof establishes that such killing was forbidden before Moses’ law. As a purified servant, Moses could not be seduced by Iblīs into sin. Like Adam’s request, his forgiveness seeks God’s covering and removal of harmful consequences, including the danger that people would discover what they considered his crime. By contrast, when he fled to Madyan and said that he stood in need of whatever good God might send down, he did not specify worldly needs such as food or lodging: he displayed poverty and remained silent, which is more fitting for worldly matters.

When charged with the mission, Moses asked for expanded breast, ease, loosened speech, and Aaron’s assistance, explaining their purpose: “so that we should glorify Thee much, and remember Thee oft; surely, Thou art seeing us.” He disclosed the purpose so that the request would not appear self-serving, and he placed himself and Aaron before God’s knowledge as needy servants. His prayer against Pharaoh and his chiefs was jointly with Aaron. It seeks destruction of their riches and hardening of their hearts until the painful punishment, so that faith then would not benefit them; this is a curse of enduring wretchedness because they had led God’s servants astray. Prayer for evil differs from prayer for good: divine mercy precedes wrath, so harm should not be sought unless an essential interest of religion or its people is known with certainty. Its ugly causes should be stated obliquely, as Moses mentioned their leading people astray rather than detailing their oppressions, and earnest entreaty should be increased by repeated invocation of “Our Lord.” God’s command to Moses and Aaron to remain upright after accepting their prayer reflects that they possessed knowledge warranting this curse.

When the seventy were struck by the earthquake, Moses first softened the setting of divine wrath before requesting forgiveness and mercy. He acknowledged that his soul and theirs were all subject to God’s will, suggested that their destruction would undermine his mission before his people, described the offenders as fools rather than a basis for destroying the community, and treated the event as part of God’s general trial, by which He guides and lets stray. Calling God their Guardian, he sought forgiveness, mercy, and good in this world and the hereafter. His words did not explicitly ask that the dead be restored, but the extremity of the situation only allowed him to indicate that need. God answered by returning them to life. In saying, “Thou makest err with it whom Thou pleasest,” Moses did not verbally ascribe misguidance to human choice because the context required emphasis on God as the ultimate Guardian and ruler, though he believed the fuller truth expressed elsewhere that only transgressors are led astray.

After the calf-worship, Moses prayed for himself and Aaron to be forgiven and admitted into mercy so that they would be distinguished from the unjust people upon whom wrath would descend. When his people refused to enter the holy land, his words that he had control only over himself and Aaron mean that only they obeyed him; he thereby alluded to withdrawing from further proclamation after their gross refusal and returned judgment to God by asking separation from the transgressing people. “Control” here is control of obedience, not independent creative possession.

Shu‘ayb’s prayer, “Our Lord! Decide between us and our people with truth; and Thou art the best of deciders,” asks for the fulfillment of God’s promise after he lost hope that his people would respond. He joins the believers with himself because they too were threatened with expulsion, leaves the unbelievers in their wrongdoing, and invokes the name “the best of deciders” as an adjuration appropriate to his request. Unlike Moses’ words about separation, it is an actual prayer.

David and Solomon thanked God for the knowledge by which He made them excel many believing servants. Their praise attributes the gift to God and merely acknowledges a particular blessing; it is not arrogance. Solomon, when the ant’s words recalled his great kingdom and power, remembered them as God’s favor upon him and his parents rather than becoming forgetful of servitude. He therefore sought the ability to thank, to do good that God is pleased with, and to enter through God’s mercy among His righteous servants. Good conduct is especially required of one possessing such authority, and his addition “as Thou art pleased with” shows that his concern is God’s pleasure rather than goodness considered apart from it.

Jonah’s departure after God removed the punishment from his repentant people represented the state of a servant displeased with his Lord’s decree and fleeing his service. God disciplined him by confinement in the whale, where he could not move and was surrounded by darkness. His invocation, “There is no god but Thou, glory be to Thee; surely I am of those who make themselves to suffer loss,” taught him that God can seize and confine him wherever He wills and that none can flee God except to Him. Unlike the other prophetic prayers, it does not begin with “Lord,” for its emphasis is that God alone is worthy of worship and no one escapes His servitude. Jonah glorifies God from injustice and admits injustice to himself. Ashamed and remorseful, he does not explicitly request restoration to his former station of servitude, considering himself unworthy to ask; God’s response and his return to his people show that this was his unspoken need.

Job, afflicted with illness and loss of property and children, said only that harm had afflicted him and that God is the most Merciful of the merciful. Like Adam, Noah, Moses, and Jonah in requests connected with worldly affairs, he did not state his need, viewing himself as unworthy of attention and his concern as too slight to mention. Naming the affliction and the mercy that calls forth response makes the need clear more eloquently than an explicit demand; to spell it out would suggest that those two matters did not themselves suffice to evoke the mercy of the most Merciful.

Zachariah’s prayer for an heir was prompted by what he saw of Mary’s worship and the direct provision granted to her. He longed for a pious child to inherit him and worship God in a manner pleasing to Him, while old age, weakness, and his wife’s barrenness made this seem remote. He described his weakened bones, white hair, lifelong prayer, fear concerning his relatives after him, and God’s habitual response to his supplication in order to awaken mercy, not to place God under an obligation. His astonishment when God granted the request shows that sorrow and yearning had impelled his prayer before he reflected on its extraordinary character. His request that the heir be “one in whom Thou art well-pleased,” read with “good offspring,” indicates an offspring good and pleasing to Zachariah, rather than a claim that his previous service entitled him to an answer.

Jesus’ request for a table from heaven reformed the disciples’ difficult request. Their words, “Is your Lord able to send down to us food from heaven?” were improper because they questioned, or at least badly expressed a question about, God’s power, and because they sought a new sign while Jesus’ signs already surrounded them. Jesus first warned them, but when they persisted, he transformed their proposed miracle into an ‘īd for himself and his followers, condensed their stated benefits—reassurance, confirmation of his truthfulness, and witnessing—into “a sign from Thee,” placed their wish to eat after its religious purpose, and restated it as the fitting request for provision. He ended by praising God as the best of providers and began, because of the gravity of the matter, with “O Allah, our Lord!” rather than only “My Lord” or “Our Lord.”

Jesus’ answer to God’s future question about his and his mother’s alleged divinity displays the highest manners of servitude. He begins by declaring God’s transcendence. Rather than bluntly saying, “I did not say it,” he considers himself too low even for the allegation to require such a direct denial: “it did not befit me that I should say what I had no right to (say).” He denies its cause, for he possessed no such right; then denies its concomitant, for if he had said it God’s encompassing knowledge would know it. He gives its opposite: he said only what God enjoined, “That worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.” He was their witness only while among them; when God took him away, God alone watched over them with everlasting and universal witnessing. Finally, if they strayed, Jesus is separate from their affair: if God chastises them, they are His servants, whose Master may punish their disobedience and association; if He forgives them, none can reproach Him, for He is the Mighty, the Wise, who does not act vainly or unwisely. Every stage combines denial of the accusation with praise of God.

The Qur’an also presents Muḥammad and the believers as models of divine manners. They believe in God, angels, books, and messengers without differentiating among messengers; they say, “We hear and obey,” seek forgiveness, and acknowledge their final return to God. This contrasts with the People of the Book who differentiated among angels, books, messengers, and commands, and who said, “We hear and we disobey,” presumed forgiveness, claimed self-sufficiency, or minimized the Fire. The believers recognize themselves as servants owned by their Lord and do not treat their faith and obedience as claims against Him.

“Allah does not impose upon any soul a duty but to the extent of its ability” follows from the fact that divinely imposed responsibility accords with the nature God created and with the felicity for which it is equipped. Yet a master may, under secondary circumstances, impose greater precaution where a matter is important, or impose added difficulty because servants have departed from natural servitude through disputation and persistent questioning, as occurred among the Children of Israel. The statement may be the believers’ praise before asking not to be punished for forgetfulness or error, or a divine insertion between their prayers that both teaches and supports their plea. Their request concerns such secondary rulings, arising from the situation of the obligation or the obstinacy of those obliged rather than from arbitrary divine burdening. Their repeated pleas for pardon, protection, mercy, and help express humble acknowledgment of God’s ownership and guardianship; repetition of forgiveness is fitting in prayer and in the passage’s contrast between them and the People of the Book.

God trained His Messenger through the praises and prayers recorded in the Qur’an, and he exhorted his community to observe the same manners. The prophets also preserved these manners while addressing people; this is practical tablīgh, more effective than verbal proclamation alone. Noah told his people that only God would bring the punishment if He pleased, that they could not render Him incapable, and that even Noah’s advice would not profit them if God intended them to go astray. He thereby negated power from himself, affirmed it for God, and grounded it in God’s lordship and their return to Him.

The prophets’ words and deeds, in all states, arise from awareness of servitude. Moses, though angry with his people, did not forget their Lord’s promise; Joseph, in the private temptation of the wife of ‘Azīz and in forgiving his brothers, retained piety and referred matters to God; Solomon, when the throne of the queen of Sheba stood before him, called it grace from his Lord and a test of gratitude rather than a ground for pride. This differs from Nimrod and Pharaoh, who attributed their authority to themselves and displayed arrogance despite the signs confronting them. Muḥammad likewise remembered God in danger in the cave and referred knowledge of a concealed matter to “The Knowing, the One Aware.”

In their dealings and debates, prophets did not answer abuse, mockery, and accusations with obscenity, insult, or debasement; they replied with sound speech, sincere counsel, and gentleness, as Moses and Aaron were ordered to speak gently even to Pharaoh. They considered themselves equal in standing with ordinary people and spoke to each group at the level of its understanding. A report transmitted by both sects attributes to the Prophet the saying that prophets were commanded to speak to people according to their understanding.

Nevertheless, their mission rested on guidance through truth, not accommodation with falsehood. Falsehood cannot be used even to aid truth, because a truth reached through falsehood is not complete truth. Prophets fear only God, do not fear the consequences of declaring what is true, and are promised divine help. Thus their clear denunciation of ignorance, forgery, extravagance, idolatry, and perdition can depart from the flattering social manners of societies built on desire and indulgence of falsehood. Divine manners mean following pure truth in belief and action, choosing its best and gentlest permissible form—such as soft speech over harshness and prompt good over delay—but never mixing truth with falsehood. What lies beyond truth is error.

Their servitude also produced equal respect for weak and powerful, rich and poor, ruler and subject, man and woman, master and slave. Where distinction exists, it belongs to knowledge and piety, not wealth or power. The strong and wealthy must exchange arrogance for humility toward truth, forgiveness, mercy, and striving in good. Prophets showed at least equal, and often greater, mercy and generosity to the weak. Noah refused to drive away believers despised by his people, since they would meet their Lord and God knew best what was in their souls. Shu‘ayb sought only reform and relied on God. Muḥammad is described as grievously concerned by people’s distress, compassionate and merciful to believers, of sublime morality, and a mercy to the worlds. Though such descriptions are principally traits, manners themselves are branches of such traits.
